title: Portraits of American women
abstract: retirement in the Quincy home.She was always adequate to every situation and said the word and did the deed that dignity and high patriotism required of her.But it is impossible to read her many letters and not feel that through it all she was charmingly and delicately a woman.She herself understood and appreciated the softer•elements of the feminine character.In England she complains somewhat of the lack of these qualities : " The softness, peculiarly characteristic of our sex, and which is so pleasing to the gentlemen, is wholly laid aside here for the masculine attire and manners of the Amazonians."^Sheherself is feminine in the deeper things of life, in the tenderness of her affection and in the bitterness of her mourning, when those she loves are lost to her, as in her profound grief over her mother's death.She is just as feminine in those lighter trifles of fashion and dress which are supposedby mento form the chief part of woman's conversation and correspondence.She was a thorough woman in her domestic interests, in that busy, often trivial, care which sustains the un- conscious felicity of home.She looked after her husband's comfort as well as his greatness.In the midst of shrewd advice as to his moral bearing among those ABIGAIL ADAMS "5 who were makingtheAmericannation, she murmurs a housewife's anxiety about his personal appearance : " I feel concerned lest your clothes should go to rags, having nobody to take any care of you in your long absence ; and then, you have not with you a proper change for the seasons."^She feels, sometimes a little impatiently, the hurry of nothing which m.akes up domestic life.Her health ?She believes she has little health." Much of an invalid," ^she calls herself casually, and elsewhere admits that her "health is infirm," and that she is not "built for duration."^But,bless me, she has no time to think about health, or talk about it, or write about it.The machine must go as long as it will.How apt and vivid is her sketch of the interruptions that puncture the whole course of her home existence!She rises at six o'clock and makes her own fire, "in imitation of his Britannic Majesty."She calls her servantsrepeatedly, and notes that in future she will hire only those who will stir at one call.Breakfast gets on the table.She would like to eat it.A man comes with coal.A man comes with pigs.Another man comes for something else, and another.Meanwhile, where is breakfast?And what flavor has it?"Attended to all these concerns.A little out of sorts that I could not finish my breakfast.Note; never to be incommoded one is untimely snatched away.She herself superin- tends their early studies, and most thoughtfully and carefully.She does indeed regret her own lack of book learning, because she has none to impart to her daugh- ters; but perhaps, even in this regard, she was less deficient than might be thought.She keeps little Johnny at her knee reading aloud Rollin's "Ancient History,"and hopes that he will come to " entertain a fondness for it."^She vastly prefers Dr. Watts's " Moral Songs for Children " to modern frivolities of " Jack and Jill " and " Little Jack Horner."^Would she have liked " Rollo," I wonder, or would she not?Whatever the value of her literary teaching, her moral lessons were as homely, as sturdy, and as lofty as those of a matron of Plutarch.On this point she was fully supported by the resonant precepts of her husband : "Root out every little thing.Weed out every meanness.Make them great and manly.Teach them to scorn injustice, ingratitude, cowardice, and falsehood."^**But she needed no precepts from any one.Out of her own heart she taught these things, and her apostrophe to her son, when he left her for the great world, is simply the flower of lessons and influences established many years before : " Dear as you are to me, I would much rather you should have found your grave in the ocean you have 8 PORTRAITS OF AMERICAN WOMEN crossed, or that any untimely death should crop you in your infant years, than see you an immoral, profligate, or graceless child."^Îf one wants evidence of this maternal loftiness and maternal tenderness combined, one has only to open the Diary of John Quincy Adams and to see how reverent, how affectionate, and how obviously sincere are the numerous references to his mother's care and devotion." My mother was an angel upon earth.She was a min- ister of blessing to all human beings within her sphere of action. . . .She has been to me more than a mother.She has been a spirit from above watching over me for good, and contributing by my mere consciousness of her existence to the comfort of my life."^^" There is not a virtue that can abide in the female heart but it was the ornament of Marry a quean and be merry: How objective are our notions of causation?
venue: Evolutionary Anthropology Issues News and Reviews
abstract: A now little-known Oxford don, Robert Burton (1577–1640) (Fig. 1A) wrote what may be the longest, and now also little-known, medical treatise in history (Fig, 1B). The Anatomy of Melancholy,1 first published in 1621 was more than 1,400 pages long. It is a rambling, chaotic, sometimes riotous concatenation of quotes, often in Latin, from the most diverse set of sources any one person may ever have cited. Burton scavenged the Bodleian library at Oxford for its treasures, noting whatever he came across that was relevant, and traveling vicariously around the world and through the minds of previous thinkers. Over sequential editions Burton added and added, but had not the patience to organize or cut. Melancholy was arcane even in Burton's own time. It cannot be read through like a normal treatise, but if browsed slowly it is interesting and often very funny. Robert Burton (1577-1640) and cover page of first (1638) edition. “I confess it again, I as mad, as foolish, as anyone.” Burton was read, or at least routinely mined for pithy quotations he had gleaned from countless other authors, like a Bartlett's of his day, and praised by many well-known scholars and thinkers. I will use Melancholy to frame the thoughts to follow because of its conceptual similarity to views on genetic causation and evolution today. Burton lived far before evolutionary ideas, much less genetics, came along in any modern sense, but his relevance is interesting, if perhaps in a whimsical way. His tome documented the endlessly diverse ways a person can become “melancholy,” or depressed, and what can be done about it. Melancholy was frustratingly hard to define. “Tis hard, I confess,” he wrote, “yet nevertheless I will adventure through the midst of these perplexities, and, led by the clue or thread of the best writers, extricate myself out of a labyrinth of doubts and errors, and so proceed to the causes.” Table 1 provides a rather sketchy and incomplete list of those countless causes. Burton discussed them in great detail, giving them nuanced treatment and clearly recognizing that they needn't be mutually exclusive. For example, there are hundreds of pages explaining how one can be melancholy because of being too zealous about religion (witchcraft, spiritualism, and such). But the cause might instead, or also, be sexual jealousy, digestion, drink, the geography of America, or being too deeply involved in reading or scholarship, as he described himself to be. Essentially, each person's melancholy was different, so it's not surprising that melancholy could affect almost any part of the body in almost any way. And, as Burton noted, the reverse is also true: bodily ills could cause mood problems as well as being caused by them. A point I'll return to is that his causal explanations largely rested on the classical but still-current Galenic principle of disease as an imbalance among the four humours: heat and cold, and yellow and black bile. Burton was not a physician, but a major objective of his work was to provide a lengthy treatise on cures he or others had suggested, which could be specific to the cause of a given case of melancholy. He acknowledged that the breadth of causes and types of melancholy that he included made this a challenging task: “In such obscurity, therefore, variety and confused mixture of symptoms, causes, how difficult a thing is it to treat of several kinds apart; to make any certainty or distinction among so many casualties, distractions, when seldom two men shall be like effected per omnia [in all respects]?” At least, he found the effort therapeutic for his own personal case: “I write of melancholy, by being busy to avoid melancholy. There is no greater cause of melancholy than idleness, no better cure than business….” In our modern scientific age, we expect higher standards of evidence than in Burton's time, when it sufficed to quote previous experts. Or do we? The scientific causes of melancholy should be objective and biological: We can't find the cause, much less the cure, of something until we know what that something is. In practice, this means that cause rests, to a substantial extent, in the cultural nature of the trait itself. With changing standards, treatments, and expectations, the diagnosis of disease changes, so that, in a way, the diagnosis becomes the phenotype. We see this regularly today in efforts to define what constitutes obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and many other disorders. The trait itself is variable and often difficult to measure, especially when its primary pathogenesis is complex or unknown. Modified measurement or improved technology leads to better or different diagnostic tests, which in turn typically lead to the definition of numerous sub-traits. Changes in definition affect who's diagnosed, at what age, and why. This then changes who gets screened and how often; that is, how intensively we search for the trait. More intense screening leads to increased diagnosis and even to changes in behavior, as people react to what they're told about themselves or what they read in the news media about the trait. The disease itself is not entirely physical. Thus, if there is a change in the cutoff level of glucose or blood pressure used to diagnose diabetes or hypertension, a person's traits may instantly switch from benign to pathological. This doesn't mean there aren't reasons for the change, or that there isn't an actual disorder, but it does mean that the connection between putative causal agents, including genes, and the “trait” differ for cultural reasons, and that, to some extent, means biologically arbitrary reasons. Culturally based diagnostic changes may be based on statistical judgment, and thus on the quirks of how we choose the data to study a problem. For example, traits like hypertension are defined on notions of increased risk—probability—of a future disease outcome like stroke. But that risk is a subjective judgment based on an estimate derived from a specific set of data, about the cutoff level above which risk is “significantly” elevated. Statistical significance is, of course, a subjective judgment.2 Furthermore, because even if it's estimated stably and accurately, risk is a probability, a point on a continuum from 0 to 1. Consequently, we are imposing culturally derived definitions on the individual, based on samples of population data, and what we choose to consider as serious, and that is more than just a reflection of improved technical knowledge. There are plenty of good reasons for making such decisions, but despite the changeable nature of the definitions, we view a trait as objective and invest intense research effort to define its genetic and environmental causes, as if there really is an “it”. While these statements apply to physical traits such as obesity or diabetes, behavior is much more vulnerable to these problems because it is based, to a considerable extent, on judgments about what constitutes appropriate social interaction. Autism, dementia, bipolarism, and other disorders are clear examples. They may have started out their history as serious, unambiguous diseases. We have all been touched by the tragedies of individuals with such conditions who were clearly debilitated. But, like Burton's melancholy, even the clear-cut severe cases, when looked at closely, vary greatly. This has led to the carving up of diagnoses into increasing numbers of subtypes; it also has meant that the discovery of simple or single causes, genetic or otherwise, has been elusive. Further, in our technical age, the definition of what constitutes a condition has expanded. Everyone is unhappy sometimes, and like melancholy to Burton, can be brought under the umbrella as a potential candidate (or should I say customer?) for therapy. You've seen the ads in which someone, usually, a nubile woman, puts the back of her hand against her forehead and gives you a pained expression, while the announcer asks whether you have ever felt depressed and, if so, hurry to your doctor to get ReLaX®. Pharma naturally wants you on lifetime medication. In a sense, we are in an epidemic of mental illness,3, 4 with expanding definitions that become codified (until the next revision) by a select inner circle of experts who presumably are disinterested. The results are published as the guidebook known as the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders5 a growing tome that is today's version of Burton. The shifting sands of diagnosis, compounded by various cultural factors and vested interests, make current study designs and the interpretation of previous studies difficult. This may be one major reason why cause and treatment remain elusive. Other issues arise, such as whether one seizure automatically makes a person an epileptic or whether one episode of memory loss or confusion constitutes a diagnosis of dementia. Currently, cultural factors have led to the medicalizing of increasing numbers of traits, physical and behavioral, in increasing numbers of people and at diminishing ages. Behavior, which is inherently sociocultural, is vulnerable to these dynamic changes in definition and even in state itself. The traits of schizophrenia may be real, and severe. But are schizophrenics ill, or do they have special insights so as to be priests or shamans or political tyrants? Is their reproductive fitness reduced because they behave weirdly and are sexually intimidating, or are they sexually intriguing and have enhanced fitness? Though hard evidence is scant, evolutionary anthropologists have repeatedly raised both arguments. Autism, which involves impaired social interactions, has been rapidly rising in frequency. But what is it? Is autism really more common or is the increased prevalence due to changes in diagnostic criteria, increased awareness, or intensified screening? Is the increased incidence a product of the press of advocacy groups or neuroscience centers to increase their scope? All of these changes have been occurring in recent decades. And then what about the cause? In Burtonesque fashion, autism has been attributed to heavy metal (for example, mercury) toxicity in the environment or in vaccines, to other kinds of vaccines, hypothyroidism, thalidomide exposure, use of valproic acid (an antipsychotic medication), maternal alcohol use, congenital cytomegalovirus exposure, measles infection, alleles that are responsive to pesticides, a large gene duplication, regulatory gene mutations, early watching of television in rainy climates, not having a fever, low intelligence, and probably more. In the face of this “clarity,” it has become fashionable to speak of autism spectrum disorder, an evasive way of saying that autism is on a continuum of social interaction that is extremely diverse, that each case is different, and that it has no single trait and no single cause, genetic or otherwise.6 If the increase in frequency is really just an artifact of detection or changing diagnostic criteria, one would not focus searches for causes among activities that have recently been increasing. But that is what's going on today. When it comes to cause, there is a current desire to turn all traits into genetic traits, which has an aura of mechanistic rigor and fits well within our current molecular view of life. Because genes are inherited, genetic causation would suggest that traits are inherent and could be detected by the promised “personalized genomic medicine” from DNA sequences, even before birth, leading to presymptomatic diagnosis and inevitably suggesting a need for ever-earlier, even lifetime therapy. When the frequency of a trait changes dramatically, we know it can't be genetic in the usual sense because the gene pool is very slow to change. But the fallback position is to insist that the trait is still genetic, but now in the sense that there is always relevant variation in a population that responds to changing environments, whatever they are. This idea receives general support from artificial or experimental selection, a kind of environmental change: the population of plants or animals, or even bacteria, almost always shows a response to selection. Similar issues apply to behavioral traits like criminality, political and economic behavior, addictability, abusiveness, response to abusiveness, adventurousness, and a host of others for which genetic causation is currently being claimed. Exactly what kinds of traits are these, and who defines them or decides how to measure them? The problems are rather obvious: If people are in the slammer today for drug offenses, then a genes-for-criminality study would call them “cases” and assign them a criminality genotype. But if Congress were to legalize recreational drugs, those who had previously had criminal genotypes would suddenly be in the normal category. With slippery and changeable cultural definitions it is no surprise that people can find what they want to find. Whether you want to call a disease or behavior genetic or environmental often becomes a matter of rhetoric or politics, not science. This doesn't mean that the trait doesn't exist or has no cause, nor that genetic variation is not involved. It means we're in elusive causal territory, partly of our own making, if we expect causation to work in a law-like way, like gravity or the ideal gas law. Clearly, it also means that, with the exceptions that always exist in the extreme of distributions, the tea-leaves of your genome do not spell your doom. Interestingly, what goes around comes around. In addition to the definitional problem, there is another way in which we're not so different from Burton as we may think. We smile patronizingly at medicine based on Galen's four humours, but we view traits, including behavior, as what amounts to imbalances of modern molecular humors, like insulin, neurotransmitters and their receptors, elevated salt concentration, or the wrong balance of vitamins, anti-oxidants, or food groups. The genetic mechanisms underlying any trait are closely connected to its evolution because evolution works through genes. Interestingly, impersonal natural selection is surprisingly similar to the cultural effects we have been considering. We humans define today's diseases or behavioral traits, but who defines the traits in terms of their evolutionary past? Nature does that, not scientists, because fitness—evolutionary adaptation—is strictly based on the realpolitik of survival: diagnosis and “therapy” wrapped into a single judgment. The way we may see the trait today need not be how nature saw it yesterday. Nature need not have seen it in the same way at all times, or even in only one way at any given time. Unlike human traits, traits out there in nature are at each time defined de facto rather than de jure. Any trait here today must have been both lucky and good enough to pass through whatever selective screens its ancestral manifestations faced in the past, and that was their only definition. We're not able to see into the past directly, but our guesses should at least be informed. Unfortunately, it can be hard to refute or choose among scenarios that might seem plausible. Rationales can always be constructed to defend an adaptive hypothesis, in the way Burton can claim that almost anything can cause melancholy. A trait, even melancholy, may seem obvious until you think about it. The problem can be seen with what might be considered a standard, safe trait to understand. Take, for example, the baboon skull shown in Figure 2. Is the skull a trait? Since a head does many things, perhaps we could agree that we should restrict our attention to something less amorphous, like the measures of face length shown in Figure 2. Many papers have been written on face length and its variation in humans and primates.7, 8 The same landmark points and distances between them can be found on other species, from aardvarks to zebras. That seems pretty empirical and objective, and since they're just straight lines, highly replicable measures. They must be valid traits. What could be simpler? Some standard craniofacial landmarks (dots) in a baboon, and lines connecting them as measures of face length. Computerized tomography scan, courtesy Joan Richtsmeier. [Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at wileyonlinelibrary.com.] But consider the top line. The face has to accommodate the eyes, chewing, vocal, and defense apparatus, salivary system, brain, olfactory and inspiration processing systems, tactile sensation, visual appearance, and more. Traits like face length or prognathism are defined in textbooks as if they make sense to us here and now, and their evolutionary adaptiveness is explained. But each function involves multiple physical components, including various bones, cartilage, muscle attachments, vascular and nerve pathways, teeth, soft tissues, and brain, as well as their proportions and relation to posture. A face has obvious behavioral uses, like being scary or sexy. Using the same length measure, the history of the assemblage as a whole can be seen in fossils and comparatively among living species. But what is it that nature screened, and when, and by what criteria, and how variably over time? Since each component and function involves the effects of many genes having partly overlapping tissue-specific expression patterns, each adaptive context may have involved different variants in different genes (in different populations). So is the top line actually a trait in nature's eyes, as it seems to be in ours? Now think about the bottom line in Figure 2. It's also clearly replicable and objective to measure. It should be statistically correlated with the length of the top line because the two lines reflect some similar morphological aspects of the skull. Some of the same genes affect both. But is there a correlation between them because they reflect the same functions? Or is the correlation forced on the two measures because, even though they reflect different functions or adaptations, they must be consistent to work together on the same head? To the extent that this matters, there is no genetic basis for the trait, because the trait is a construct of our imagination. It is not necessarily blind nature, but we today who subjectively impose the definitions, and hence define what's important or real and then try to explain it, accounting for its adaptations. How can we prove our understanding or prove it to be wrong? This is science, after all, isn't it? The elusiveness of the definitions of biological traits is likely one of several reasons why direct evidence of adaptive natural selection, which has pushed a trait to a new function, is difficult to find. (In contrast, it's easy to find evidence of purifying selection, which rejects new variation in existing genes, presumably to retain existing function). Such evidence is likely to be weak if many different genes contribute to a given trait9 because natural selection will move variation in any or all of them in the favored direction, spreading the favors among them so to speak. But evidence of selection will be even more elusive if the trait that we define as unitary is actually a compound of multiple components or functions, past or present. If the causal landscapes are slippery in these ways, one can alter one's phenotypes, without any genetic change, by altering one's environment. Burton had a fine solution for one of the many sources of melancholy that interested him so much. This was the melancholy a man felt upon discovering that his spouse was being sexually unfaithful (how women felt about their spouses is beyond the scope of this article and this author). The cause of infidelity melancholy was possessive jealousy. title: The Solitary Mind in the Anatomy of Melancholy
abstract: When I go musing all alone, Thinking of diverse things fore-known, When I build Castles in the air, Void of sorrow and void of fear, Pleasing myself with phantasms sweet, Methinks the time runs very fleet. All my joys to this are folly, Naught so sweet as melancholy. When I lie waking all alone, Recounting what I have ill done, My thoughts on me then tyrannize, Fear and sorrow me surprise, Whether I tarry still or go, Methinks the time moves very slow. All my griefs to this are jolly, Naught so sad as melancholy.2 Much could be said about these lines, but my concern here is with the relationship they thematise between melancholy, self-reflection and solitude. The rest of the poem leaves us in no doubt that Burton regards solitary meditation upon oneself as an integral part of the ‘abstract’ of the melancholic pathology (‘When to myself I act and smile / With pleasing thoughts the time beguile … When I lie, sit, or walk alone, / I sigh, I grieve, making great moan … Friends and Companions get you gone, / 'Tis my desire to be alone; / Ne'er well but when my thoughts and I / Do domineer in privacy …. I am a beast, a monster grown, / I will no light nor company, / I find it now my misery’).3 The special significance of solitude in the Anatomy is also announced on its illustrated frontispiece, produced from Burton's instructions by the Frankfurt engraver Christof Le Blon, and first appearing in the third edition of 1628 (Figure 1). Again, when Burton provides his readers with a guide to the contents here, the importance of solitude is reflected in the fact that it is given its own panel (Figure 2), together with depictions of the main types of melancholy discussed in the book, and two famous herbal therapies (borage and hellebore), set beside portraits of the author and his ancient philosophical predecessor Democritus.4 Solitude here is depicted, as Burton explains in another poem added in 1632 (‘The Argument of the Frontispiece), ‘[b]y sleeping dog, cat: Buck and Doe, / Hares, Conies in the desert go: Bats, Owls the shady bowers over, / In melancholy darkness hover’.5 All of these creatures were traditionally associated with both solitude and melancholy, and it is perhaps also notable that all the human figures on the frontispiece are alone.6 In this essay, I explore the pathological aspects of solitude in The Anatomy of Melancholy. The first part outlines Burton's account of the medical dimension of solitude, in which the desire to be alone is, according to the teachings of physicians from antiquity to the seventeenth century, a prominent symptom of the melancholic disease. Here, the Anatomy draws on a range of medical authorities to connect solitariness with the characteristically melancholic passions of fear and sorrow. However, when analysed in conjunction with physical idleness and excessive thinking, solitude could also be regarded as part of an unhealthy physical and psychological regimen, and thereby come to be a cause of melancholy. As we shall see, Burton is particularly interested in the effects of solitude upon the mind of the melancholic sufferer, and describes the process of ‘melancholizing’, the passage from pleasurable meditation to painful mental fixation, as one of the intrinsic dangers of the voluntary withdrawal from the external world. In the second part of the essay, I turn to the spiritual significance of solitude in Burton's work. Whilst solitude had been regarded for many centuries as an important part of Christian devotion, its potentially hazardous dimensions had also long been recognised, particularly in early accounts of acedia (sloth) and diabolical temptation. This perspective on solitude was incorporated in Protestant writing about melancholy, especially in English works concerned with the ‘afflicted conscience’. These sources provided the background for Burton's account of ‘religious melancholy’, which combined spiritual and medical ideas about solitude to describe its destructive function in generating superstitious delusions and mental self-torment. Bringing the theme of melancholic solitude in the Anatomy to prominence serves to illustrate important features not only of this work, but of the premodern understanding of melancholy more generally.7 Burton wrote his extraordinarily large and polymathic book partly, as he says, to alleviate his own melancholy, having been ‘left to a solitary life, and mine own domestic discontents’, but also to help treat it in others by presenting and analysing the encyclopedia of human knowledge about the disease, from antiquity to his day.8 My assumption here, then, is that the Anatomy can serve as useful, even privileged vantage point from which to view the broader history of the relationship between melancholy and solitude. At the same time, Burton's account of this relationship brings particular features of his understanding of melancholy into closer focus.9 Perhaps most importantly, we can see that for Burton, as for his contemporaries, although the melancholic disease had a physical and corporeal basis – most famously, but not exclusively, in the humour black bile – some of his most pressing concerns related to the effects of melancholy on the mind. The physicians, after all, agreed that melancholy was properly defined as a form of madness (delirium) that affected both body and mind, but also that in the disease the primarily ‘affected parts’ were the powers of imagination and reason in the brain.10 In solitude, I suggest, the workings of melancholy upon the mind are most clearly seen, and presented by Burton through his medical and religious sources as a destructive form of introspection. Since antiquity, the desire for solitude had been identified in medical works on melancholy as a symptom of the disease.11 In the Subsection on the ‘Symptoms or Signs in the Mind’ in the main treatise of the Anatomy (1.3.1.2), it is presented as primarily a by-product of the psychological perturbations that arise from the damaged imagination; it is also linked to the effects of the humour black bile upon the mind, and with the celestial influences of Saturn and Mercury.12 In the first place, following the authority of the Hippocratic Aphorisms (6.23), Galen (On the Affected Parts 3.10), and their legions of followers in neoteric medicine, are the symptoms of persistent fear and sorrow, generally regarded as ‘most assured signs, inseparable companions, and characters of melancholy’, and, according to Burton, the cause of the melancholic wish to be alone.13 The fearful melancholic is often groundlessly distrustful of others, to the point that ‘[h]e dare not come in company for fear he should be misused, disgraced, overshoot himself in gesture or speeches, or be sick; he thinks every man observes him, aims at him, derides him, owes him malice’.14 Other psychological symptoms are intensified in solitude, or serve to reinforce the tendency of the sufferer to withdraw from company. The sadness of melancholics, Burton observes, is accentuated ‘if they be alone, idle, & parted from their ordinary company’; their suspiciousness prompts others to shun them; their inconstancy and restlessness means that they can abide ‘no company long’; and their dejected bashfulness means that ‘they dare not come abroad, into strange companies especially’ and ‘can look no man in the face’, ‘cannot speak, or put themselves forth as others can’, ‘seldom visit their friends, except some familiars’, and are ‘oftentimes wholly silent’.15 They delight in floods & waters, desert places, to walk alone in orchards, gardens, private walks, back-lanes, averse from company, as Diogenes in his tub, or Timon Misanthropus, they abhor all companions at last, even their nearest acquaintance, & most familiar friends, for they have a conceit (I say) every man observes them, will deride, laugh to scorn, or misuse them, confining themselves therefore wholly to their private houses or chambers, fugiunt homines sine causa (saith Rhasis) & odio habent … they will diet themselves, feed and live alone …16 Just as the melancholic passions of fear and sorrow could ‘tread in a ring’ and be both symptoms and causes of melancholy – in the latter case by affecting the spirits and humours – so being solitary, according to Burton, could itself lead to the disease.18 Here, however, he was stretching his medical sources, or at least developing their concern with the detrimental effects of physical inactivity.19 Certainly contemporary physicians warned of the dangers of idleness, which, we are told (1.2.2.6), quenches the natural heat of the body, dulls the spirits, and hinders digestion, and fills the body with ‘crudities’ and ‘obstructions’; by generating and corrupting black bile in the body, it is, in the opinion of al-Rāzī in the Comprehensive Book (the Liber continens in the medieval Latin translation), ‘the greatest cause of melancholy’.20 To similar effect, physical idleness induces potentially harmful motions in the mind, for ‘what will not fear and fantasy work in an idle body?’21 In Burton's translation of the opinion of the Portuguese converso Elijah Montalto in his Archipathologia (1614), ‘[t]hey that are idle are far more subject to melancholy, than such as are conversant or employed about any office or business’.22 This consideration of inactivity as a cause of melancholy leads Burton to its frequent accompaniment: ‘[c]ousin-german [that is, “near relative”] to Idleness’, he writes, ‘and a concomitant cause, which goes hand in hand with it, is nimia solitudo, too much solitariness’. Here the citations of learned medical authority – that of the contemporary physicians Montalto, Nicolas Le Pois and Girolamo Mercuriale – are creatively misleading, because these authors actually confine themselves to the technical category of ‘motion and rest’, without referring to solitude as causes.23 Nevertheless, it is not difficult to find solitude included amongst the causes of melancholy in other works of learned medicine in this period.24 It may not quite have been ‘the testimony of all Physicians’, then, but few would have disagreed with Burton's argument that the solitary life was a potential cause of melancholy because of its association with physical inactivity. Voluntary solitariness is that which is familiar with Melancholy, and gently brings on like a Siren, a shoeing-horn, or some Sphinx to this irrevocable gulf, a primary cause Piso calls it;26 most pleasant it is at first, to such as are melancholy given, to lie in bed whole days, and keep their chambers, to walk alone in some solitary Grove, betwixt Wood and Water, by a Brook-side, to meditate upon some delightsome and pleasant Subject, which shall affect them most; amabilis insania [a lovable madness], and mentis gratissimus error [a most agreeable delusion]: a most incomparable delight it is so to melancholize, to build castles in the air, to go smiling to themselves, acting an infinite variety of parts, which they suppose, and strongly imagine they represent, or that they see acted or done: Blandae quidem ab initio [agreeable indeed at the beginning], saith Lemnius, to conceive and meditate of such pleasant things, sometimes Present, past or to come, as Rhasis speaks.27 So delightsome these toys are at first, they could spend whole days and nights without sleep, even whole years alone in such contemplations, and fantastical meditations, which are like unto dreams, and they will hardly be drawn from them, or willingly interrupt, so pleasant their vain conceits are, that they hinder their ordinary tasks and necessary business, they cannot address themselves to them, or almost to any study or employment, these fantastical and bewitching thoughts so covertly, so feelingly, so urgently, so continually set upon, creep in, insinuate, possess, overcome, distract, and detain them, they cannot I say go about their more necessary business, stave off or extricate themselves, but are ever musing, melancholizing, and carried along, as he (they say) that is led round about an Heath with a Puck in the night, they run earnestly on in this labyrinth of anxious and solicitous melancholy meditations, and cannot well or willingly refrain, or easily leave off, winding and unwinding themselves, as so many clocks, and still pleasing their humours, until at last the Scene is turned upon a sudden, by some bad object, and they being now habituated to such vain meditations and solitary places, can endure no company, can ruminate of nothing but harsh and distasteful subjects. Fear, sorrow, suspicion, subrusticus pudor [rather awkward shyness], discontent, cares, and weariness of life surprise them in a moment, and they can think of nothing else, continually suspecting, no sooner are their eyes open, but this infernal plague of Melancholy seizeth on them, and terrifies their souls, representing some dismal object to their minds, which now by no means, no labour, no persuasions they can avoid, haeret lateri lethalis arundo [the lethal arrow sticks in the side], they may not be rid of it, they cannot resist.28 In Burton's account, this psychological dynamic is prominent in forms of the condition that afflicted those with lifestyles or professions that were associated with seclusion – most famously, philosophers and scholars. Again, his view is built upon teachings that had been long established in medical circles. According to the influential ancient Greek physician Rufus of Ephesus (fl. c.100 CE), ‘no-one who devotes too much effort to thinking about a certain science can avoid ending up with melancholy’.29 Thus, whilst the melancholic humour was sometimes seen to be the physiological cause of extraordinary intellectual achievements, the solitary contemplative life was also viewed as intrinsically hazardous to one's health.30 Indeed, it is no accident that the most famous formulation of the notion of melancholic ‘genius’, in the first book of the De vita libri tres (1489) of the Neoplatonist title: Man Meets Machine
abstract: Who will stand up to the juggernaut of artificial intelligence (AI) and strike a blow for human intelligence? Gerd Gigerenzer, in How to Stay Smart in a Smart World, rises to the challenge. How is a Streitschrift in the best polemical tradition. It takes aim at the postscientific paradigm of AI and the culture that has grown up around it, critically examines its assumptions and pretensions, asks tough questions about its epistemological, technological, and ethical implications, and explores ways that might take us to a better place. How delivers plenty of shock value. AI has produced successes and failures that will startle many readers. How can it be that after plenty of deep learning AI can beat any grand master at chess but mistakes a school bus for an ostrich if patterns of pixels have been added to the photo in a way that makes no detectable difference to the human eye (Szegedy et al., 2014)? A pragmatic conclusion would be to let AI do whatever it does best and leave the rest to human decision makers.There are two problems with this. First, AI is greedy; its mission is not to creep but to rush, with the prospective outcome being an ever-shrinking domain in which native human intelligence can work its own magic. Human intelligence seems condemned to the fate of a “god of the gaps,” that is, an agent that is limited to take care of whatever cannot be done mechanically. Second, the current state of AI technology is not one that people might find acceptable, particularly after reading How. Actual and potential surveillance, the hollowing out of conventional notions of privacy and personal dignity, have reached apocalyptic dimensions. Gigerenzer reports that turned-off smart TVs record our living room conversations, while toy dolls record the babblings of the next generation. The Samsung website he cites states, “Please be aware that if your spoken words include personal or other sensitive information, that information will be among the data captured and transmitted to a third party through your use of Voice Recognition” (retrieved at https://www.samsung.com/hk_en/info/privacy/smarttv/). Smart homes and smart cars are about to arrive. The price of convenience is a loss of freedom. Do we want to pay this price?Gigerenzer sketches his story in an introduction and lets it unfold in 11 topical chapters. Of these, the first six chapters explore “the human affair with AI.” It is not a love affair, although at times it seems that way and although AI promoters may want it to be. Along the way, we learn about how fundamentally different human—and especially social—intelligence and artificial intelligence are. That one intelligence can be reduced to or explained by the other is a myth to be debunked. Yet the final five chapters explore the vulnerability of the human variant of intelligence to be reduced by the artificial one. Here, not only failures of human rationality play a role but also myopia, sloth, and other animal passions.The picture that emerges is dark, and one wishes Gigerenzer had stronger medicine to offer for the emancipation of the human spirit. He does have advice, but it is modest. We should pay for services such as internet searches, services that are currently covered by the revenue coming from the selling of our personal data. We should reject cookies, which spy on us. As to love, we may want to get out of Tinder and instead ask trusted friends and family to find us a match. Alas, getting off the grid is made hard by clever algorithms and human web designers, if there are any left. They have a vested interest in keeping us hooked, and so they shape our “choices” with “Like” buttons and “cookies.” Haven't psychologists shown that rejecting cookies is hard (Mischel, Shoda, & Rodriguez, 1989)? Gigerenzer suggests that what we are witnessing is a late victory of Skinnerianism. The managed organism has no freedom or dignity and does not know it.The introduction anticipates many of the substantive points How explores at length. A chief concern is that AI aims to predict and control human behavior. Many of our behaviors, such as whether or for whom we vote and whether or whom we might kill are increasingly predictable. Personal freedom and agency diminish as a consequence, and ethical questions otherwise left to science fiction (e.g., the moral status of a “precrime unit”; Dick, 1956/2002) become pressing. The dystopia of prediction and control is partly offset by a suite of egregious and often hilarious AI failures. To unlock my iPhone, all I need to do is look at it. This does not work on a sunny day, however, because my sunglasses render the algorithm impotent. Still, the master narrative is that AI is getting better all the time and that this is a good thing. If artificial intelligence solves all the important problems, human intelligence will be regarded as inferior, or, more generously, as a subvariant of true intelligence, which is artificial.So far, the failures of AI have not gone away, and big failures have big consequences. Predictions fail when low-probability and high-impact events burst on the scene. Algorithms did not predict the crash of the financial industry in 2008, but then again, neither did a significant number of highly compensated economists. Nevertheless, AI has ushered in an era of mass surveillance, a development that has met with little resistance. People, their attention and data, have become the product, and government by algorithm is morphing into a veiled form of authoritarianism, lulling us to sleep in front of our watchful smart TV. If only this were paternalism in the literal sense, but the pater has left the building. The new god is disembodied, and unlike the god of old-time religion, he does not care about us—because he can't.Gigerenzer emphasizes that AI cannot be fully human; that is, there will be no “strong AI.” Computations can't “care” even if they can learn human preferences deeply and base decisions on them. AI advocates might see this as an advantage. Why bother with the baggage of “will and representation”? When predictions are accurate and choices are optimal, simulation is all that is needed. The intuition that human sentiments (“caring”) matter, or the more modest claim that they are irreducible to mechanical computation, must therefore be defended. Leibniz (1719) was an early critic of the mechanistic worldview; more recently, Frankfurt (2004) argued that human preferences and desires are necessary for any intelligible or “meaningful” action to occur. AI needs such input to get off the ground. Why would AI predict human crime and recommend sentencing someone who has not yet committed a crime if there is no human endorsement of such a strategy? Matters will turn darker once AI generates its own preferences. Were this to happen, how would we infer or know that AI “cares”? AI might well pass a Turing test by leaving us unable to tell whether it does care or merely acts as if it did (Searle, 1980). Again, however, AI enthusiasts will insist that this is the wrong question, or rather, that it is one question too many.How gives much attention to the notion that AI does not “really see” anything, that it has “no conceptual representation,” and that it does “not really know” anything in the way that natively intelligent earthlings do. Compelling as this contrast may seem, its force is limited. It is but an appeal to our self-conscious pride and intuition. It glosses over the difficult problem of other minds (Avramides, 2020). If I can't prove that David next door has a mind similar to my own, my inability to prove that a computer has a self-conscious mind does not amount to a strong condemnation of AI. Again, an AI zealot will not “care” whether the algorithm thinks or knows anything; she will look for her proof in the pudding of successful prediction.It is for this reason that the success of the attack on AI depends on how poorly AI does on its own turf. Gigerenzer dedicates the first topical chapter to AI's spectacular failure to advance the cause of monogamy. Romantic matching is a good choice to make the argument because it is here that humans with their animal passions want to succeed badly and are thus uncritical in their acceptance of AI's promises. But there is no deliverance. Gigerenzer estimates that the probability of being successfully matched within a year is about 5%, a bar that conventional methods of matchmaking can clear as well. AI's problem is twofold. First, even if learning is deep, the data are shallow. Profile similarity retains a prominent role in prediction, neglecting that over time similarity loses its importance. Second, once people meet, they enter games of interdependent action, which provide rich reserves of uncertainty (Krueger, Heck, Evans, & DiDonato, 2020).When uncertainty enters the picture, algorithms lose traction because they depend on the “stable-world assumption.” This is the chief explanatory concept How brings to the table. Prediction works well inasmuch as things stay the same. Then, validation data resemble training data, and the past predicts the future. In a world of noise, or worse yet, a world of shifting biases and disruptions, predictions fail and the good fits obtained with training data turn into embarrassing cases of overfitting, overconfidence, false-positive errors, and detections of “crud” (Meehl, 1967; Wilson, Harris, & Wixted, 2022). Gigerenzer notes that that in spite of decades of relevant research on the matter, AI designers (human or otherwise) have not come to grips with the fine art of cross-validation (Mosier, 1951). The standard procedure is half-baked; it is to gather a large amount of data and use one half to train an algorithm and the other half to assess the quality of its “out-of-sample predictions.” This sounds better than it is. If the data come from the same population, out-of-sample does not mean out-of-population. Instead, what is made to look like an exercise in cross-validation reduces to a check of split-half reliability.The difference between internal reliability and external validity cuts to the heart of inductive inference. If worlds are not perfectly stable and if we seek to predict the future from the past, we must acknowledge that the populations from which we sample to learn are not the same as the populations for which we make predictions. One would wish to have a prior estimate of the degree of similarity between these populations, at least in an ordinal sense. If women and men form different populations, then old men and young women form populations that are even more different. In cross-validation research, the result of interest is how much greater the loss of accuracy in out-of-population predictions is than the accuracy loss expected a priori.Solving the problem of cross-validation is a technical challenge, and the finding that most AI work has settled for fitting models and maximizing reliability does not mean it can't do better. AI's statistical myopia is not an intrinsic impediment to its success. Leveraging the argument of the “stable-world assumption,” Gigerenzer suggests that many of the critical to-be-predicted outcomes in the human scene are fraught with uncertainties that even the most sophisticated cross-validation models cannot overcome. In contrast, native human intelligence has access to a toolbox of simple heuristics that need little data as input and that work well even when things change. They do so because they ignore information that may look relevant in a sample from one population but add no value in a sample from another.Gigerenzer can draw on decades of research conducted at the Max Planck Institute in Berlin, research that has mapped the conditions under which fast and frugal heuristics do as well as or better than exhaustive quantitative algorithms (Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011). Mate selection, entertainingly discussed in the first chapter, is a case in point. Satisficers do well here, in part because they have abandoned the belief that the perfect soulmate can and must be found (Todd & Miller, 1999). If there is still a surviving strand of “psychological AI,” as Gigerenzer notes, then why is it not possible to use the fast-and-frugal framework to design algorithms? Like algorithms, heuristics are quantifiable computational rules. Thus, if native human intelligence is characterized by the use of heuristics in an uncertain world, then why can't a psychological AI mimic it?Given the desire for human intelligence not to be supplanted by artificial intelligence, any argument that there is something irreproducible is attractive. Humans might delight in the conveniences AI brings, laugh at its failures, and reassure themselves with the thought that the algorithm du jour cannot savor a Montrachet or recognize a faded photo of grandma with speed and ease. In How, Gigerenzer shows how inefficient and error-prone today's type of AI can be. His exploration of how smart—and scary—AI might become if it were built around the same capacities and shortcuts that mark human intelligence is more tentative. Where we will stand 10 years from now is an inductive question, and as we have seen, predicting an uncertain future requires a nimble form of intelligence as well as luck.
