title: Cotingas in Aviculture, Part II
abstract: Part I, published in the Watchbird XXXIV Number 2, included a history of cotingas in aviculture, and an overview of their diets in captivity. Accounts of cotingas now present in American public or private collections follow, with four species discussed here. Screaming Piha (Lipaugus vociferans) Of cotingas currently in aviculture, this species stands out for its superficially appearance. From pictures, it appears gray and thrush-like In life, it is more reminiscent of a New World Flycatcher (to which cotingas are, after all, closely related). Its large dark eyes are an immediately attractive feature. On the other hand, what is not at all ordinary is its very loud, three-note whistle (scarcely a scream), performed in a lekking display, one of the typical jungle noises across its enormous South American range. It occurs east of the Andes, including eastern Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, as well as the Guianas, Venezuela, Brazil, and Bolivia. Specimens in aviculture originate from Suriname, from where softbills continue to be commercially exported. I am unaware of any arriving in Europe or the U.S. before the 1990's. As of May, 2006, the International Species Information System (ISIS) listed three specimens distributed between two European zoos. Aside from a male at the National Aquarium in Baltimore, the U.S. zoo population was concentrated around the Great Lakes. A pair was exhibited at the National Aviary at Pittsburgh, while single birds were kept atToledo, Madison, and the Lincoln Park Zoo in Chicago. As of late 2007, ISIS lists a male and an unsexed bird at the National Aquarium, and single birds at the National Aviary, Toledo and Madison. In 2007 The Dallas World Aquarium received four birds from Suriname. So far as I know, nothing has been written about this species in captivity. I am therefore most grateful to Lori Smith, Senior Aviculturist at the National Aquarium in Baltimore for providing data about the pi has there. A single pair maintained in the Aquarium's rain forest hatched one chick each year from 2000 through 2003, with a fifth hatched in 2005. To my knowledge, this is the only captive propagation to have occurred. The chick hatched 22 October 2000 drowned immediately after fledging, on 22 November. The same fate overtook the bird hatched 14 May 2001, which died 4 June. The chick hatched 29 October 2002 disappeared the day it hatched, while the chick hatched 14 September 2005 disappeared after two days. The chick produced 31 August 2003 hatched in an incubator and was hand-reared, but died after three days, having difficulty passing feces. The breeding female died in 2006. The pair shared the 519,060 cubic foot rain forest with a free-ranqinq pair of Golden Lion Tamarins, a Two-toed Sloth and seventeen other species of birds, including seven species of tanagers (four of which are Tangaras), Blue~headed Pionus, Sun Conures, Red~capped Cardinals, Saffron Finches, Blue~crowned Motmots, and white-tailed Trogons (which successfully bred here for the first time in captivity). While in general, cornpatibility problems have not been an issue, the male Piha proved intolerant of male Spangled Cotingas, actually repeatedly killing them before it was decided to no longer maintain Spangled Cotingas (which had bred there) in this exhibit. I have found the birds at The Dallas World Aquarium remarkably tame, leading me to suspect they may have been collected from the wild as fledglings. They spend most of their time in the highest parts of their aviary, but when new diets are placed in the feeding station, they drop straight down in a swoop, again rerniniscent of tyrant flycatchers, and commence eating, not minding at all if I stand inches away. The ones I work with avidly eat crickets, but seem uninterested in giant mealworms. Other preferred foods are blueberries and Mazuri ZuLiFe Soft-bill Diet pellets. Spangled Cotinga (Cotinga cayana) Although this species made its avicultural debut in 1929 when the department store magnate J. Speden Lewis donated a pair to the London Zoo (Seth-Smith. 1930), it was an extreme rarity in captivity until the 1980's, when Dutch dealers began exporting it from Suriname. It has remained commercially available, with specimens arriving in the U.S. directly from Suriname since 2006 (as a result of European import bans for fear of bird flue). While ISIS, in May 2006, indicated only three European zoos held it, eleven U.S. and one Canadian collection were listed, making it the most well represented Cotinga in North American zoos. (The ISIS listing of 33 specimens at the Dallas World Aquarium is an error, six pairs being actually present then). In late 2007, it was present in nine U.S. institutions, as well as one Canadian, one British, four Continental European, and one South African collection, along with the Jurong Bird Park in Singapore, according to ISIS.

title: Boomerangs and International Plastic Surgery
abstract: Recently I had the privilege of attending an international plastic surgery meeting in Sydney, Australia. When most Americans think of Australia, they often think of the unique and fascinating boomerang; so while there, I purchased a boomerang for my son and me. The art of throwing a boomerang and making it come back is difficult to master. It is much like trying to walk when you are accustomed to crawling. At first you want to throw it like a Frisbee, which is wrong. You must hold a boomerang at a slight 15- to 20-degree vertical angle, depending on the velocity of the wind. The propeller balances the force of gravity so that the boomerang is not pulled to the ground before it makes a complete circle. According to local history, boomerangs were invented by primitive hunters who came up with a nonreturnable form that was used as a crude tool or club to hurl for protection. By accident, one of these bent sticks came back. The hunters then carefully constructed sticks with better curves that were thinner and longer in order to achieve optimal return on a reproducible basis. The oldest nonreturnable boomerang was found in Poland and dates back more than 20,000 years. These nonreturnable boomerangs are called kylies. The Australian Aborigine people are associated with the kylie in the shape of a boomerang. As the kylies were carved with more of a curved shape, they would come back to the thrower. They are the first flying machine recorded by man. Boomerangs are unique. Initially they appear to be easy to master, but the actual accomplishment is very complicated. Plastic surgery looks easy to some, but the actual accomplishment is a long and arduous journey. Like mastery of the boomerang, when one does master plastic surgery, it returns so much to you in so many ways. It becomes a natural part of you, like breathing in and breathing out. It changes your life. At the 2000 Olympic summer games, Australians became known worldwide for their hospitality. They set a new model for how Olympic games should be organized and played. This model must have been used by the International Confederation for Plastic Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgery (IPRAS) for their recent meeting in Sydney. It was incredible. Once every 4 years, IPRAS holds its international meeting. This year it was held in Sydney, Australia. It was a phenomenal success primarily due to the efforts of the organizing committee hosted by the Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons. The congress presidents, Drs. Ian Taylor and Wayne Morrison, deserve much of the credit, along with their organizing committee chair, Dr. Norman Olbourne. They planned an unbelievably comprehensive educational meeting that included a phenomenal scope and depth of information for every aspect of plastic surgery. Despite the long and difficult travel time (a 15-hour flight from Los Angeles), it was impressive to see the passion with which plastic surgeons from around the world came and participated in this educational event. The subjects covered spanned the entire international spectrum of plastic surgery, from perforator flaps to new innovative techniques in cosmetic plastic surgery, such as fillers and advances in craniofacial and pediatric plastic surgery. The meeting was highlighted by the beautiful backdrop of Sydney, a phenomenal city in an incredible country. Australia is the sixth largest country in the world, the same size as the 48 mainland states of the United States. It is 50 percent larger than Europe, but it has the lowest population density in the world per square kilometer. Among Australia’s more notable unique qualities are that it has 95 percent of the world’s precious opals, the kangaroo, the koala, and, of course, the boomerang. Australia’s history goes back more than 50,000 years to the aboriginal people who lived in a unique and challenging natural environment. They are believed to be the world’s oldest civilization. Australia was not officially discovered until Captain James Cook arrived in Botany Bay in 1770. The Australian people are gregarious, outgoing, and welcoming. Their lifestyle is very appealing. My only regret is that I could not spend more time enjoying the beautiful scenery surrounding this wonderful meeting. This global event for all of plastic surgery was not only educational but also a truly eye-opening experience. We heard colleagues share common problems ranging from scope of practice to ethics issues in plastic surgery today. Our cultures may be different, but the problems we face in our academic and clinical settings each day are virtually the same in every country. I strongly encourage more plastic surgeons to attend the next IPRAS meeting, to be held in Berlin in 2007. We especially need a greater representation of American plastic surgeons. Plastic surgeons from the wealthy countries of North America were very few at the Sydney meeting compared with the contributions of smaller, developing nations, who sent their plastic surgeons in numbers. We must applaud these plastic surgeons who, through no small effort and with minimal resources, came to this meeting for a once-in-a-lifetime educational experience. I look forward to the next IPRAS meeting and hope to see you there.

title: TagGen
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: TagGen: Source Code Archive This archive contains the complete source code for TagGen v1.2.0, archived at the time of publication of: Chowdhury F, Swain T, Shirokikh R, Rudler DL, Fox AH, Cleynen A, Shirokikh NE. (2026) TagGen: High-Performance Barcode Generator and Demultiplexer for High-Throughput and Long-Read Sequencing Applications. F1000Research -- Software Tool Article. The live TagGen repository (including future releases) is available at: https://github.com/Arnaroo/taggen Contents Source Code (source/) File Description source/app.d Application entry point; GUI initialisation and main event loop source/tagcore.d Core barcode generation engine: Monte Carlo candidate generation, greedy diversity selection, Hamming and Levenshtein distance utilities, exclude-sequence filtering, TSV/FASTA/matrix export source/cli.d Command-line interface: full parameter parsing (getopt), JSON config loading/saving, ASCII heatmap output, verbose statistics reporting source/benchmark.d Standalone benchmark binary entry point (no GTK dependency) source/embedded_resources.d Compile-time embedding of GUI resources (icons, logo) via D's -J import path source/version.d Version string and version info banner Demultiplexer (source/demux/) File Description source/demux/demux_main.d Demultiplexer entry point: DemuxParams struct, CLI argument parsing, pipeline orchestration for GUI, CLI, and standalone invocation source/demux/demux_index.d 8-mer k-mer index construction over the tag set; candidate barcode lookup and hit-count ranking source/demux/demux_match.d Banded edit-distance alignment (Stage 2 matching): position estimation from k-mer votes, confidence scoring, ambiguity detection, tag trimming (none/ends/all) source/demux/demux_io.d FASTQ reader (plain and gzip), per-sample FASTQ writers, read annotation, unassigned read collection source/demux/demux_stats.d Per-sample assignment statistics: read counts, expected vs. observed, mean Q-scores, TSV export source/demux/demux_pod5.d POD5 co-demultiplexing: read-ID routing to per-sample directories via the pod5 subset tool Build Configuration File Description dub.json DUB package manifest: dependencies, build configurations (linux, windows, benchmark), release and optimised build types (release-static, release-zenplus) dub.selections.json Locked dependency versions for reproducible builds build-windows.bat Windows build script: compiles TagGen with LDC2 + MSVC linker and packages a portable ZIP (optionally an Inno Setup installer) repackage-windows.sh Helper script to repack the Windows ZIP from a pre-built binary WINDOWS_BUILD.md Step-by-step instructions for building TagGen on Windows (MSYS2 + Visual Studio Build Tools + LDC2) Installer (installer/) File Description installer/taggen-installer.iss Inno Setup script for the Windows installer installer/package-windows.sh Shell script to invoke Inno Setup from the build pipeline Resources (resources/) File Description resources/taggen-logo.svg, taggen-logo.png TagGen logo (vector and raster) resources/taggen-icon.svg, taggen-icon.ico, taggen-icon-48.png, taggen-icon-128.png Application icons at multiple resolutions resources/arnaroo-mascot.png Arnaroo mascot image resources/README.md Notes on resource files Pre-compiled Binaries File Description taggen Pre-compiled Linux x86-64 binary (dynamically linked, GTK3 required) taggen-v1.2.0-windows-x86_64.zip Portable Windows ZIP including the GTK3 runtime DLLs taggen-windows/ Unpacked Windows distribution (executable + all required DLLs and GTK resources) Building from Source TagGen is written in D and uses the DUB package manager. The GUI module requires GTK3 via the GtkD bindings. A CLI-only build (no GTK dependency) is available via the benchmark configuration. Prerequisites Linux (Arch): sudo pacman -S ldc dub gtk3 Linux (Ubuntu/Debian): sudo apt install ldc dub libgtk-3-dev libgtkd-dev Linux (Fedora): sudo dnf install ldc dub gtk3-devel macOS (Homebrew): brew install ldc dub gtk+3 Windows: See WINDOWS_BUILD.md for full instructions. Build Commands (Linux / macOS) # Standard release build (GUI + CLI) dub build --compiler=ldc2 --build=release # Statically linked portable binary dub build --compiler=ldc2 --build=release-static # Optimised build for AMD Zen+ processors dub build --compiler=ldc2 --build=release-zenplus # CLI-only benchmark binary (no GTK dependency) dub build --compiler=ldc2 --config=benchmark --build=release Build Commands (Windows) From an x64 Native Tools Command Prompt with LDC2 on the PATH: build-windows.bat :: Build + portable ZIP build-windows.bat --installer :: Build + ZIP + Inno Setup installer Quick Start Launch the GUI ./taggen Generate barcodes (CLI) # 96 barcodes, 14 bp, minimum Hamming distance 4 taggen --cli -n 96 -l 14 -d 4 -o my_barcodes # 96 barcodes, 20 bp, Levenshtein distance 8 (recommended for ONT) taggen --cli -n 96 -l 20 -d 8 --metric levenshtein --minGc 40 --maxGc 60 -o ont_tags -v Demultiplex reads taggen --demux --tags my_barcodes.fasta --reads reads.fastq \ --mode end --trim-mode ends --outdir demux_results/ Full CLI reference: taggen --help and taggen --demux --help. Software Architecture TagGen implements a two-phase barcode generation algorithm and an anchor-free demultiplexer pipeline, both described in detail in the accompanying manuscript. Barcode generation: - Phase 1 (Monte Carlo candidate generation): Parallel random sequence generation across all CPU cores, validated in real-time against GC content, homopolymer, and exclude-sequence constraints. - Phase 2 (Greedy diversity selection): Iterative selection of the candidate maximising the minimum pairwise Hamming or Levenshtein distance to all previously selected barcodes, using cached minimum-distance updates for O(n·k) total complexity. Demultiplexer pipeline: - Stage 1 (k-mer voting): Pre-built 8-mer index maps query read k-mers to candidate barcodes; hit counts estimate barcode location. - Stage 2 (banded edit-distance alignment): Sliding-window Levenshtein or Hamming alignment at the estimated position; reads are accepted only if the edit distance is below threshold, the best-to-second-best margin is ≥ 2 (ambiguity guard), and the confidence score exceeds the minimum. Dependencies Dependency Version Purpose LDC2 ≥ 1.30 D compiler (LLVM-based) DUB ≥ 1.34 D package manager GtkD ~> 3.10 GTK3 bindings for GUI GTK3 ≥ 3.18 Cross-platform GUI toolkit The benchmark build configuration has no external dependencies beyond the D standard library. Changelog v1.2.0 "Wombat" (2026-03-08) Position masks refactored from exclude to include semantics GUI: 3-mode anchor selector per zone (From 3' end / From 5' end / Custom range) CLI: --position-mask accepts 3p:N and 5p:N shorthand Comprehensive demux test framework with parameter sweeps v1.1.3 "Echidna" (2026-03-08) Positional mask for full-mode demux: constrain tag search to specific read regions Post-demultiplexing statistics window with four visualisation tabs v1.1.2 "Platypus" (2026-03-05) Integrated demultiplexer (GUI tab + CLI --demux mode) POD5 signal file co-demultiplexing Tag trimming modes: none, ends, all Confidence scoring with ambiguity detection v1.1.1 "Billabong" (2026-03-05) Levenshtein edit distance for tag selection (--metric levenshtein) Greedy selection performance fix: O(n·k) cached min-distances v1.1.0 "Outback Explorer" (2026-01-16) Interactive heatmap visualisation of pairwise tag distances Exclude sequences feature with sliding-window comparison for longer reference sequences v1.0.1 "Unlimited Outback" (2025-10-15) Increased maximum tag limit to 1,000,000 v1.0.0 "Kangaroo Launch" (2025-10-15) Initial release: GUI, parallel generation, greedy diversity selection, TSV/FASTA export License Source code is available under the MIT License. title: How to Build a Grocery Delivery App: A Complete Development Guide
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In today's fast-paced world, convenience is king, and grocery delivery apps have emerged as a vital solution for busy individuals and families seeking to streamline their shopping experience. With the rise of e-commerce and changing consumer habits, the demand for efficient and user-friendly grocery delivery services has never been higher. This comprehensive development guide will walk you through the essential steps to create a successful grocery delivery app, from understanding the market and defining key features to selecting the right technology stack and executing effective marketing strategies. Whether you're a budding entrepreneur or an established business looking to expand, this guide will equip you with the knowledge and tools needed to navigate the complexities of app development in the grocery sector. Understanding the Grocery Delivery Market Market Trends and Growth Potential The grocery delivery market is riding the wave of convenience, and it's not slowing down! Thanks to hectic lifestyles and a dash of pandemic-induced habits, online grocery shopping has become as essential as that morning coffee. Market research shows that the global grocery delivery market is expected to hit billions (yes, with a 'B') in the coming years. This growth isn’t just a passing trend; it's a sign that people are craving the ease of ordering groceries from their couches like they order pizza. Target Audience Analysis When diving into the grocery delivery pond, it's vital to know who’s swimming in it. Your target audience ranges from busy professionals and parents juggling work and kids to tech-savvy millennials who prefer clicking over carting. Don't overlook the elderly population, who may see grocery delivery as a lifeline. Tailoring your app to meet the needs of these diverse groups will help you reel in loyal customers faster than you can say "two-for-one deals." Competitive Landscape The grocery delivery arena is crowded, with big players like Instacart and Amazon Fresh flexing their muscles. But fear not! The competition isn’t just about who can deliver faster; it’s about unique selling points. Perhaps your app has customizable subscriptions, local farm partnerships, or eco-friendly delivery methods. Know your competitors well to find that sweet spot where you can stand out and capture the market's attention. Defining Key Features for Your App Essential Features for Customers Customers are the lifeblood of your grocery delivery app, so roll out the red carpet! Essential features include a user-friendly interface, a smart search function, personalized recommendations, easy payment options, and real-time order tracking. Let’s not forget a review system to keep customers happy and a loyalty program to turn occasional buyers into regulars. Make sure their experience is smooth—like butter on warm toast. Admin Panel Features Behind every successful grocery delivery app is a robust admin panel that keeps the ship sailing smoothly. Key features for admins include inventory management, order tracking, customer support tools, and analytics for performance tracking. Add in the ability to manage promotions and user roles, and you’ve got a control center that even NASA would envy. Driver and Delivery Features Don’t forget the backbone of your delivery service—the drivers! Equip them with features like route optimization, real-time GPS tracking, delivery scheduling, and a user-friendly interface. A robust communication tool will also help them stay in touch with customers to ensure smooth deliveries, especially when navigating the chaotic maze of a city’s streets or the suburban sprawl. Choosing the Right Technology Stack Frontend Technologies Your app's face should be as appealing as a freshly stacked grocery aisle! For frontend development, consider popular frameworks like React, Angular, or Vue.js to create a responsive and interactive user interface. Remember, the goal is to make the shopping experience as delightful as finding a coupon for your favorite snack! Backend Technologies The backend is where the magic happens (a.k.a. the stuff users don't see). Choose robust backend technologies like Node.js, Ruby on Rails, or Django. These frameworks allow you to handle user requests, process payments, and manage databases with ease. Opting for cloud solutions like AWS or Google Cloud can also enhance scalability, because, let’s be honest, who doesn’t want the ability to grow? Database Options Now, let’s talk storage—of the data variety. For databases, you can choose between SQL options like PostgreSQL or MySQL or go with NoSQL databases like MongoDB, depending on your data structure needs. The goal is to select a database that provides speed, reliability, and easy data management, ensuring that every grocery item is neatly cataloged and accessible at lightning speed. Designing an Intuitive User Interface User Experience (UX) Principles An intuitive user interface is like a good grocery store layout: easy to navigate! Applying UX principles such as simplicity, consistency, and accessibility will enhance user satisfaction. Keep load times down, buttons large, and processes straightforward. If users can find their favorite snacks without breaking a sweat, they’ll keep coming back—no one enjoys a scavenger hunt for avocados. Wireframing and Prototyping Before diving headfirst into design, create wireframes and prototypes! These handy tools allow you to sketch the app's layout and functionality before investing time in visual design. Use tools like Figma or Sketch to map out the user journey—this step is crucial for ensuring your app flows like a well-oiled machine. Visual Design and Branding Last but not least, let’s talk aesthetics! Your app’s visual design should reflect your brand's personality while being inviting and easy on the eyes. Choose a color palette that evokes freshness and trust (think greens and blues), and make sure your branding is consistent across all materials. After all, a recognizable brand can turn “just another grocery app” into “the one I can’t live without.” Developing the Backend Infrastructure Setting Up the Server First things first, your app needs a server that won't throw a tantrum at peak hours (we've all been there). Choose a reliable cloud service provider like AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure, and set up your server environment. Consider using Docker for containerization; it keeps your app running smoothly in any environment, just like a well-organized pantry. API Development Next up: creating APIs that are as smooth as butter on warm toast. Your app will need endpoints for user registration, product listings, cart management, and order processing, among others. RESTful APIs are a popular choice here, allowing for easy integration with various frontend technologies. Make sure they are well documented—nobody wants to decipher a mystery novel when troubleshooting! Database Management Your database is like the secret ingredient in grandma's famous recipe: critical and best kept organized. Choose a robust database system like PostgreSQL or MongoDB, and structure it to easily handle user data, product inventories, and order histories. Implement efficient query mechanisms and think about scalability; you’ll want your database to keep pace as your user base grows—because nobody enjoys a slow checkout process! Implementing Payment and Delivery Systems Choosing Payment Gateways Pick your payment gateway like you'd choose a partner for a three-legged race—strong, reliable, and able to get you through the finish line without tripping. Popular choices include Stripe, PayPal, and Square. Ensure they offer features like fraud protection, multiple payment options, and easy integration into your app. A seamless payment experience means happy customers—and happy customers mean repeat business! Delivery Logistics Solutions Now it’s time to tackle delivery logistics, which can be trickier than finding a parking spot at a busy grocery store. You can either partner with third-party delivery services like DoorDash or Uber Eats, or manage deliveries in-house. Evaluate each option based on cost, coverage, and reliability. Whatever route you choose, make sure you create a system that delivers groceries as fast as the speed of light—or at least faster than a sloth. Order Tracking Features Order tracking features are like the GPS for your grocery delivery app—customers want to know where their groceries are at all times! Implement real-time tracking so users can see their order status and estimated delivery times. Consider sending notifications (without going overboard) when their order is out for delivery or if there’s a hiccup along the way. Everyone loves a little heads-up! Testing and Launching Your App Types of Testing Testing is like taste-testing a new recipe—absolutely essential! Start with unit testing to ensure each component works as intended. Then move on to integration testing, functional testing, and user acceptance testing, making sure everything avoids the culinary disaster zone. Perform load testing, too, to prepare for that sweet rush of customers when you go live. Beta Launch Strategies Beta launches are your app’s time to shine (or get a reality check). Start with a closed beta, inviting a select group of users to test the app and provide feedback. After addressing any major issues, roll out to an open beta, but keep the audience small enough to manage. This phase is key for ironing out kinks and ensuring your grocery delivery service is ready for the big leagues! Gathering User Feedback Receiving feedback is like attending a friend’s dinner party—you never fully know what you’re walking into! Use surveys, social media, and in-app prompts to gather user insights. Analyze this feedback with an open mind, and be sure to make necessary adjustments based on what users loved (and hated). title: About Teaching
abstract: Observe the typical seating arrangements for grand rounds or the weekly departmental teaching conference. The very senior physicians and those who are retired sit in the front rows (presumably for better hearing and vision as those faculties begin to fade). Chief residents and senior residents are in the middle, while at the very back are the first year residents and medical students. It is a seating arrangement based on straightforward fear. Typically after the case presentations, the discussion is led by the professor, who often fires factual questions at individuals in the audience. If the professor is challenged as to the effectiveness of this approach, he or she would probably explain this tactic as use of the Socratic method, but this is often patently untrue. Socrates asked questions of his students to stimulate them to reason with the facts, not simply to find out if they knew the facts. The senior physicians and retirees are not attacked out of courtesy. Attendees who know the most facts have less to fear and therefore sit closer to the front, where they might be noticed by the professor. Those who know the least sit at the back and hope to avoid notice. There are two things that make this sort of confrontational teaching painful, not only for the hapless student who doesn’t know the fact but also for the rest of the audience who must witness it. First is the pain of seeing someone undergoing grueling embarrassment in public, and second is the tremendous waste of everyone’s time. As the question goes unanswered, and the student is left to twist slowly in the wind, the rest of us wait, and wait, and wait. Even if the student knows the right answer, it is often reduced to an inaudible mumble because the student fears being pilloried if he or she is wrong. It is clear that during this time no teaching is going on, and it is a rank discourtesy to all those present. As a first year medical student, I had the dubious fortune to draw the chairman of the Yale Department of Physiology, Professor C. N. H. Long, as my quiz section instructor. We students were at first fearful and a bit awed to find ourselves dealing with the professor himself at close quarters, but we soon came to realize we were the lucky ones. As an example of his style, consider this kind of question he once asked the class: “What is the main stimulus to breathe?” Someone said, “Low oxygen.” The rest of us felt we had an idiot among us, but Long replied, “Well, yes, a low oxygen level in the inspired air is a stimulus to breathe, but it is not very strong. I should have emphasized more that I was looking for the chief stimulus, which is carbon dioxide.” Superficially, that exchange is not very remarkable, but I would urge a closer look. Dr. Long was Oxford trained, professor and chairman of the department, a former dean of the medical school, and a member of the National Research Council. He was obviously not a man who had to suffer fools gladly, but he was a true gentleman, and extraordinarily kind in not snapping out quick put-downs or using sarcasm or a derisive tone of voice. Further analysis reveals that he even suggested he was partly to blame for the student’s failure to have the right answer by implying that it was the way he asked the question. In the case above, the student was dull or unprepared, and Dr. Long’s question was unambiguous, but Long never seemed to lose sight of the fact that the whole purpose of the quiz section was to teach, not solely to probe weaknesses in the students’ preparation. He did not hesitate to give the right answer immediately when it was not forthcoming from the class. The quicker we had the correct facts, the more time we would have to discuss their implications. His quiz sections were a joy to attend. If one made a mistake, one was never attacked or made to look incompetent. Dr. Long never implied that we shouldn’t read the textbook, but he felt that if you missed a fact in the text, it wasn’t necessarily bad if the professor told you the right answer. If a student did not have the right answer, the student embarrassed himself, but the teacher did not also embarrass him. Those of us who teach in medical schools have no formal training in the art or science of teaching, and there is no requirement to take a medical education major or the education courses required of public school teachers before we attempt to transfer our knowledge to students. For those on the receiving end, it is a matter of luck if they get an effective teacher or a poor one. I have made a few observations over nearly 45 years of clinical teaching (and having many mentors myself). Drawing on my experience with Dr. Long and others like him, I try to avoid inciting fear in my students. No question is foolish. If I ask the class a question of fact or even of reasoning and the answer is not forthcoming within 5 to 6 seconds, I either give the answer or give additional clues. I try to avoid showing impatience or giving the answer derisively. What good does that do, other than discourage class participation? If you actually time 6 seconds, it is surprising how long it is. For the student who doesn’t know the answer, it is a seeming eternity. When a student gives the wrong answer, I try to find part of it that would make sense under certain circumstances, and suggest that that was what the student was thinking. This is not wasted time but is as useful as running down the pros and cons of a differential diagnosis. There are lazy, inept, and poorly prepared students. Conclusions about the student can be drawn from his or her participation or performance in rounds or the operating room. The student must obviously be made aware when he or she is not performing up to standard. However, lectures, grand rounds, the operating room, and the bedside are not the proper venues to make known one’s negative judgment of the student. This should be accomplished privately in the office, where one can ask questions to determine whether there are emotional or situational factors involved in the lack of performance. Instead of being a simple “chewing out,” it can also let students know you care, and they may redouble their efforts to please. I have often wondered why the confrontational approach is encountered so often in the teaching of medicine. It is an obvious ego trip for the teacher, be he a clinical instructor or the departmental chair. Being able to easily demonstrate one’s own vast knowledge compared with another’s is always ego boosting. Some view it as a necessary tactic to make students stingingly aware that they must know all the facts. The practice of medicine and surgery is, after all, a life and death business, with no place for sloth. On a more subtle level, many probably justify it by thinking, “I remember having it done to me and that is how I learned, so I’ll do it to my students.” I have observed that good teachers often illustrate key facts with colorful or memorable case histories to provide “hooks” on which to hang the facts. This is a very effective technique when many facts are being brought out at once. It reduces confusion and reinforces long-term memory. There is an immense amount of material to learn in the practice of medicine. It has always been taught by individuals without specific teaching credentials. Nevertheless, some outstanding teachers who have never taken an education course have mentored me over the years. Formal education credentialing is not necessarily a requirement. On the other hand, it is worthwhile to point out some of the basic elements that make for effective teaching. My hope is that this essay can, in part, contribute to that end.

title: So, You Followed Your Husband to Hadley – Lake Lennucks and He Still Won't Take You to the Animal Emporium?
abstract: Listen, girl, Hadley – Lake Lennucks isn't exactly a place twentysomethings flock to. As your new husband surely knew when he proposed this move, most people your age are moving to the big city, not away from it. But that doesn't mean you have to feel like you're stuck living in the old folks’ home.Hadley – Lake Lennucks is one of the Adirondacks’ top tourist towns, which means there's plenty to get up to. We've got hiking, swimming, rafting, tea rooms, arcades, Victorian photo parlors, a spa — even a river cruise. Whatever you want, you can do, including checking out all the amazing animals at our local big cat zoo: Boyd's Corner's Exotic Animal Emporium. How many times did your man sell you on a date here, back before you two actually moved?But if your man seems intent on sitting around like a bump on a log, you may start wondering why you two moved all the way out here in the first place. After all, back in the big city, couch-potatoing was the only thing you guys could afford to do.So, if your man refuses to pop the only question that matters — “Hey, babe, want to go to the Animal Emporium today?” — here are a few ideas to get you both moving in the same direction (toward Boyd's Corner, obviously).After all, maybe your new husband feels bad that you dropped literally everything — your three-bedroom (and both roommates) in Flatbush, your budding career as a vintage lounge singer, your friends, your volunteer work, your city-based hobbies. Meanwhile, he had everything literally handed to him the moment he agreed to move back to his hometown — his job at the family restaurant, a cute little fixer-upper house, a secondhand BMW, even — by his Monopoly Man father and the entire extended Montague family.Yeah, maybe he does feel bad. Bad that all his promises have so far come to nothing. “Oh, you'll make friends so easily!” With whom? There's no one your age to befriend! “You'll get a singing job in no time!” Yeah, at his dad's Food Event, but who the fuck else in Warren County is looking for lounge acts? Why can't nepotism help you too? “We'll spend so much time together — we'll do so many new things. Hiking. Scenic mountain drives. Tubing. Whitewater rafting. Hell, I'll take you to the Animal Emporium. You'll love the Animal Emporium,” he said. But will you? You wouldn't know, now would you?No, no. You're being unfair. You agreed to this move. You wanted this move. And you know the house and car were handed to you, too. So . . . okay, tone it down a notch. Maybe ask him about himself. How's he doing? You two have been here for only six months now. Is he feeling unsettled? After all, home renovations aren't easy — and while, yeah, you're doing most of the metaphorical heavy lifting, you can't do everything (including actual heavy lifting) and he often comes home from work just to roll into doing more work. Aren't you supposed to have dinner waiting on the table for him or something? Maybe a more experienced wife — one who has been a wife for longer than six months and that one week spent honeymooning across France on Daddy Montague's dime — would know how to do this without both a properly functioning stove and a kitchen table. But hey, he brings leftover food home with him every night from the Food Event. Maybe he's tired of filet mignon and lobster mac and cheese?Nope. You're being unfair again. Maybe he's overwhelmed working for his dad. Managing a restaurant's finances — and stock, and catering, and special events — probably isn't easy, and his dad has been talking about opening a second location recently.Ask him if it's hard being back in his hometown again. Maybe what for you is a step forward is for him a step back in time. He's got friends he grew up with here — some of whom have never left — and you've seen how he struggles to talk to them sometimes, how he falls back into old thought and speech patterns and then turns to you, startled, because he never thinks of himself as a “bro” — a “Broseph,” a “Broleo” — with you. His grandma still pinches his cheeks, even though he's nearly thirty, and his mom talks to him sometimes like he's five — “Leo, baby, you gotta stop leaving your water cups all over the house” — and sometimes like he's fifty — “Leonardo Luca, why haven't you set up your retirement account yet? What's your beautiful wife gonna say when you're sixty-five and can't afford to retire?”That's gotta be frustrating, right? You're frustrated by it, and you're just the “beautiful wife.”Or, you know, maybe he's just a butthole who thinks now you're married, he doesn't have to take you on dates.Okay, so maybe he's overwhelmed and needs a break. He's too tired to plan a date, but you're no trad wife. You can do it, can't you?Buy tickets online — maybe splurge for the Sloth Encounter (it's for four people, but it'll still be fun with just two!). The website says plan to stay several hours or so, and to avoid the crowds, get there when they open at ten — which means plenty of time to head up to the Traveler's Rest for a nice lunch (that, you know, isn't the Food Event). He'll still have the whole afternoon to himself.Then, on Saturday morning, just tell him to get ready — you have a surprise planned. Everybody loves a surprise, right?So, okay, he refuses to go. Has plans already with his parents, and insists he can't cancel. Even though he was stuck at the Food Event till well past closing last night; his dad, on a whim, wouldn't let anyone leave till the walk-in freezer was deep-cleaned.But, girl, you can still go by yourself. The tickets are still valid. He isn't stopping you; he just can't (or won't) come. Get brave and get going. The Animal Emporium awaits!Yeah, you've heard the stories of Hadley – Lake Lennucks's rival tourist attractions — Haight's Corner and his Rollercoaster and Thrill Park, versus Boyd's Corner's big cat zoo. How they're situated on opposite, otherwise isolated hills. How Boyd and Haight built their empires to spite each other — and now everyone in the sister towns has their favorite, which they cling to (half in jest) to fuel that rivalry. And maybe you'd like to weigh in, and have an opinion, and be a part of this stupid feud, too. It's no fun being left on the outside of a long-running, town-wide inside joke.But what's more, you could never have afforded these tickets in the city, let alone the added extras. And even if you could have paid your own way, not one of your friends would have gone with you. You'd follow them all the way to Brooklyn, or the Bronx, for happy hour pricing, but in all the time you lived there, they couldn't be assed to go a block out of their way for a museum or a park or any new thing you wanted to do — something that just maybe, if you tried it, would mean something to you.They'd laugh at you now, if they knew what you were up to.When you park the BMW, odds are good you're going to be like “What the fuck?” Because of this feud — the hype around these institutions — you're probably going to be expecting, you know, a zoo, not a dirt parking lot and a dinky path past some ramshackle sheds. Yep, it looks like someone's backyard, and dollars to donuts you're going to wonder if you're about to be a witness to obvious animal abuse. Maybe this is why Leo hasn't wanted to take you, once push came to shove — because how are you gonna look at him, and your new town, the same again knowing they're all complicit in rampant animal abuse?But listen. They already have your money. Why not just show your e-ticket to the yawning man working the turnstile? If it's as bad as you fear, you can leave. Besides, if you need to file a complaint with the ASPCA or wherever, it's best they know what they're dealing with.Doubled-up chain-link fences enclose “habitats” the size of your postage-stamp backyard, and restless big cats pace along them. You're the only one here, and the tigers huff, as if to say they will not be your tourist attraction. In a cage near the entrance, some kind of sickly looking dogs — dingoes, maybe — trudge back to their plywood den. The only sign tells you not to feed them — though with what? And why would you? — because they're under veterinary care. And no wonder they're ailing, wasting away, with their only company the geese and drooping peacocks and buzzards roosting overhead in the trees.In the adjacent row, over the duck pond and past the shell-scarred and shambling tortoise, a baboon shrieks and rattles its confines, and this sign warns you not to make eye contact. These creatures, it says, become easily agitated and quick to take offense — and who wouldn't be, when they're meant, by nature, to live not down here, stuck with man, but high among the branches and leaves?Go ahead: Think about shrieking, too — just like you did on the drive over here.Instead, you're drawn to a tucked-away glass enclosure, near the vending machines, and the tiny sun-colored tiger hobbling within upon a narrow, slatted boardwalk. There's something wrong with her back legs, her hips dropped low to the ground, her stricken tail quivering.“What have they done to you?” you ask, this poor trapped soul, stuck behind glass and then ignored. Left to wallow and founder, broken by her years bound in by the narrow perimeters of Hadley – Lake Lennucks.You turn to go. They can keep your money — and choke on it.A teen in a bright-red shirt comes bouncing up, beaming a golden grin. He introduces himself as Cox, this year's intern, and laughs, and slips through a door into the enclosure. Bouncing still, he tells you about this tiger, named Edith, to whom he beckons, and she — miraculously — limps right on over, to rub her cheek against his fingers, and — you're flummoxed — you think she even purrs.You've never heard a tiger purr before, you say, or seen one this up close, cuddling a zookeeper and ready to play. Tigers can't “purr,” he corrects you, as she thumps to the floor of her enclosure, and asks, inexplicably, for belly rubs. But rather, they “chuff,” in which they blow shortly through their nose, often lifting their head; a greeting, a comfort, a sound of joy. Stroking her red-striped stomach, he tells you she's a Golden Tabby Bengal, and like the famed white tigers, this gentle sunburst color is due to a recessive gene.You stand there, clutching your little park map, and she rolls over and hops, heavily, her back legs dragging, back onto the plank trail. The teen says she limps and hobbles because she lived the first years of her life in a backyard cage, under someone's porch — because someone thought, as you have, in daydreams, that a tiger would make a great pet, and then actually went out and had to learn the hard way.“Mr. Boyd rescued her,” he says; he blows her a kiss as he steps back through the door and bolts it. “He rescued all of them. We're the number one wildlife sanctuary upstate. This here's Dumas,” he says, pointing, and just like that, you're on his tour. “Our ti-liger.” A cross between a tiger and a liger (already tiger and lion), and a victim of irresponsible breeding.There are Barbary Lions brought back from the edge of extinction, and white tigers rescued from photo op companies; even the dogs at the entrance — New Guinea Singing Dogs — came from another zoo, forced to close its gates. Big cats play with cardboard boxes — soaked in donated perfumes and essential oils; “enrichment” he calls it, and most enclosures hold more than one. The white-handed gibbon habitat boasts homemade bunting and paper ribbon, a sign that reads Happy Birthday, George & Eliot. He says they're hosting a party at noon and invites you to join; you can buy a feed cup in the gift shop, he says, and throw them “a confetti” of peanuts.“Look there,” he says, of a little double-wide at the corner of the property. “That's where Boyd lives, with his son, Ranlo. I know a lot of guests think we look sketchy as hell, but that's only because Mr. Boyd spends every penny we earn on the animals, not aesthetics. One leopard came to us with a severely broken leg — we thought it'd have to be amputated, maybe even put the poor thing down. But Boyd took care of him day and night and hired a specialist with the funds earmarked for repaving the parking lot; heck, I think Ranlo even offered to dip into his college fund.”“Did it survive?” you ask. “Did it keep its leg?”“Oh yeah,” Cox says, and changes course. “He's right over here — Dostoyevsky.” He's cozily snoozing against his glass windowpane, all four of his legs in the air. “We're like a big family, here. Us and the animals,” he says, and you feel it — this place that is not the prison you first thought, but a home. A chance at a new and better life.They don't let you do the Sloth Encounter alone. You and Cox are joined by the man who'd been working the ticket booth — and this, you learn is Boyd himself — and a bevy of volunteers, bored while the park has slowed, post-season, and they all laugh with you as you coo at the little sloth hanging upside down from a rope line, and they pet his bristly fur with you and snap photos with your phone and swap stories of zookeeping wins and woes.And you remember now why you left the city — why you're so glad you did. You could never have had this in the city — not you — because, even if, magically, you and your friends had been able to go, and to make it past the parking lot, and the shabby structures, not one of them would have had a kind word to say about any of it. Not about Cox, nor about Edith the chuffing tiger, not even this contented, leisurely sloth, unhurriedly accepting your proffered watermelon, and munching. They were so relentlessly negative, in the city, and never wanted to try new things.And, you know, you became a naysayer there, too.“Are you looking for new volunteers?” you ask.You go home singing. You sing for the first time in months, excepting prime rib nights at the Food Event. They are always looking for new volunteers.Your husband emerges from the dining room smiling, happy to see you so happy.“How did it go?” he asks, and then his gaze drops, to the plastic feed cup you brought home as a souvenir. His smile, too, drops when recognizes the emblazoned logo: the big cats prowling the bridge above the River Ames.“Your surprise was the Animal Emporium?” he asks, his composure breaking.You nod and add, “And the Sloth Encounter.” But you don't say it shittily — rather, earnestly, gleefully, so eager are you to tell him all about it. The names of the animals and their stories and the kindness of the volunteers — complete strangers — and their enthusiasm for your enthusiasm and how you think you just might want to volunteer, too.He tells you that's great, that he's so glad you had such a good time, that you should volunteer if that's something you'd like to do, and you hug him and he hugs you. But, you notice, he won't quite meet your eye, and when he thinks you're not looking, the corners of his mouth pull down.“What did you and your parents do today?” you ask — again, not bitchily; you do want to know. And that's when you hear the fumbling in the unpacked dining room, and the footsteps, and:“Leo, baby, what's taking so long? Honey,” your mother-in-law appears and says to you, “come on in!
