title: Notes on Contributors
abstract: Francesca de Lucia holds a master's degree from the University of Geneva, Switzerland, and a PhD from the University of Oxford, UK. She was an associate professor at Zhejiang Normal University, Jinhua, China, and has taught at Minzu University of China, Beijing. She is the author of Italian American Cultural Fictions: From Diaspora to Globalization (Peter Lang, 2017) and of articles on different aspects of ethnicity and American identity in literature, including “Ethnic Investigations of the American Crime Scene: Comparing Domenic Stansberry and George Pelecanos” (2022).Joe De Quattro's fiction is published in a number of literary magazines and has received nominations for the Pushcart Prize as well as The Best American Short Stories. He is a lecturer in writing at the University of California, Berkeley.Gerald R. Gems is a professor emeritus at North Central College in Naperville, Illinois. He is a past president of the North American Society for Sport History, past vice-president of the International Society for the History of Physical Education and Sport, and a Fulbright Scholar. He has authored or edited more than 250 publications, including thirty-one books.Roland Merullo is the author of twenty-eight books and the recipient of numerous prizes, including Massachusetts Book Awards in both fiction and nonfiction. His books have sold over half a million copies and have been translated into twelve languages. He's made sixteen trips to Italy for both business and pleasure and has set several of his novels there, including a trilogy of World War II historical fiction. His most recent novel is Dessert with Buddha. He can be reached via his website, RolandMerullo.com.Robert J. Romano, JD, LLM, is an assistant professor of sport management at St. John's University where he writes on various sport law and sport history topics. He is of Italian descent on his father's side. His great-grandfather Raffaele Romano, a tailor, emigrated from the town of Scafati, Italy, to New York City around the year 1911.Featured Poet Gerry LaFemina's most recent books are After the War for Independence (poetry, Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2023) and The Pursuit: A Meditation on Happiness (creative nonfiction, Madville, 2021). His previous books include a novel, a collection of short stories, and over a dozen poetry titles. He's served on the board of directors of the Association of Writers & Writing Programs, edited numerous literary journals and anthologies, and founded the Center for Literary Arts at Frostburg State University, where he is a professor of English. He also serves as a mentor in the MFA program at Carlow University and is a current Fulbright Specialist in Writing, Literature, and American Culture.David Albano is a joyful dad because his children love stories, poetry, and pizza as much as he does. His poetry appeared in Italian Americana once before. He has taught literature in a variety of places—from Malawi to the Navajo Nation—and to a variety of students. His favorite place to teach is under a tarp in a thunderstorm on a canoe trip.Joel Allegretti is the author of, most recently, Platypus (NYQ Books, 2017), a collection of poems, prose, and performance texts, and Our Dolphin (Thrice Publishing, 2016), a novella. He is the editor of Rabbit Ears: TV Poems (NYQ Books, 2015). The Boston Globe called Rabbit Ears “cleverly edited” and “a smart exploration of the many, many meanings of TV.”Gabriella M. Belfiglio is an Italian American, queer artist, and activist in Brooklyn, New York. She's a winner of the W. B. Yeats award and is a Saltonstall fellow. Her work has been published widely—including in The Centrifugal Eye, Folio, Avanti Popolo, Poetic Voices without Borders, Lambda Literary Review, and The Paterson Review. She's part of the poet trio, The Ferlinghetti Girls, with Paola Corso and Phyllis Capello.Grace Cavalieri was Maryland's tenth Poet Laureate. She's written several books and chapbooks of poetry, plus short-form and full-length plays. Her newest poetry publication is The Long Game (2023). Her latest play was “Quilting the Sun” (NYC's Theatre for the New City, 2019). Grace founded and still produces “The Poet and the Poem” on public radio and podcasts, celebrating forty-six years on-air in 2023, now recorded at the Library of Congress.Marc Alan Di Martino (translator) is the author of the collections Love Poem with Pomegranate, Still Life with City, and Unburial. His work appears widely and has been nominated for the Pushcart Prize and Best of the Net. His translation Day Lasts Forever: Selected Poems of Mario dell'Arco will be published by World Poetry Books in 2024. Find him at marcalandimartino.com.Though his last name, Glaser, doesn't reflect it, Elton Glaser is descended from his paternal grandmother, Josephine Lala, whose parents came from Sicily. All the cultural traditions in the family, especially concerning food, were distinctly Italian. Glaser has published eight full-length collections of poetry. A new book, Ghost Variations, was published by the University of Pittsburgh Press in October 2023.Bart Mallio has just published his first volume of poetry, Out on the Rim of the Now, via Damianos Publishing and Silver Street Media. He studied Chinese history and English literature at Bowdoin College, and he lives on Long Island with his wife and cats. Days, he works as a computer network defender; nights, he writes poetry and listens to jazz.David Masello writes about art and culture and is currently Executive Editor of Milieu, a national print magazine about design and architecture. Many of his short plays have been performed by theatre companies in New York and Los Angeles, and his essays, poems, and features have appeared in many publications and anthologies, including The New York Times and Best American Essays (multiple editions). His website is davidmasello.com.Susan Tekulve's newest book is Second Shift: Essays. She's the author of In the Garden of Stone, winner of the South Carolina Novel Prize and a Gold IPPY Award. She's also published two short story collections: Savage Pilgrims and My Mother's War Stories. Her poems, short stories, and essays have appeared in journals such as The Georgia Review, The Louisville Review, and Shenandoah.

title: Noir II – the art of murder
abstract: Red Fox was parked in a plaid, upholstered lounge chair under the flare of a lobby light like a sample on a confocal stage and gave me the nose-to-toe before flashing her dazzling smile. “Hiya, Mole,” she said. “You look terrible.” “Yeh, crummy beds in this half star hotel,” I retorted, not as wittily as I would have liked, “and you look whatever the polar opposite of terrible is.”If you are just joining us, we were talking about the very noir process of reviewing, that thing we scientists do and have done to us, complain endlessly about when it goes the wrong way on our end, and then use to get a bit of schaudenfreude when we do it. And we do it for free, because the tens of millions of semolians the publishers earn through subscriptions, page charges, and advertising is all used up in the high cost of electrons on line (or something). We talked about reviewing papers (in black and white with shadows and low camera angles), but today RF and I were not here to do that. We were reviewing grants.Along with RF and yours truly, there were 25 of us holed up in this shabby, over-priced hotel where we had sherpa'd our bags, fetched our key cards after initialing here, here, and sign here, dropped our cargo into our respective rooms (my light was out and the shower had been new in 1990), and met in the hotel bar (nothing on tap) to drink away our pain, and prepared for this morning in the hotel ‘conference room.’ “Ready?” said the Fox, and we walked into the room together (should have brought a java, I had forgotten that it isn't supplied), at five minutes to eight. In the freakin’ morning.The pleasantries started as usual. We introduced ourselves. There was The Rat, Salamander from Chicago, Big Squirrel, Little Gorilla, Sloth Three-Toes from the Bay, and a woman they just called Carnivore. And there, at the head of the table, was Frog, who snatched flies out of the air as he smiled at the assembly. We were there to do a killing, although only some of us knew it. But what they didn't know was that RF and I were there to see to it that it didn't happen. It was Study Section, grants panel, review committee. A Consortium of Murder. But not today.“Scores!” shouted Frog, as we were off and running. Three reviewers perked up to answer, while twenty other pairs of peepers returned to their e-mails. “One,” said Cricket, with a chirp. “One,” agreed Panda the Chemist, all smiles. “Four,” countered Chameleon, turning red. And there it was. You see, the scores are the scores, the lower the better, and they generally don't change very much from the preliminary to the final. One is as good as it gets. Four, well, see ya next time, ya mook.Cricket and then Panda made their cases, briefing us on the basic plan and their “score drivers,” those positive and negative bits of arcana that pushed their numbers around. The grant before us was innovative, creative, strongly supported by preliminary data, and had the potential to change the way we think about a small but important corner of our biomedical universe. “And it was a pleasure to read,” concluded Panda. We turned to Chameleon. At least those of us who weren't immersed in our laptops.He took a hard look at each of us, his eyes pivoting around the table as he savored his moment. “I disagree,” he said. The Rat made a yipping sound, the Carnivore licked her lips. “I found it diffuse and overly ambitious,” Chameleon continued. “In one aim alone an analysis is proposed for 60 cell lines, with extensive validation and testing,” he paused for effect, “in vivo.” He slammed in the blade with a killing stroke. “I'm tempted to move my score to six, four was too generous.” He sat back, dangling the baited hook, and looked back at his adversaries.“Well,” returned Cricket, taking it line and sinker. “It is ambitious.” Panda, her smile fading, added, “And the assays, while rigorous and sophisticated, are not simple. Figure twenty three is a bit blurry, and the applicant could have added more data.”In study section in my country, we review in order of the average preliminary scores, starting with the best, and discuss them until we've covered about half of them (the rest are ND, ‘not discussed’). Most tend to cluster around the threes and fours; good, but not good enough. Close only counts, as they say, in horse shoes and hand grenades, and we weren't playing gin rummy. This was high stakes poker, and Chameleon's hand was winning. Frog looked at him, then at the group. “This grant is open for discussion.”There are rules. Anyone around the table who hadn't read the grant (since they had so many of their own assignments to read) could ask questions of the reviewers, but could not offer opinions. This one was already fitted with cement overshoes, and once the discussion was over and the final scores stated, it would be dropped into the river to be nibbled by fishes. But not just yet. I could feel RF's big green eyes on the side of my head, and I cleared my throat.“I wasn't a reviewer,” I started, “but I did read this grant carefully.” I saw Chameleon not-smile. “The proposal is focused, but expansive, not diffuse.” I warmed up. “And yes, it is ambitious,” I leaned towards Cricket, “but when did we decide that research shouldn't be ambitous? It is only overly so when we think that the applicant cannot actually do it, and this one has clearly shown us that she can. Her publications show it, her data show it, and I know I want her to move the field forward. I think you, and you,” looking at Panda, “would like to see her do it, too.” I saw them each nod, and I sat back, giving Red Fox her opening. She leaped into it.“Like Mole, I also read this grant, and it is amazing. The applicant should get to work doing the research, not rewriting the application.” Red Fox was on a roll, supporting my argument, and turning the tide. “I wish we had more ambitious proposals like this one.” Now there were nods around the table. “Okay,” said Frog, “final scores please.”“I'll stay with one,” said Cricket, and I gave an inward sigh of relief. Too often the tendency is to slide to the halfway point, killing fortune. “One,” agreed Panda, assertively. Chameleon had turned a pale blue. “Well,” he said, looking down, “I could move to a three.”“Wait,” countered Red Fox, “you didn't make your case, you can do better.”“No,” returned Chameleon, “I gave it a four, I can't go lower than three.”“Yes, you can,” said RF.“Fine,” Chameleon relented. “Two.” We had foiled a crime, and nobody outside of the room would know it.Our job in reviewing grants is not to find reasons not to support outstanding research efforts, but to find ways to point out the best work and ensure it proceeds. An ambitious project that will be done is far better than a cautious proposal that advances the field incrementally. Our colleagues, experienced in the ways of grant review mishaps often advise us to be ‘safe.’ But those of us who want to see great things happen in this enterprise in which we travel together have to push back. If you happen to be reviewing grants, Red Fox and I implore you to read the grants you weren't assigned if they show promising but disparate preliminary scores (we get to see these some days before the formal session), and weigh into the discussion. It is the only way to turn us back from the cautious, safe path to take some chances on the great projects with longer odds.Today, RF and I will have some chances to do this, winning some and losing many. We had decided in advance to read a few grants we hadn't been assigned and argue if we disagreed with the way the discussion was going. Maybe next time, a few others will join us. Perhaps even you. After a very long day, tonight we will drink bubbly drinks and maybe watch what promises to be a nice sunset over the buildings of Bethesda.

title: Next chapter for Veterinary Medicine and Science
abstract: Veterinary Medicine and Science launched in 2014 as an online, peer-reviewed, open access, truly international journal covering all aspects of veterinary science. The latter statement could not be more correct…..the journal accepts articles on all species and in my short time of accepting articles I have overseen ones on the species you would expect (dogs, cats, cattle, pigs, poultry, horses) all the way to rail (small to medium-sized, ground-dwelling birds) and pangolins. We look forward to this breadth of species submitted to the journal to continue. The journal has become established over the last five years under the leadership of Professor Ed Hall, as Editor-in-Chief, an extensive group of Associate Editors and an experienced Editorial Board. They have worked tirelessly to publish over 100 original articles, reviews and case reports over this time and deserve thanks from all. VMS has been accepted for indexing in the Science Citation Index Expanded (SCIE), and therefore the journal will receive its first Impact Factor in 2019. This will be a testament to and based on the work of Ed and his team. My vision for the next three years will be to build upon this benchmark. I completed a large animal (food animal and equine) internal medicine and emergency and critical care residencies at the Royal Veterinary College, London. I am also an associate diplomate of the European College of Veterinary Diagnostic Imaging primarily for my interest and publications in food animal ultrasonography and hold an RCVS certificate in veterinary anaesthesia. My interests and clinical expertise thus encompass several species and areas, which I hope will be an asset to the journal. However, one person cannot manage the number and breadth of articles submitted alone. As such, a small, select, species-specific group of Associate Editors have been selected, and I would like to thank them all for the work that they have done so far and for what is to come. Professor Mark Bowen is staying on from the original Associate Editor team to handle equine, internal medicine and education submissions. The new Associate Editors are Prof Markus Freick, HTW Dresden, who will be managing reproductive and food animal papers and is our European representative; Dr Chris Luby, University of Saskatchewan who will also manage food animal papers and be the North American representative; Dr Cara Hallowell-Evans, based in private practice in the UK, will be managing exotic animal papers; Dr Katie Nash, based in private practice (VETMED) in Arizona, will handle the small animal papers; she also brings expertise from her time spent growing up and practising in Australia; Dr Mark White, who is a pig consultant based in the UK, who will manage the porcine papers and Dr Will Garton, who leads the Avivet poultry and gamebird team in the UK, will manage the poultry papers. Hopefully, this breadth of experience and geographical variety will provide support to authors in all areas of veterinary science from across the globe. Veterinary Medicine and Science aims to publish good quality articles from all aspects of veterinary science. One of the unique selling features of this journal is that it aims to publish sound science, where research integrity and ‘technical quality’ are more important than novelty or perceived (citation) impact. The editorial team aims to support authors to ensure science is published and are looking for reasons why an article could be accepted rather than rejected. We aim to work closely with authors to help revise their manuscript, with the assistance of reviewers, into a format suitable for publication. We are accepting original articles, reviews and also case reports. Case reports have been accepted by the journal previously, but we hope more will be submitted in the future. Many journals have stopped accepting case reports unless they are very novel or are a case series, which in my opinion limits the dissemination of unusual cases or case presentations to the veterinary community. Case reports are also a publication option or requirement for many professional qualifications, and there is a dearth of options of where to publish these; we hope that VMS will become that ‘go-to’ journal for many. VMS is a truly international journal accepting articles from all over the globe. It receives many articles from the United States, Africa and the Far East. We hope that with the support from the editorial team and with the acquisition of an Impact Factor in 2019 that this journal will also have appeal to currently under-represented regions such as Europe. Lastly, the journal would not be able to exist without reviewers, and I wish to thank all those that have reviewed previously and those that will review in the future. I have only been in this role a short time, and before it, I had been an active and frequent reviewer, but had minimal editorial experience. Wiley has supported me regarding training and technical aspects that I need to become a productive and successful editor in chief. However, no-one but you can help me with the biggest challenge I face, and that is recruiting appropriate reviewers. As an author, I want my papers to pass swiftly through the review and publication process. This, however, cannot happen if no-one is willing to give up their time to review. Reviewing papers, as well as being an opportunity to give back, is also an educational experience and provides opportunities to identify limitations in other peoples’ research which should allow you to improve your studies and manuscripts and ensure that they need fewer revisions. I would, therefore, like to reach out to the research and veterinary community and particularly to anyone who has complained about how long their paper has been in review to accept requests to review. I hope that anyone who submits to VMS will be willing to review for us. Every paper I review, I learn more. I look forward to working with authors, Associate Editors and reviewers over the next three years and hope to be approachable and supportive of a broad scope of veterinary research and will be happy to help if I can.

title: Between Logic and the World: An Integrated Theory of Generics
abstract: Bernhard Nickel's Between Logic and the World looks at genericity, the phenomenon underlying what philosophers and linguists call generic statements. It is the first ever such book intended specifically for a philosophical audience, and we are long overdue for one.Intuitively, a generic statement is a loose generalization that can tolerate certain exceptions but still be true, such as:(1) a. Ravens are black. b. Rattlesnakes are poisonous.We know about albino ravens, and yet we still believe (1-a) to be true. We know that rattlesnakes sometimes have their poison glands removed, and yet that does not prompt us to reconsider whether (1-b) is true. So, somehow, a generic is a general statement that can allow for certain counterexamples, which is a bit of a mystery. And that puzzle is just the tip of the iceberg—although generic statements are utterly ubiquitous in everyday reasoning, it has been astonishingly difficult to pin down what exactly a person is saying when they utter one.Nickel's theory is impressively deep and sophisticated, and if I tried to present it in full, I doubt I would have the space to do anything else. So in the interest of plunging right into thinking about it, let us consider the following simplified version. His core idea is that generics make claims about what is normal for members of a kind. That makes (1-b) a statement about what is normal for rattlesnakes, however exactly we decide to cash that notion out.The first component Nickel adds onto the core idea is that there's no such thing as being normal simpliciter—rather, there is only such a thing as, for example, a normal raven or a normal snake. That seems intuitive, given that it's normal for snakes to have scales and for ravens to have feathers, but not for snakes to have feathers or for ravens to have scales. The second complication he introduces is that in addition to being relative to the kind of thing we're talking about, normality is also relative to a more general property. Thus, it becomes possible for the same entity to be normal in some ways but abnormal in others. For example, an albino raven is abnormal with respect to color, because it is white, but normal with respect to means of locomotion, because it has wings and can fly.Having thus introduced two parameters of variation into the notion of normality, Nickel proposes that generic statements involve a second-order existential quantification over ways of being normal. So a generic ‘As are F’ is true, modulo a few further details we are abstracting over, just in case:For some way of being a normal A with respect to a determinable of the property F, every A that is normal in that way is F.The view gets an unbelievable amount of mileage out of this second-order quantification. Going this route allows Nickel to explain why ‘Chickens lay eggs’ is true even though there is intuitively nothing abnormal about a rooster that can't lay eggs. It puts him in a good position to say why ‘Mosquitoes carry malaria’ can be true even when a vanishingly small percentage of mosquitoes are infectious. And it opens the door to an extensive discussion of how the generic construction ties into other well-studied semantic phenomena, such as plurals, free choice permission, and comparatives/equatives.Part 1 contains a detailed presentation of Nickel's semantic analysis, which is based on previous work published in both philosophy and linguistics settings. This section develops a view not just about the truth conditions of a generic, but about how those truth conditions are derived compositionally from the way the words in a generic statement are put together. This is especially welcome given that previous research on generics within both fields has often shied away from such details. Part 2 turns to an absolutely fascinating discussion of normality itself. In this section, the concept is defined in terms of families of questions that are proper to each area of study, families of strategies for answering them, and the causal mechanisms that an area of study can explain aspects of. The book concludes by using the discipline of linguistics itself as a case study in how families of explanatory strategies can evolve historically around a single worldly phenomenon, whatever the explainers' level of informedness or ignorance about the phenomenon may be.This is an important book along a number of key dimensions. One is that it serves a deep need in the profession. I am constantly hearing from curious parties in search of reading recommendations on generics. We find them intriguing because they seem to be the natural grammatical home for ceteris paribus hedges in scientific laws, they are the medium via which we teach children about biological kinds and their defining properties, and they seem to have something to do with how we form prejudices about social groups. Does our cultural preoccupation with what is normal or abnormal afford us a useful tool for understanding the natural world, or perhaps for understanding the social world? The literature on generics promises to help make inroads on these burning questions.Up until now, I have never been quite sure what to recommend to my colleagues, given how bewildering the literature within linguistics, computer science, and psychology can be even to specialists on the topic. But I am pleased to report that at long last, we have a book that fits the bill. Between Logic and the World serves admirably both as an overview written specifically for a general audience and as a detailed elaboration of Nickel's picture from both a semantic and a metaphysical vantage point.A more telling sign of its importance is that it reveals a way of doing natural language semantics that is distinctively philosophical. Nickel is as thorough in his semantic analysis as one could hope to be, having spent time steeping himself in the latest research on genericity, gradable adjectives, vagueness, loose talk, plurals, scalar implicature, and free choice permission. And although the analysis he offers will not appear at all foreign to an audience of linguists, the book does not read like a linguistics paper. It explores the topic with a view to explaining what kinds are, how different disciplines provide explanations, how explanatory purposes can vary from conversation to conversation, and whether there are objective facts about what explains what. The reason the book pours so much effort into compositional semantics is that doing so can help clarify which aspects of our truth-value judgments are tracking metaphysical phenomena and which aspects of our truth-value judgments are tracking other independent semantic phenomena.I think that is really the book's crowning achievement, amid a great number of original contributions. It shows that by paying careful attention to the workings of natural language constructions, we can isolate the intuitions we are having about genericity itself from the intuitions that arise out of the interaction between distinct linguistic phenomena. For instance, a close look at how the comparative construction works can show us why the statement ‘ravens are bigger than toasters’ is ascribing a characteristic size to ravens—not a characteristic size relative to toasters.Anyone who wants to give a unified semantics for generics that makes the right predictions about all the canonical examples is inevitably forced to make bold decisions, and Nickel is no exception. I would argue that the risks he takes in this regard pay off. The boldest decision, which I suspect is likely to garner resistance from certain quarters, is to give an account that validates the following inference rule:Kind Percolation:Let A, B be kinds where A is a subkind of B.Then if ‘As are F’ is true, ‘Bs are F’ is true.Kind percolation harks back to the left upward monotonicity of quantifiers like some or at least three, except that in lieu of the subset relation, the pattern is governed by the much more restrictive subkind relation. To take one example, the rule allows us to deduce (2-b) from (2-a):(2) a. Platypuses lay eggs. b. Mammals lay eggs.Although that sentence seems false—one would think that snakes or codfish were better candidates for being egg layers than mammals—Nickel thinks that it is true but seems false because it gives rise to a misleading quantity implicature. In other words, it is a bit like saying ‘Evelyn, Vivian, and Ashley came to the party’ when Whitney also came. You didn't technically say that nobody else came, but in most contexts, the person you were speaking to would assume that that was what you meant to suggest. Similarly, when you say ‘Mammals lay eggs,’ all you are literally saying is that for some way of being a reproductively normal mammal (in this case, the platypus way), every thus reproductively normal mammal lays eggs. You may be implicating that that is the only way of being a reproductively normal mammal, but the implication is defeasible.I don't find that part of the story particularly worrisome, because although our intuitions about these cases are somewhat elusive, Nickel has done all the necessary legwork. The theory is supported with ample linguistic evidence and a helpful appendix provides derivations to show how everything works at a lower level. Furthermore, the payoff of having a unified semantic analysis that uses this story about examples (2-a) and (2-b) to capture so many other data points is too substantial to be dismissed out of hand.That said, further investigation into the validity of kind percolation might still be warranted, especially when it comes to morally and politically charged examples. Consider the following pair:(3) a. White women are oppressed. b. White people are oppressed.If white women are a kind of white person, then the truth of example (3-a) plus kind percolation should imply example (3-b). And yet I can think of a lot of people who are willing to sign up for (3-a) without being willing to sign up for (3-b), and I'm not so sure that when they do, it's because (3-b) is a true statement bearing the misleading quantity implicature that (roughly) the only way of being a normally politically enfranchised white person is one that leads all of those white people to be oppressed.Another class of cases that poses questions about Nickel's analysis are what we might call ‘unintended effect’ generics, such as (4):(4) Clowns are creepy.People with coulrophobia, at least, would happily grant that (4) is true. But is there a way of being a normally emotion-eliciting clown such that every clown that is normal in that way is creepy? It is difficult to tell. I suppose I would have thought that the most obvious way to be a normally emotion-eliciting clown was to be funny. One option for Nickel might be to exploit the apparent assessment-sensitivity of predicates like creepy, and argue that this is another kind of interaction effect. Another might be to draw on the fact that he does not cash normality out in terms of an accessibility relation on possible worlds, the way most other theorists who take this approach do. This is a very interesting feature of his semantics. Each possible world just comes with its own ways of being normal, and that might make it easier to argue that there simply is a way of being a normally emotion-eliciting clown that leads to this result. Nevertheless, I find it hard to shake the feeling that some further effect is at play in this type of example, beyond the general tendency for a sentence that takes the form As are F to describe a way of being F-normal for an A.In any case, what is clear is that this book brings an incredible mass of seemingly heterogenous data under the scope of a single theory that is beautifully argued for, while providing a fleshed-out story about the metaphysics of normality to boot. What more could we ask for?

title: La Pastorela
abstract: El Teatro Campesino (ETC) is most well-known globally for their actos, short political satires that the company developed in support of the Delano grape strike (1965–70) and nationally for its groundbreaking Broadway production and subsequent Warner Brothers film, Zoot Suit (1981). However, at home in San Benito County and the surrounding Salinas and Silicon Valleys, the company is also revered for its rotating winter productions: the operatic miracle play La Virgen Del Tepeyac and La Pastorela were performed inside the Mission San Juan Bautista church. In 2019, a renovation of the Mission San Juan Bautista church forced ETC’s La Pastorela into their ninety-nine-seat playhouse. I was lucky enough to witness this beautiful and dynamic reimagining of La Pastorela in-the-round that year. The following year, the COVID-19 pandemic forced the cancellation of so much live performance across the globe, and the production staff at El Teatro Campesino recorded a radio version of La Virgen Del Tepeyac. La Pastorela is often presented bilingually, however, the true language of the live version is spectacle. There is spectacle, of course, in the staging of battles and angelic apparitions, but there is also a spectacle of community when gathered together in large numbers to view a production.In 2021, ETC transformed its long-running live version of La Pastorela and produced La Pastorela: A Spanish Radio Adaptation, which aired on local station KKUP (Cupertino, CA) at midnight on December 18, 2021. The choice to broadcast on the airwaves was an important gesture. Perhaps a reminder that although we can’t be together in person to marvel at the eloborately staged fights, beautiful costumes, and dynamic lights, we can still share stories. The radio drama and digital theatrical content has become an act of care in these times of great precarity.Radio and digital formats allow theatre companies including ETC to continue creating, this digital shift also allows ETC to fulfill its mission to “create vibrant community” without putting artists or audiences in harm’s way. The radio play was rebroadcast on National Latino Public Radio’s Radio Bilingüe on December 22, 2021. After these initial broadcasts, the show was uploaded to ETC’s Soundcloud account, where it was available from December 23 until January 6, 2022, which is the Catholic feast day of the Epiphany, or Three King’s Day.For ETC, the tradition of producing a nativity play goes back as far back as 1966, the year after founding artistic director Luis Valdez began creating actos on the picket lines of the Delano grape strike. In 1966, the company produced The Wakefield Mystery cycle play The Second Shepherds’ Play. ETC staged its first La Pastorela as a puppet show, which is how the play was first performed in the Americas. In 1977, La Pastorela returned to San Juan Bautista as a street pageant before its inaugural production in the Mission San Juan Bautista church. ETC’s La Pastorela also received a film adaptation in 1980 staring Linda Ronstadt and Cheech Marin. I trace this chronology in order to illuminate that, for ETC, this play has always had a genre malleability that various artistic teams have embraced across decades of the company’s history. While it may have been motivated by the constraints that COVID has placed on live performance, the 2021 La Pastorela: A Spanish Radio Adaptation is just one on a string of ETC-produced pastorelas that shift to meet the moment. This legacy of adaptation related to the pastorela tradition hemispherically can be traced back to the early adaptations mentioned above. While stories of shepherds in some relation to Christ’s nativity proliferate across Europe, it is not until the story of the nativity is deployed as part of the Catholic Church’s proselytizing efforts in Mexico that it begins to include the biblically out-of-place battle between heaven and hell. In the Bible, the nativity lives in the gospels of Matthew and Luke. The battle between Satan and the Archangel Saint Michael is only mentioned in the book of Revelation—never in conjunction with the Christ narrative.Generally, pastorela plays center the journey of a group of shepherds who end up caught in the battle between heaven and hell for the souls of humanity. Each adaptation also includes, omits or reimagines a variety of secondary narratives. In ETC’s adaptations, the plays inciting incident is Archangel San Miguel, voiced by long time company member Anita Reyes appearing to Gila (voiced by Sammy Cardoza), a young female shepherd early in the play. San Miguel sings “No Temais Pastores (Shephard’s have No Fear)” before announcing the birth of the Christ Child. Gila goes back to tell the rest of the shepherds, but while she was gone, the group has gained a member. A hermit, El Hermitaño (voiced by Ray Rios), has broken his solitude in the mountain caves after also having had a vision of Christ’s birth in a dream. The group is excited to welcome the Christ Child to the world, with the exception of Gila’s father, Bartolo (voiced by Daniel Valdez). Bartolo has succumb to a spell of the devil and is too lazy to start the journey. In this version, the shepherds sing a song, “En Belen Esta La Gloria (The Glory Is in Bethlehem),” and the spell is broken. The play marches on toward a climax through similar interactions. Satanas (voiced by Katrina D. Valdez), tries over and over again to tempt the shepherds and lead them astray; ultimately the spells cast by Satanas are broken, and the shepherds press on to Belen (Bethlehem). When Luzbel (voiced by Anahuac Valdez) finally becomes tired of Satanas’s missteps, he takes things into his own hands. Luzbel appears to the shepherds, interrupting their journey one last time to narrate the tragic passion of Christ’s crucifixion to the shepherds, emphasizing that this young king will die alone, wearing a crown of thorns, again, conveyed through a song, “Una Corona de Espinas (A Crown of Thorns).” At this point, the Archangel San Miguel intervenes with all of her angels, and the battle between heaven and hell ensues. Sonically, the battle is represented by layering the sounds of swords clashing, with instrumentation and narration that offers blow-by-blow commentary to craft a dynamic and exciting moment of radio narration. When the battle is over, San Miguel claims victory with a moving song that tells the shepherds to continue their journey. The shepherds make it safely to Bethlehem to offer humble gifts of song and well-wishes to the holy family. The story ends, but La Pastorela always includes an epilogue, a moment of direct address delivered by an ensemble member. In the epilogue, the actors wish the audience happy holiday season, a Merry Christmas, and a Happy New Year!The radio version deviates from the standard, scripted greeting, to offer listeners the following message: “Humanity is resilient. Our faith cannot be absent. My friends, please listen, search for your star, for the universe can save us. Continue on your journey; you will come to that happy Bethlehem with time. That is how we will achieve all of the good that is ours.” This final incantation reminds audience who might be listening in isolation or quarantine that even though the continuing COVID-19 pandemic makes it hard for people to come together, we can still be in cosmic community under the same stars, and through the airwaves, until we get through these challenging times.What struck me most about this production was the new ways the writing team, Kinan Valdez and Christy Sandoval, reimagined this story for 2021. The most immediately noticeable change is the addition of a narrator, who is tasked with the significant labor of translating the visual cues an audience would have taken in from watching a live production. The narrator almost plays the role of lighting and designer, telling our minds eye what to focus on, as well as when and what resonate sensorially. The narrator’s work is significant for a show whose prior iterations relied so heavily on spectacle, and it is done with aplomb by core company member Cristal Gonzalez Avila. Her work is shared by a team of musicians (led by Daniel D. Valdez). The live version of ETC’s in person productions of La Pastorela makes expert use of the shepherds’ journey to tell the story. Since a group of people have to move en mass around the mission church, they hold the audience’s focus by dancing through the space with large, colorful, walking sticks and singing. Travel is central to the story and easy to track visually when the show is performed live and in-person. In this radio version, the songs are truncated and are used to carry the listener from one vignette to the next, until we finally arrive at the site of Christ’s nativity with the shepherds.Much of the narrative framework for contemporary pastorelas can be traced back to a play titled La Noche Mas Venturosa, ó El Premio de la Inocencia (The Most Venturous Night, or the Prize of Innocence), written by Mexico’s first novelist, José Joaquin Fernandez de Lizardi, in the early 1800s. Lizardi’s play was the first adaptation written explicitly for an acting troop. The play is replete with misogynistic humor, beginning with a young shepherd, Bato, threatening violence on his wife, Gila, for not cooking enough food. Since the devil tries to indulge the characters in each deadly sin, pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, anger, and sloth are prominent character flaws of the shepherd’s cohort. Echos of the Lizardi play have been a part of the ETC production for years.One way that Lizardi’s text has haunted ETC’s productions emerges in the marriage subplot between Bato and Gila. In ETC productions past, the impending marriage of Bato and Gila was an essential part of the story. However, the 2021 version has done away with the marriage storyline between these two young shepherds. Instead, the song that used to be sung as a duet between the two lovebirds, “Oir, Cantar,” is now a truncated solo sung by Gila. The lyrics are rewritten as a vehicle for Gila to communicate that she has heard the angel’s announcement and now has to sing the mission to her kin. The marriage storyline pops up later in the play, but it’s a joke made in passing by one of the shepherds to get a rise out of Bartolo. These changes evidence reflexivity in the current company who is thinking about the ways that rigid divisions of between devotion and sin still resonates in new ways as we question, what stars we have chosen to follow. The choice not to include these echos of gendered violence reminds audiences that we don’t have to carry everything with us as we pilgrimage into the uncertainty that is 2022.

title: Gluttony and Gratitude: Milton’s Philosophy of Eating. Emily E. Stelzer. University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 2017. Pp. vii+364.
abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeBook ReviewGluttony and Gratitude: Milton’s Philosophy of Eating. Emily E. Stelzer. University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 2017. Pp. vii+364.Bruce BoehrerBruce BoehrerFlorida State University Search for more articles by this author PDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreAt last we have a book comparing Milton to a cow. The comparison occurs near the end of Emily Stelzer’s Gluttony and Gratitude, where Stelzer remarks that “like a cow,” the poet “would consume, ruminate, digest, transform, collect, and secrete thoughts and language” (276), and while one might observe some inaccuracy in the parallel (cows don’t secrete language, for instance), the point is better taken than might at first appear. It was Milton himself who, while awaiting a tardy amanuensis during the composition of Paradise Lost, “would complain, saying he wanted to be milked” (276), nor would he have seen any inherent impropriety in the analogy. In a monist universe, after all, both cows and angels are compounded of the same first matter, divinity and bovinity joined at the protocellular level.In pursuit of this vision, Stelzer engages not only with her title sin of gluttony but also with Milton’s philosophy of eating in the broadest sense. The first three of her six core chapters confine themselves to eating in its sinful dimension; the final three then sketch out a model of temperance that Stelzer associates with the prelapsarian world of Paradise Lost. Together, the six chapters make the case that food occupies a central place in Miltonic cosmology, exerting both a physiological and a spiritual influence upon the consumer, enforcing our collective participation in a Great Chain of Being that is also a “Great Chain of Eating” (170). Within this system, one may understand our dietary interdependence either as “a dynamic of generosity, grace, and gratitude, of symbiotic giving and receiving,” or as a “predatory food chain” of exploitative selfishness (171). For Stelzer, this is our central moral choice, configured in Genesis through the fruit of the tree of knowledge.Chapters 1–3 explore the demonic valence of this choice. Here Stelzer begins with patristic theories of gluttony, which tend to regard “Adam’s gluttonous eating, avaricious curiosity [about the forbidden fruit], and selfish pride” as encompassing “all sin in the single act of the fall” (27). Thus the act of overeating itself serves as only one manifestation of gluttony, which becomes equally visible in the “love-drunkenness” of “Adam’s uxoriousness” and in the “psychological delicacy” of “Eve’s presumption for forbidden knowledge” (39), to say nothing of “the intemperate pursuit of glory in battle, … or the luxuriant sloth of peacetime” (76). Nor are the effects of gluttony confined to the body of the glutton. On the contrary, “when Milton describes Nature’s response to human intemperance, he imagines pure regions vomiting out the impure inhabitants,” with “the environment imitat[ing] the vomiting gluttons within” (73). For Satan and the fallen angels, who lack the prevenient grace bestowed on fallen humankind, the consequences of gluttony prove even more severe, extending to various sorts of corrupt embodiment. Thus the demons are thrust to hell in a grand “metaphor of celestial defecation” that parallels the “metaphor of Edenic vomiting” applied later to Adam and Eve (119). Once expelled from heaven, in turn, the fallen angels become subject to myriad processes of physical imbruting that render their being ever more feculent and foul.By contrast, the unfallen world of Paradise Lost reconfigures the food chain as a ligature to unite the entire living creation. If Raphael holds out to Adam and Eve the possibility of “human transformative ascent” up the Great Chain of Being (164), that is because human beings and angels alike “were created to physically return to God” (166); they inhabit a continuum of being created from the same divine substance. Thus Raphael finds no inconvenient diet in Adam and Eve’s earthly repast—although, to preserve the parallel, one would expect Adam and Eve to be equally able to graze on grass with their bovine companions. (Again, it seems, the matter comes down to Milton’s relationship with kine.) In sum, Stelzer argues, “In Paradise Lost humans were created to ascend to the heavens by merit and sustained obedience substantially exemplified in decisions made about eating” (175). Within this scheme of things, “one being’s superfluity provides sustaining nutriment for a higher being, uniting all creation through a system of symbiotic giving” (188).To imagine an unfallen universe whose elements all sustain each other symbiotically through grateful mutual consumption is to envision a prelapsarian ecology. In this sense Stelzer’s argument leads from food studies to ecostudies, and Milton’s philosophy of eating participates in the grand tradition of stewardship theology, with its efforts to imagine biological interdependence as something other than competition and exploitation. But for Milton as for most of his contemporaries, I suspect, the stewardship ideal vanished with the fall, replaced by a universe of suffering and strife from which death alone will free us. Gratitude still matters in this universe, but not as much as faith and prayer and the stoic determination to suffer as to do.Amid all this, Stelzer reveals herself to be a medievalist at heart, particularly adept at tracing the Miltonic influence of writers like Augustine and Aquinas, Dante and Chaucer. Her work is at times more syncretistic than original; her treatment of demonic scatology in Paradise Lost, for instance, draws heavily on the prior scholarship of Michael Lieb and others. And, in the way of most academic writing, Stelzer’s can be both overwrought and obvious, as when she cites a plague sermon by Lancelot Andrewes as “exemplifying that systems of thought connecting exhalation and worship in perfumed prayers extended beyond paradisal contexts” (200). On the whole, though, Gluttony and Gratitude is quite a good book of its kind, its particular virtue being the scope of its inquiry, which extends from heaven to hell and from the garden of Eden to the fallen present, in the process offering an integrated overview of the role of dietary concerns in Milton’s work. title: A World Art History and Its Objects by carrier, david
venue: Journal of Aesthetics and Art Criticism
abstract: CARRIER, DAVID. A World Art History and Its Objects. Pennsylvania State University Press, 2008, 170 pp., 11 b&w illus., $55.00 cloth. David Carrier is that rare creature, a philosopher who writes art history. Most philosophers who have written on art have been content to remain philosophers, among them Richard Wollheim and Arthur Danto, whose work Carrier uses heavily in this book. Most art historians of a philosophical bent, such as Michael Baxandall (also a museum scholar) and Ernst Gombrich, both of whom Carrier cites, consistently maintained their identities as art historians, purposefully avoiding identification with philosophy as a discipline and a profession. In pursuing his ambition, Carrier has, in a sense, leapt over the Warburg Institute generations represented by Gombrich and Baxandall to connect with an earlier time when scholars such as Erwin Panofksy, Edgar Wind, and Ernst Cassirer could move freely among wissenschaftlich disciplines, including philosophy and history of art. But Carrier's publisher, Pennsylvania State University Press, firmly classifies his new book as philosophy, not as art history. It does not even appear in both lists. Is this fair? Carrier is at his greatest ease and is most authoritative when he turns to decidedly philosophical matters—although he is in no sense at a loss when discussing art and its histories. In this book, he sets out to define conditions for a certain kind of art history that scarcely exists—a world art history—so his text is about conditions, premises, and, in the end, predictions for the practice of a range of arthistorical methods. To this extent his text is appropriately philosophical, and Carrier's analytical skills carry him a great deal further than many art historians who have explored the puzzles arising from ambitions to address art worldwide. The title of the book might lead some readers to be disappointed by its contents; yet this would be unfair, for from the outset Carrier makes it clear that he is writing no more than a prolegomenon in which he seeks to describe the conditions in which the future writing of a world art history might be feasible. Further, some readers may be disappointed that by “world art history” Carrier does not mean the world in its human entirety, but only parts of it: Europe, China, India, and the Islamic world alone. He is clear, though, about his reasons for omitting great tracts of the globe. It would be impractical, he contends, to extend the examination to each and every human society at present. While admiring his ambition, and respecting his prudence, one can question his choices. Discussions of art are exercises of power. Carrier sees world art history as part of the process of globalization, though more in sorrow than in approbation. Placing the discipline in the context of European travel, trade, and conquest, he contends that “the expansion of art history from [Giorgio] Vasari's story focused on Tuscan art to our multicultural narrative is inseparable from that history. As capitalism seeks new markets, leaving no part of the world unexplored, so Western art history now looks to all cultures, interpreting exotic art in ways guided by its own precepts” (p. 120). This may be so, but are the philosopher and the art historian compelled to acquiesce? Why not place art (to call it such while acknowledging the extent of the definitional puzzles that the term presents) from societies at the greatest disadvantage in the picture from the very beginning? Why exclude the subaltern, to use Antonio Gramsci's term to encompass groups including, but not confined to, indigenous peoples who are at a disadvantage to those exercising power? Carrier is far from alone in describing the consequences of globalization for historical study. The anthropologist Jack Goody makes a similar case in respect of the character of an entirely Eurocentric history in The Theft of History (Cambridge University Press, 2006). He contends that Asia—China, India, and the Islamic world—has been traduced owing to insidious Eurocentrism, according to which the technological rise of the West was ordained by a lack of capacity owing to perceived Eastern sloth and tyranny, a myth effectively exposed by Edward Said in Orientalism (Vintage, 1978). Goody unmasks three great twentiethcentury scholars—Joseph Needham, Norbert Elias, and Fernand Braudel—as “thieves” from Asia of science, civilization, and capitalism, respectively, by their concealed application of Eurocentric assumptions. As Carrier acknowledges, and Goody argues, European particularism has been enormously damaging. As a corrective to the view of Europe as a special, inevitably privileged case, there is much to be said for regarding the Eurasian landmass plus the entire Mediterranean and east African littoral functioning as one cultural unit between about 500 and 1500, with only a few pockets of peripheral eccentricity, such as much of Western Europe (excluding the Iberian peninsula before the socalled Reconquista, or al‘Istirdād). In When Asia Was the World (Da Capo, 2008), Stewart Gordon has argued that the widely shared cultural norms of this huge area allowed the midfourteenthcentury Moroccan Ibn Battuta and his like to find patronage and employment from Timbuktu to Beijing. Gordon holds that only the arrival of the Portuguese compromised widely shared conventions, which until then had promoted a degree of social cohesion. The Portuguese, who journeyed into the Indian Ocean from 1498 onwards with consequences that were catastrophically disruptive to the societies they encountered, were ignorant of conventions such as the giving and receiving of robes of honor. They compromised a system of which they knew nothing by ignoring or controverting its conventions through the exercise of raw power. While acknowledging his own European identity and inevasible Eurocentrism (as shared by the European diaspora in North America and elsewhere), Carrier implicitly subscribes to this Eurasian worldview by giving privilege to China, India, and the Islamic world. Carrier's vision is not the result of any want of consideration, but is, in part, a consequence of his conception of both philosophy and art history. “The philosophers and the art historians have different goals,” he writes. “The philosophers seek a completely general definition, while the historians [properly, art historians] want to explain the relationship of successive works of art on the various time lines” (p. 109). Philosophers ask, “What is art?” whereas art historians pose what Carrier characterizes as “more parochial questions”: What is Chinese art? What is Indian art? What is Islamic art? That is, insofar as artists make art by responding to other art, notably that of their predecessors in an at least partially selfcontained system of imitation, emulation, and innovation, each such system within any given society should be comprehensible by means of a timeline: one for European art, another for Chinese art, yet another for Indian art, and yet another for Islamic art. These timelines are reductions of, or can be elaborated to produce, necessarily Westernstyle causal narratives. On this account, need art history be anything more than what Arnold Toynbee feared some thought history to be, “just one damn thing after another”? Carrier's analysis is certainly reductive, but, as far as the Western practice of art history goes, largely justifiable. If we adhere to a recent, modern Western notion of a hierarchy of media (in play since the later seventeenth century, subsequently coalesced by Immanuel Kant) that places fine art before decorative art, with painting at the top, it would be difficult to refute the claim that until the recent past art practice proceeded on a series of such timelines (a far larger number than Carrier discusses, of course), each in isolation or near isolation from the other. In this case, Carrier's claim that “[t]here is a difference in kind between occasional exchanges between traditions, which occur throughout history, and what happens when previously parallel time lines intersect” (p. 41) is plausible; but, if we do not subscribe to such a hierarchy, and in consequence adduce numerous exceptions, the condition of isolation applied to societies in contact with one another, pursuing tradition under blinders, begins to look distinctly suspect. By relying on an outmoded notion of artistic hierarchy, Carrier neglects to give enough weight to a broad range of visual cultural exchange. For instance, the spread of blueandwhite ceramics from China to Persia, and eventually to Western Europe, and the attendant search for the secret of porcelain, entail the intersection of the art history timelines of all four of Carrier's societies—Europe, China, India, and the Islamic world—in a hugely consequential way. Carrier consistently underestimates contacts and responses among these societies, I suspect largely because they occur in visual rather than textual terms: that is, members of these societies may have known a wide range of each other's visual products, but not each other's writings about them. The worlds of artworks and other artifacts in these societies were far more intertwined than Carrier allows. He makes much of the exoticism in Europe of carpets from the Islamic world, and their depiction in European paintings, but does not fully take into account their actual use, and even their commission . In 1634, Robert Bell gave the Girdlers' Company (one of London's guilds and livery companies), of which he had been master, a monumental floral and armorial carpet that he had commissioned from weavers in Lahore, then in the Mughal Empire. It remains in the possession of the company. Such an object was and remains inherently crosscultural, conceived, designed, and used differently from contemporary Islamic prayer carpets, but sharing in the conventions of Mughal floral carpets no less than in those of Western European armorial representations. In the very same year, in Rome, Gian Maria Roscioli acquired a new painting by Nicolas Poussin, The Saving of the Infant Pyrrhus (Musée du Louvre, Paris). As an artwork, the Bell Carpet is neither more nor less significant, interesting, arresting, or aesthetically valuable than the painting by Poussin (an artist on whose work Carrier has written illuminatingly). The relative oversignificance that Carrier attaches to the works of socalled canonical Western painters such as Poussin emerges fully in the thought experiment that constitutes the finale of the book. Here Carrier notes that, thanks to a Chinese scholar, Ding Yuchang (Carrier's invention), “we finally have a satisfactory account of Nicolas Poussin's landscape paintings. What had puzzled the earlier European commentators, the relationship of these pictures to his scenes of pagan mythology and classical history, now becomes clear thanks to Yuchang's inspired recognition of their affinity with Chinese landscapes” (pp. 147–148). Carrier is perceptively making the serious point that we shall not be able to speak properly of a world art history until European discourse on European and nonEuropean art is fully and equitably complemented by nonEuropean discourse on not only nonEuropean art but on European art, too. Attractive as this notion may be, postulated as it is on a mutual cultural respect that Carrier advocates, it fails to take into account both the fatal power disparities among artmaking societies and social groups (that is, all human societies and social groups) and the sheer longevity of human existence. Humans and other hominids have made aesthetically charged artifacts for an almost unimaginably long time. Consider, for example, the symmetrical, likely nonfunctional hand axes produced by Homo ergaster, Homo erectus, and Homo heidelbergensis up to 1.4 million years ago, discussed by Marek Kohn and Steven Mithen. The mere thousand years of panEurasian mutual cultural intelligibility between 500 and 1500 looks very “parochial” (to use one of Carrier's terms) in this context. The challenge of conceiving, let alone producing, a world art history is on a far larger scale than Carrier perhaps dares to acknowledge, even despite his sincere disclaimers regarding the limitations of his preliminary case studies, for such an art history must not only address all humans ever, but also take us beyond what we comfortably recognize as human. Philosophers are trapped by reliance on the written word; so are most art historians. It is no coincidence that Carrier concentrates on societies with written commentaries on visual art, whether by Giorgio Vasari in sixteenthcentury Tuscany, or Tsung Ping in fifthcentury China. In doing so, Carrier adheres to a questionable view of “civilizations,” seeing them in essentialist terms, as when he claims “Chinese culture has a certain distinctive essence” (p. 37) or, when quoting Laurence Sickman and Alexander Soper, The Art and Architecture of China (Yale University Press, 1971), he claims that “the Chinese possess the longest continuous cultural history of any of the peoples of the world” (p. 43). This would come as news to many other peoples, the Pintupi of the Northern Territory and Western Australia, for instance, or the Hupa of northern California, to pick two (almost) at random (see Byron Nelson Jr., Our Home Forever: The Hupa Indians of Northern California [Howe Brothers, 1994]). As Western art historians such as Richard Farris Thompson in the case of the Yoruba in Nigeria, Howard Morphy in that of the Yolngu in Australia, and Sally Price for the Suriname Maroons have demonstrated (among many others), peoples long without writing can have a complex aesthetics regarding the things they make, often not for purely functional purposes, articulated both visually and verbally: art. Rather than leave definitions to Western scholars alone, various subaltern groups have taken charge of their own cultural interpretation in institutions that deal with visual arts. Prominent examples are the national museums Te Papa Tongarewa, Wellington, Aotearoa (New Zealand), with a prominent Māori presence, and the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C., and New York City. A tribal example is the Haida Heritage Centre at Kaay Llnagaay, Haida Gwaii, British Columbia, Canada. If we would make philosophical claims about visual art, those claims must not only be generally true, true in all possible worlds, but also true in real societies, such as those of the Yolngu in Arnhem Land, and the Haida in Haida Gwaii, no less than in Ming China, Mughal India, and Renaissance Florence. They must be true not only today, but also yesterday, and each yesterday before that as far as 1.4 million years ago. No wonder we blench. As well as taking many of the steps Carrier eloquently and rightly proposes, we can take others yet more radical. We need not acquiesce in globalization, but can resist its power inequalities by rejecting notions of centers and peripheries, no less than oppositions between sophisticated civilizations and primitive cultures. We can question the ascription of superiority to urban over agrarian peoples, agrarian over huntergatherer peoples, even settled over nomadic peoples. Europeans can make imaginative attempts to see themselves at an unfamiliar cultural disadvantage to indigenous peoples, for instance in situations of dependence such as Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca and his surviving companions experienced between Florida and northwest Mexico between 1528 and 1536 (see Andrés Reséndez, A Land So Strange: The Epic Journey of Cabeza de Vaca [Basic Books, 2007]). Such exercises are salutary and might remind not only Europeans, but also Chinese, Indians, and inhabitants of the Islamic world that their ways of doing things—including artmaking and artwriting—are not the only ways, nor invariably the best. David Carrier has characteristically and admirably set himself a heroic task, like Raven stealing the sun, moon, and stars, or Herakles fulfilling the tasks set by Eurystheus. As one of our most deft philosophers of art, he sorts out various puzzles arising from an ambition to create conditions in which a world art history might be possible, including distinguishing between relativism and pluralism, for instance, propounding the appreciation of “exotic” art without necessarily accepting the worldview of its creators (though the same should hold for the appreciation of European art in relation to the worldview of its creators). This book is a necessary preface to the project he, and many others, have in mind: a world art history, but, finally, we must realize that he, like others who seek to combine philosophy with art history, is obliged to work under difficulties that might confound any thinker. As a philosopher, Carrier tests his claims against particular instances, so he cannot be wholly comfortable in that role; as an art historian, Carrier tests his claims against wouldbe universals, so neither can he be comfortable in that role. Yet such discomfort is only a mild foretaste of the challenges to cherished fundamental assumptions—in art history, philosophy, and worldview generally—that those who would join David Carrier in his great venture must inevitably face.

title: Of Beasts, Kids, and Science as a Method
abstract: The Beast in You! Activities & Questions to Explore Evolution. Marc McCutcheon. Williamson Publishing, Charlotte, VT, 1999. 96 pp., illus. $10.05 (ISBN 1-885593-36-8 paper). As everyone knows, evolution is under attack. This is by no means an assault based on cogent scientific arguments, theoretical or empirical. More simply, it is an aggressive stance that is ideologically motivated and rooted in two positions that make for rather amusing and quite strange bedfellows: religious fundamentalism and left-wing political correctness (Cartmill 1998). On the one hand, the fact that evolutionary biology contradicts the most cherished beliefs of people who interpret the Bible (Gish 1995) or the Koran (Yahya 1999) literally has led to a more than century long crusade against Darwinism. On the other hand, the esoteric intellectual movement of deconstructionism has attempted to show that science is just another cultural construct, with no better claim to truth than myths and psychic predictions (Levitt 1998). Despite all of this, creationists have been repeatedly defeated in court (Larson 1997) and evolution is still being taught in all major colleges in the United States. However, the movement has not died; rather, it has simply found new ways to subvert what its adherents perceive as the plot of countless atheist professors bent on brainwashing American youth. The new creationist strategy has evolved along two directions: by attempting to gain some academic respectability by clogging the discussion with pseudo-religiously neutral terms such as “intelligent design” (Pigliucci 2000), and by influencing the minds of young people by polluting the science literature for children with books portraying dinosaurs and humans walking side by side. It is therefore with a sigh of relief that I came across The Beast in You!, by Marc McCutcheon, a wonderful book meant to clearly explain what evolution is all about to children and to promote critical thinking about the scientific enterprise in general. The book gets its title and underlying theme from the simple observation that if one pays close attention to his or her own image in a mirror, he or she can easily see a benign “beast,” the vestiges of the wild animal that humans were not long ago, before MTV and McDonald's. For example, simply smile at your mirror and you will see a pair of teeth known as canines, which offer a simple yet wonderful opportunity to talk about predators and prey, dogs, tyrannosaurs, and even—considering the word's instead of the tooth's roots—of ancient languages such as Latin and Greek and their place in scientific terminology. A few pages into the book, the reader starts finding interesting little sidebars such as the series “The Evolution Solution,” which explains a scientific puzzle and offers a tentative explanation in terms of evolutionary theory. The first such puzzle is the existence of the appendix, which the author uses to get into the idea of vestigial organs and of evolution as a suboptimal, and therefore natural, process. More importantly, McCutcheon never overstates the case and makes clear that some of the ideas discussed in the book are tentative and await confirmation—and he insinuates that such confirmation may very well come from one of the bright girls or boys intent on reading the book. What an idea! Science as a fascinating process rather than a boring accumulation of facts. Telling scary stories around a campfire is a favorite pastime for many children, but how many realize that the chill running down their spines is a remnant of the almost universal fight-or-flight response? Behavioral repertoires evolve too, and they leave a mark on modern civilized humans, no less than canine teeth and appendices do. Again, McCutcheon further exploits the topic by proposing simple experiments, such as testing one's own fight-or-flight response while learning how to check one's pulse. Far from being a sociobiological fundamentalist, the author clearly nudges the child toward understanding that biology does not mean strict determinism: how much the better to keep your nerves under control the next time that somebody bothers you at school, knowing that you are dominating an instinct that is millions of years old! Basic principles of evolution, such as variation and natural selection, are explained not only by observations that anyone can carry out in his backyard, but by involving the child in direct scientific experiments. For example, everyone knows that rabbits come in different colors. Does the color of their hair make a difference? One of the experiments directs readers to carve three rabbits out of paper; color them white, yellow and brown; and then paste them at the base of a tree. Then, readers are encouraged to place themselves at a distance of 15 meters and imagine they are hungry coyotes. Which rabbit would they spot more easily? One of the most recurring arguments of creationists is that if evolution is occurring now, how come we don't see intermediate forms? McCutcheon convincingly informs his readers that even a child can see these intermediate forms clearly. Penguins' bones are hollow, as if they were adapted for flying, but the birds don't use their flippers to take off, preferring instead a semi-aquatic life. Why is it that only female wasps can sting? Does this have something to do with the fact that the stinger evolved from an egg-laying organ? And why do boa constrictors have remnants of legs, as if they once were lizardlike animals? Not to mention, of course, moles and cave salamanders, which still carry leftovers of eyes no longer used, or the fact that baby anteaters develop teeth that disappear before birth. The Beast in You! very appropriately includes a chapter on human evolution, in which the myth of cavemen fighting against dinosaurs is debunked for what it is and the science of paleontology is presented as equivalent to the job of a detective who has a series of clues and has to determine what happened by solving a gigantic puzzle of geological proportions. In the meantime, readers learn how to take a core sample from their backyards as well as how to make casts of footprints in a fashion similar to the methods of the scientists who uncovered Lucy, the remains of an Australopithecus who lived in Africa approximately 3 million years ago. Of course, appropriate Web sites are also referred to throughout the book, a good thing given the propensity of so many people to go to the Internet first and accept whatever garbage they happen to stumble on as a reliable source. Another feature of the book designed to instigate critical thinking appears as sidebars called “Think About It!” One of these invites the child to consider the claims reported by the media about Bigfoot, a humanlike creature that allegedly represents the remnant of some earlier stage of our own evolution. McCutcheon does not provide dogmatic answers, but simply points his readers toward considering alternative hypotheses, how reliable the evidence is, and how to go about investigating the matter further. If only college textbooks were written with the same underlying philosophy, I would experience much less pain when teaching my introductory ecology course. McCutcheon doesn't stay clear of controversy either, and devotes a few pages to the evolution–creation story and to John Scopes and his trial. This is something that more educators should allow in the classroom. There is no question that teaching creationism is not only illegal, it is nonsensical given our state of knowledge in the field. But that is not to say that teachers should ignore a cogent national debate, or the fact that up to half of their children may in fact harbor strong feelings against evolutionary biology. The classroom is a place for informed discussion and formation of critical thinking skills, not the locus of boring lectures designed to have the audience swallow the status quo just because some vague and unrecognized authority says so. Although I did find minor points in McCutcheon's book that needed further explanation or perhaps a different approach, I think The Beast in You! should be the prototype of a new generation of science books not only for children 7–14 but, as the song goes, from one to 99. I certainly wish I had access to this kind of book when I was a child, and no doubt will give a copy to my daughter as soon as she is old enough to turn one page at a time.
