title: The Doctor as Pain Management Scapegoat
abstract: I see a lot of patients with slurred speech. Not the kind of slurred speech that makes me contemplate thrombolytics. Not the kind of slurred speech that makes me wonder if they have botulism. Their slurred speech comes from the use of pain medications. In our rural county, there have been several overdose deaths in the past few years. They weren't people who left a note, distraught, intending to end their misery. They were people who probably said to their families, with slurred tongues, “This pain is killing me. I'm going to take something.” And they did. They took their pain medicine, over and over, and the other pain medicine they received from various doctors. And in the morning, their family looked at them sound asleep, breathing quietly on the couch, and went to work. And when they came home, they were dead. I'm tired of this pain dance that we all have to learn. I'm tired of the pain scale, which is almost always reported as a 10/10. I'm sick of hearing physicians accused of ignorance and cruelty in the management of pain. I'm shocked that so many organizations, whose representatives frequently aren't evaluating pain on a daily basis, feel free to evaluate emergency physicians in this arena. The joint commission, CMS (via EMTALA), nursing associations, and various pain management and pain advocacy groups all consider us inept in managing pain, both acute and chronic. These groups are counterbalanced by federal and state controlled substances policies, state medical boards, and investigators for both, who are eager to find patterns of overprescribing. And, of course, there are always lawyers anxious for a hint of liability in either direction. I admit, some doctors are bad at pain management. Some doctors I see consulting in the ED don't know the doses of common narcotics, especially for children. Some surgeons I have known simply think that large wounds and fractures just aren't that bad. Some internists fail to appreciate the horrible pain of metastatic cancer. But these are exceptions. On the other hand, I believe that emergency physicians as a group believe in giving comfort to the suffering and that we do it well. Some think we are abysmal failures, however. The thing is, pain is not objectively quantifiable yet. There isn't a painometer that we can attach to someone's scalp. All we have is the pain scale, our objective, scientific assessment of the problem before us, and our interpretation of the patient's appearance and vital signs. But most pain advocates feel that our objective interpretations are relatively worthless, that pain may be severe without an obvious physical abnormality, and so the pain scale is all that remains. And because much of the pain that we see is terribly subjective, the management of pain is difficult at best, and at worst is a daily battle to decide who is lying and who isn't. We find ourselves left with slurred speech in the young and old, who have frequently come to define complete pain relief as complete unconsciousness. Left with 21-year-old patients with chronic back pain who spend their lives passed out before the television waiting for their disability check while their families hope for something, anything, to change their lives. Left with 85-year-old patients whose spouses think they have had strokes, despite the fact that they take five different narcotics. Almost all of these patients are being treated by one or more physicians, anxious to be compassionate, even as they continue to feel that we in the emergency department are to blame if they continue to report, “My pain ith about a t-t-ten.” How about a solution? Here is a possible answer to taking the blame away from physicians in general and emergency physicians in particular. Let's legalize the over-the-counter purchase of narcotic analgesics. Now I've never really been a legalization advocate before, but it makes some sense. After all, if I can't accurately interpret a patient's pain and only he can, why shouldn't they get the drugs and get me out of the middle? We're always told by pain specialists that only a fixed number of patients will become addicted no matter what. And most of those are getting their prescriptions from doctors anyway. So let patients be in charge, in a sort of outpatient, oral PCA arrangement. There are advantages. It will save patients the cost of frequent ED visits. It will save the system the cost of uncompensated care among those who can't pay. It will help patients avoid the struggle of finding pain specialists. It can be controlled, if we like, with national tracking. If you want to buy your own narcotics, you need a narcotic purchasing card that evaluates your background and links all pharmacies. That way you can't just buy endlessly for the purpose of suicide or social occasions. If you need more than a threshold amount, you must certify that you are under the care of a pain specialist. The involvement of the pain experts is very important. I know they understand the science of pain better than I do. So let's ask the pain guys to put up or shut up. If pain is a national epidemic with untold millions of patients suffering needlessly, then do something about it. Let there be more residency slots in anesthesia or neurology. Let there be pain management fellowships for primary care doctors. Let there be more free-standing pain management facilities to guide patients who need extra help beyond their over-the-counter purchase of narcotics. Let's have an EPTA, or Emergency Pain Treatment Act, that involves nonemergency department facilities so we can stem the tide of this national crisis. We're talking about helping our fellow men and women who are unjustly neglected by hard-hearted ED types! It makes sense. But it won't happen for a couple of reasons. It isn't that the finances are a problem in terms of buying narcotics. Without the cost of doctor's visits, patients who already buy narcotic prescriptions or narcotics on the street could afford medicine more easily. There will be those who need pain specialists, however. And they don't, or won't, come cheap. Anesthesiologists would be very unhappy with anything like the arrangement we work under, where everyone gets care without cash up front. I'm afraid pain care is a lot like dental care. It's generally a nine-to-five, weekday national crisis, which is best handled by the less than capable in the emergency department during off hours. But the main reason it won't happen is that it would shift responsibility from physicians to patients. It would require that a patient be the one making the decision to use the drug, the one deciding how to use it. (This is what we're approaching already, as we assume that the patient always knows best in some twisted business philosophy gone awry.) It would mean that if adverse outcomes happened, no physician or hospital could be blamed. It would take most of us out of the middle, and drop an enormous weight of accountability into the laps of the patients whose pain we are accused of neglecting. It won't happen because despite our alleged ignorance, sloth, and willful cruelty, the system needs doctors in the middle, if for no other reason than to accept the blame for problems that other people create. And it's never more true than in the management of pain and the use of narcotics.

title: Second Opinion: Capable — and Proud of It — in a World of Voluntary Incapacity
abstract: ImageThose of us who work in emergency care are often deemed insensitive by others. When we rant about the situations we see, sensitive people genuinely believe that we're cold, uncaring, or burned out. I have been accused of ultraconservatism, right-wing lunacy, being judgmental (the worst insult a post-modern can muster, by the way) and of being a greedy, Mercedes-driving doctor. (I drive a pickup.) Someone even said my newspaper readers should ignore my opinion about medical finances because I was just “po'mouthing,” a Southernism that implies I was making my situation sound dismal when I was actually quite well off. While I'm sure that a few physicians are, in fact, cold and uncaring, most of the docs I meet are anything but. What they are, however, is possessed of the remarkable clarity about humans that can only come from working with actual people rather than theories or ideologies. It's an insight that cannot be achieved in the purely academic world, nor is it attainable in Internet chat rooms, but it isn't, as I long suspected, just doctors who deal with reality. I often speak about our struggles with a dear friend and fellow church deacon who is a manager in a local grocery store. My friend is as kind a man as you'll ever meet. Devoted to family, friends, and God, he volunteers at a local elementary school, spending time with at-risk children. He comes to church early to pray for the many things that burden his heart. He would literally give you the shirt off of his back. And he's fed up with the abuse he sees in his grocery store. He told me, “Ed, I see people using food stamps to buy food I could never afford. And I have a good job!” He recently held forth about a woman using her WIC (Women, Infants, and Children program) card to buy six gallons of milk at once. When he half-jokingly asked what she did with all of the milk, she pointed to a toddler and said, “She drinks all of it.” Later, leaving the store, the customer was heard to say, “What does he care? He ain't payin' for it!” Except, of course, that he is. My friends who are deputies and highway patrol officers feel the same, as do many of my friends whose work as attorneys puts them in contact with the welfare and social services systems. They are often frustrated by the abuses they see, by the parade of bad decisions, and by a bureaucracy that almost seems to encourage and reward the abuse of benefits and services while rarely elevating anyone. One of my own favorite gremlins is disability. Many of my patients seem to see disability as a career goal. A friend of mine is a school counselor. When she recently asked a young high school student what his post-graduation plans were, he never missed a beat. “Guess I'll get disability for my nerves, like the rest of my family.” The thing that makes those outside our circle think we're bitter is that stories like the ones above drive us crazy. Just like patients who come to the ED for routine pregnancy tests, who ask for prescriptions for Tylenol, and who seek Family and Medical Leave Act forms for ankle sprains. In the same way as the diabetic who refuses to get a $4 prescription at Walmart but regularly goes to McDonald's before coming to the ED. There are doubtless well-meaning people who will read this and still marvel at our insensitivity. So I was doing a little reflection on what it is about these situations that frustrates us. Is it, after all, about the money? Are we just mad because we aren't being paid? Well, that can't be it. My disabled and Medicaid patients all have insurance. I'm paid for seeing them! Maybe not a full market value, but something is better than nothing. Is it elitism? Do I consider myself better than these folks, who are often poor and uneducated? Probably not. My faith teaches me that we're all the same in the eyes of God. And my own grandparents were laborers and small business owners as well as subsistence farmers. I have no animosity toward those who struggle. And then it hit me! Those who struggle! I like it when people struggle, not in the sense of hopelessness or crushing misery, but meaning those who try, who set goals and go through life trying to be better, happier, more successful, more resourceful, more independent. I'm happy to help those who try, and happy to help those who are actually in need. I'll gladly give care to the truly sick. I'll stay late, bend over backwards, beg and borrow to do whatever it takes to help them. For those who try? Anything. If they're trying to do what's right, trying to get healthy, trying to rise out of generational poverty, trying to recover from an accident or mistake, a prison sentence, or a disabling injury, I'm honored to be there for them. What bothers me, what bothers us collectively, is not that people need us. It's not even that people need us for free. It's that they have begun to worship at the altar of incapacity and what wise men of old called sloth. We are an overmedicated, undereducated nation bent on proving that we cannot, rather than showing that we can. Having inverted the ethics of our forefathers, our goal is no longer autonomy, but dependence. We have abandoned the sense of guilt that in the past made our citizens try to achieve on their own to avoid being burdens. We have, in fact, abandoned the entire idea of guilt in exchange for a kind of social lovefest, where anything goes as long as we want it. And nowhere do we see the results of this experiment more clearly, more painfully, than in the emergency department. Young and old alike swamp our departments, convinced that someone owes them money and compassion for their own dysfunctional life choices and beloved incapacity. It isn't that we're burned out. It isn't that we're cold. It's just that we understand better than most what it means to try. No one told us that not trying was an option. And we're just weary of being responsible for an endless parade of patients who believe we owe them something and who consistently refuse to do anything for themselves. So don't let anyone call you bitter, shallow, greedy, or anything else. Gather your friends, business people, police officers, and social workers; collect their stories and pass them on. Explain that you aren't the only person frustrated with our deteriorating social situation. And be proud that in a world of epidemic and voluntary incapacity, you remain capable and proud of it.Dr. Leap: is a member of Blue Ridge Emergency Physicians, an emergency physician at Oconee Memorial Hospital in Seneca, SC, and an op-ed columnist for the Greenville News. He welcomes comments about his observations, and readers may write to him at [email protected] and visit his web site and blog at www.edwinleap.com.

title: Discussion
abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeDiscussionPDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreDaron Acemoglu contextualized the authors’ paper as part of an ongoing debate about the origins of intercohort trends in labor market outcomes. He argued that differences across education groups have been studied extensively, whereas differences across cohorts are less understood. He contrasted two views on the subject. According to the first one, which he labeled the “early labor view,” intercohort trends stem from differences in protections and unionization across cohorts. The second view, which Acemoglu labeled the “Card-Lemieux (2001) view” (David Card and Thomas Lemieux [“Can Falling Supply Explain the Rising Return to College for Younger Men? A Cohort-Based Analysis,” Quarterly Journal of Economics 116, no. 2 (2001): 705–46]), imputes these trends to differences in educational attainments across cohorts. Acemoglu downplayed the importance of the first view. He suggested instead that a decrease in the relative supply of educated workers across cohorts is the most plausible explanation for the rise in the skill premium observed in the data. He noted that college graduation rates rose steadily for cohorts born before 1950, but educational attainments stagnated or even declined afterward. Acemoglu argued that the literature still does not have a good understanding of the source of this structural break. The authors agreed that the decline in educational achievements across cohorts is striking, especially because the skill premium rose over the relevant period. They would not speculate about the reasons underlying this trend but suggested that skill-biased technical changes might also have played a role for the rising skill premium.Valerie Ramey followed up on the subject and offered a tentative explanation for the decline in educational achievements across cohorts. She highlighted the role of expectations for investment in human capital. She noted that the 1960s cohort (studied in the paper) turned 18 in the late 1970s, when the college premium was low and strong unions guaranteed favorable labor market outcomes to low-educated workers. Ramey suggested that education choices based on backward-looking outcomes might have led the 1960s cohort to underinvest in education. The authors were sympathetic to this idea.Silvana Tenreyro spoke next and suggested that deviations from rational expectations might play an important role when modeling decisions related to education and health. She offered the rise in opioid use as an example. The authors acknowledged that the determinants of health outcomes are complex. In particular, they argued that there is much uncertainty in the first place about whether health outcomes are endogenous (i.e., a result of investment decisions) or mostly exogenous, as in their model. For illustration, they cited the work of Rachel Griffith, Rodrigo Lluberas, and Melanie Lührmann (“Gluttony and Sloth? Calories, Labor Market Activity and the Rise of Obesity,” Journal of the European Economic Association 14, no. 6 [2016]: 1253–86) on the source of the rise in obesity in England. Although this increase in obesity had long been largely attributed to an increase in calorie consumption, Griffith et al. (2016) found that the change in the nature of jobs (an external change) was an important factor. In the case of opioid use, the authors pointed out that prescriptions by doctors (again, an external change) might also have played a role. This uncertainty about the endogenous or exogenous nature of health outcomes justifies their modeling choice, they argued, addressing a point raised by one of the discussants, Greg Kaplan.Erik Hurst offered two comments. The first was related to positive selection into employment, and to the work of Richard Blundell, Luigi Pistaferri, and Itay Saporta-Eksten (“Consumption Inequality and Family Labor Supply,” American Economic Review 106, no. 2 [2016]: 387–435) and Richard Blundell et al. (“Female Labor Supply, Human Capital, and Welfare Reform,” Econometrica 84, no. 5 [2016]: 1705–53). Hurst noted that selection might be particularly important for female education and labor supply. Excluding the bottom 5%–6% of the education distribution would provide a conservative robustness check, he argued. Second, Hurst inquired about the role of medical expenses in the model because they are assumed to be exogenous. On selection into employment, the authors agreed that more robustness checks were warranted and welcomed Hurst’s suggestion. On the modeling of medical expenses, they reiterated that a substantial part of medical expenses seems exogenous. For instance, doctors might prescribe newer, more expensive treatments due to fear of lawsuits, even if those treatments do not have a significant effect on life expectancy.Chad Syverson noted that health shocks only take place after retirement in the authors’ model. He suggested an extension with preretirement health shocks and disability shocks. The authors were very receptive to this comment. The evidence suggests that marriage affects the response to health and disability shocks, they argued. Allowing for preretirement health and disability, and for an interaction with marriage, is a promising avenue for future research, according to the authors.James Poterba offered a comment on measurement. Referring to the work of Bruce D. Meyer and Nikolas Mittag (“Combining Administrative and Survey Data to Improve Income Measurement” [Working Paper no. 25738, NBER, Cambridge, MA, 2019]), Poterba noted that survey data might be inaccurate for individuals at the lower end of the income distribution. Furthermore, the share of individuals reporting no income in surveys far exceeds that observed in administrative data, and the survey response rates have decreased over time, he argued. Poterba suggested that taking these measurement issues seriously is particularly important when comparing outcomes across cohorts, citing the work of Fatih Guvenen et al. (“Lifetime Incomes in the United States over Six Decades” [Working Paper, University of Minnesota, November 2018]). The authors agreed that measurement across cohorts is crucial. They noted that intercohort trends have far-reaching consequences, including political polarization and attitudes toward trade and immigration policies. Measuring outcomes accurately is a required first step toward making progress on those issues, they argued. The authors also emphasized the need to account for changes in consumption baskets across cohorts to measure price indices accurately, following up on a point raised by one of the discussants, Greg Kaplan.Benjamin Friedman concluded the discussion with a remark on assortative mating, a feature of the authors’ model. Friedman noted that the degree of assortative mating has actually increased over time. He suggested that higher education institutions might have played an important role in this trend. Although university attendance has remained stable over time, he noted, individuals now tend to study farther away from their hometown. As a consequence, the pool of individuals remaining in towns without major colleges is less qualified, contributing to increased assortative mating. title: Steven Franklin Perry (1944–2022)
abstract: Steven Franklin Perry, or Steve to most of us, was born on 14 March 1944, in Brockton, MA, USA. He attended Middlebury College in Vermont, completing his BA (Biology) in 1966 with honours courses in agronomy and radiation biology at Cornell University, USA, and the University of Rochester, USA, respectively, before going on to undertake his PhD at Boston University, USA. Steve graduated in 1972 by dissertation titled ‘The lungs of the red-eared turtle, Chrysemys (Pseudemys) scripta elegans, as a gas exchange organ: a histological and quantitative morphological study’, which set him on the path to his life's work in respiratory biology. Following completion of his PhD, Steve began a post-doctoral career that saw him work with some of the world's leading respiratory physiologists, anatomists and morphologists. His post-doctoral research began at the Max-Planck Institute for Experimental Medicine in Göttingen, West Germany (1972–74), where he worked on the morphometry of lungs and gills with Prof. J. Piiper. He then moved to the University of Bristol, UK (1974–75) to work on trout gills with Prof. G. Hughes. From there, it was back to Germany to work with Prof. H.-R. Duncker (1975–77) at the Universität Giessen on the functional anatomy of lizard lungs. Steve then took up his first academic position as an Assistent at the Universität Oldenburg (1977). During his time in Oldenburg, Steve completed his Dr habil. (Zoology) through his Habilitationsschrift entitled: ‘The functional anatomy of unicameral and multicameral lungs and its implications for the evolution of the lung structure in amniotes’, published as Perry (1983), as he progressed to a fixed-term professorship (1984). Steve then moved to Calgary, Canada, in 1987 to work with Prof. J. Remmers on the morphometrics of developing sheep lungs and the neuronal control of breathing, and during this time he became a Canadian citizen. Steve accepted a permanent appointment as a professor at the Rheinische Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität Bonn, Germany, in 1994, where he was the group leader for morphology and systematics in the zoological institute. Steve remained in Bonn for the rest of his life and career, formally retiring in 2009, after which he spent a year as a visiting professor at the Universidade de São Paulo in Ribeirão Preto, Brazil.Steve was well known to everyone in the respiratory biology field and made an enormous contribution, publishing some 125 articles through his career (many in Journal of Experimental Biology) on an array of different animals and plants. Arguably one of his most important scientific contributions was the definition of the anatomical diffusion factor that described the ratio of potentially respiratory active surface area to the harmonic mean diffusion barrier thickness (Perry, 1978). This paper provides a means of quantifying the ‘hardware’ (as Steve put it) of any respiratory organ, improving our understanding of all respiratory systems. Steve never liked publishing for the sake of it and would often comment ‘well let's just do this in the Aardvark’ if we even contemplated it. A quirk of Steve's career was that he only graduated three doctoral candidates, each of us beginning with the advice that our job was to think freely and exchange our ideas with our peers, an approach that was actively supported in lab meetings with cheesecake or, even better, facilitated in a local bar.Steve established successful collaborations with several Brazilian laboratories throughout his career, resulting in a frequent exchange of students between Germany and Brazil. One of us (W.K.) examined one of Steve's lingering questions on the division of the coelomic cavity in vertebrates and how it affects the respiratory pump. This research in the tegu lizard demonstrated how this structure prevents paradoxical breathing during locomotion (Klein et al., 2003) and provided insight into one of Steve’s other passions: the evolution of the mammalian diaphragm (Perry et al., 2010). Thorough examination of long accepted paradigms was a fascination for Steve in how ideas become entrenched and accepted dogma, often with little supporting data. Research into the role of accessory breathing structures in birds (J.R.C.) was able to confirm one of his suspicions that the uncinate processes were in fact respiratory structures (Codd et al., 2005) and provided a mechanism for explaining how dinosaurs breathed like birds (Codd et al., 2008). Steve never lost his interest in reptiles or revisiting ideas he'd published, even in his retirement, to seek new and important insights. Research into the comparative anatomy of turtles (M.L.) followed on from Steve's own dissertation and demonstrated how these could be used to address systematic questions (Lambertz et al., 2010). A lesson we all learned was the incredible value of the ‘old’ anatomical literature even if it highlights Steve's early struggle with the German language, such as trying to literally translate Scheidewand. Steve searched for interesting questions, and never cared if these fitted the mainstream, encapsulated in his life's work on respiratory organs (Perry, 1989).The integrative nature of a field like respiratory biology was something close to Steve's heart and this led him to organise the International Congress of Respiratory Science, held in 2006, 2009 and 2014, where he brought together scientists from diverse fields under one roof to break down barriers between different areas of science. The publication of his book ‘Respiratory Biology of Animals’ (Perry et al., 2019) has set the foundations for this field moving forward. You can find much of Steve's philosophy of science throughout the book, perhaps best encapsulated by the quote from the preface: ‘you may not find all the answers you are interested in, but instead will be confronted with persisting questions’. Steve was something of an exception in being someone who never tried to take possession of his field and would freely share his knowledge, passion and ideas, delighting when these would take root and produce new scientific outcomes, ways of thinking and research.Steve loved teaching and got a real kick out of interacting with students throughout his career. He would begin many classes by reassuring the students that although he considered himself a Canadian, he had been speaking German longer than any of them! If you ever attended any of his classes in Bonn, these were notable for Steve's overwhelming enthusiasm for anatomy and functional morphology, which would variously include Steve breaking into song and insisting the students joined in (whether they liked it or not) with the chorus of ‘it's a long way from Amphioxus’ to making use of any unfortunate doctoral students standing around to demonstrate hypaxial musculature. A functional anatomy course wasn't considered complete unless the obligatory ‘so long and thanks for all the fish’ was inscribed onto the blackboard in thanks. One important aspect of his teaching was the full immersion of the students into an animal's Bauplan. Steve memorably used to ask the students to close their eyes and visualize in their mind as he talked them through the pathway an oxygen molecule travels until ultimately reaching the mitochondria. Steve was an excellent anatomist and would expertly guide students through their dissections and facilitate their understanding of the changes in vertebrate structure and function through evolution.Outside of his academic life, Steve had a lifelong love of music and song and was a musician at heart. Steve was a keen member of several choirs in Bonn and the Folk Club Bonn – never happier than when he could break into song, preferably wearing a flat cap and in Welsh or interchangeably with a Norfolk or West Country accent. We all have fond memories of Steve stopping by a busker on his way through the Weihnachtsmarkt in Bonn, just to get the beat.Steven Franklin Perry died in Bonn, Germany on 13 November 2022 after a long illness, leaving behind his wife Regine. Steve lived a good life and made his mark as an academic but also as a friend and mentor to many. Those of us lucky enough to have studied and collaborated with him cherish the lessons he taught us through the memories of our time with him and we proudly carry his legacy with us.Wilfried Klein, graduated 2001Jonathan Codd, graduated 2004Markus Lambertz, graduated 2015

title: The Pain Museum
abstract: In the middle of the vast Gobi Desert, the beige sand undulates like waves. Somewhere in the shadow of one such swell, Roy Chapman Andrews stands in his camp.He wears jodhpurs and a khaki shirt, open at the neck. There is no point to buttoning it to his throat. The Mongolian sand, Roy Chapman Andrews knows, will find its way into every crease. So will the night's chill—in this rain-shadow desert, the temperature can drop sixty degrees in twelve hours—and the venomous snakes seek the warmth of tents.It is June 1922, and sandstorms whirl into existence without warning. Yellow sand shreds the American flag above camp into red and blue ribbons. The men survive only by huddling in depressions, wet cloths pressed to their mouths, nearly suffocating. It sounds, to me, like certain hell. Still, Roy Chapman Andrews would rather be no other place on earth, and for this, I love him. When I was seven, my father gave me two books from his childhood, All About Dinosaurs and All About Strange Beasts of the Past. They were from the American naturalist and explorer Roy Chapman Andrews's All About series of the 1950s.All About Strange Beasts of the Past opens with a saber-toothed tiger drowning in the La Brea tar pits. The tiger struggles and dies alongside two ground sloths, one imperial mammoth, and six black vultures. Within a few paragraphs, all the animals are dead. It was, and remains, one of the formative books of my life.Roy Chapman Andrews is a good writer, especially for children. The prose is matter-of-fact: “We know that people of early times loved to eat animal brains—the bigger, the better!” He describes how early man killed woolly mammoths and rhinoceroses by driving them into previously dug pits.The texts are illustrated, and one accompanying image shows a bellowing woolly rhino at the bottom of a pit, surrounded from above by seven Ice Age-era men, each holding a spear or heavy rock. The caption: Frequently, cave men would kill a trapped rhino by dropping stones on its head and body.I traced this illustration with my finger over and over again, wanting to feel the bristle of the rhino, as if this were Pat the Bunny. The psychologist Jerome Bruner has identified two primary modes of human thought. One, the logico-scientific, seeks to fulfill a mathematical ideal of explanation. The other, the narrative mode, relies upon story, drama, and believable, though not necessarily true, historical accounts. The modes are not mutually exclusive. Both have value, or should be valued equally.The logico-scientific mode is also known as the paradigmatic mode. It is the mode of science, of logical categorizing. I imagine it was the primary mode of Roy Chapman Andrews and my father, the engineer-turned-geologist.Try as I might to be more scientific, I fail. I ascribe meaning and build story. I cannot escape narrative. How can any of us, even the most scientifically detached? What is science without story? Lately I have been thinking about the dead explorer Roy Chapman Andrews, and my living father, and how the living can feel as far away as the dead.About narrative—always narrative—and my heart, that museum of old pain. Roy Chapman Andrews on the mating habits of whales: It was positively indecent the way I pried into the private lives of whales during those days at sea. With a pair of field glasses from the masthead, I watched the love-making of a pair of humpback whales fifty feet long. An amorous bull whale may be very amusing to us but to his lady friend he is doubtless as exciting as a matinee idol is to a debutante.Roy Chapman Andrews: matinee idol. Roy Chapman Andrews was not handsome. Prematurely balding, thin-lipped. What hair he had was the color of hair. In a polo match, an opponent called him a “bald-headed bone-digger.” Even when he was a young man, his hairline sat nearly right on the top of his head, a few degrees shy of the prime meridian of his skull.Still, women wrote to him: I know from the kindness and nobility of your face that you know how to treat a lady. . . . I am sending my photograph, but it is much better to see the original. How would Friday afternoon do for tea?Another letter: I wish I could decorate you on both cheeks the way the French do, but if I ever put my arms around you I'd never want to take them away. You are a grand person, one of the world's swankiest and My Gawd, you can park your shoes next to mine anytime you feel the urge.Roy Chapman Andrews received this letter when he was approximately fifty-three years old. A photo of him at that age features him in a three-piece suit, looking like a banker or Midwestern minister, holding an elk skull by one antler. Roy Chapman Andrews: father figure. I have chosen an unlikely father figure in Roy Chapman Andrews. He loved and doted upon his two sons, George and Kevin. He and his first wife, Yvette, separated in 1930 and he remarried Billie Christmas, but his boys remained at the heart of the household. And then in 1937, Yvette showed up and told her ex-husband that Kevin was not his son, but the product of a long-term affair.After that, Kevin does not appear in any—any—of Roy Chapman Andrews's books or articles. His ex-father spends an entire chapter of the autobiography An Explorer Comes Home writing about his deaf cat, Lord Jitters, and another on a particularly sociable duck; still, he does not spend a single word on Kevin, the boy raised as his son for thirteen years.Kevin never existed. Like a desert sandstorm, he was there and howling one minute. Then he simply disappeared.Like I said: I have chosen an unlikely role model in Roy Chapman Andrews. Perhaps you are sensing a recurring motif. Perhaps you recall Electra, who plotted against her mother. (Think Greece, not Marvel.) Perhaps you worry this essay will have a section about my failed relationships, my constant search for approval.Perhaps you are writing daddy issues on your therapist's pad and underlining it one, two, three times.I haven't called my father daddy since I was eight, so I would prefer the word father, if you don't mind. You have not heard of Roy Chapman Andrews. You do not know about the Gobi expeditions of the 1920s, the line of black Dodges he drove into the desert. You do not know of the nest of Oviraptor eggs, the nest lying under sand all these years, the first dinosaur eggs ever found.You think: Indiana Jones. But there is no evidence that either George Lucas or Steven Spielberg knew Roy Chapman Andrews. There are no notes about Roy Chapman Andrews in the early Raiders script conferences.But there are notes about basing Indy on the pulpy heroes of paperbacks, dapper in their khakis and broad-brimmed hats. Those pulpy heroes, who—of course, you know this even as you read it—were based on Roy Chapman Andrews, the American swashbuckler of the 1920s.Roy Chapman Andrews was not afraid of snakes, as Indiana Jones is. Still, he did not particularly enjoy the night he camped near the Flaming Cliffs and was visited by forty-seven pit vipers. There is a difference between playing a phobia for comedic effect and having to kill venomous snakes that have wrapped themselves around the legs of your cot.Roy Chapman Andrews found the fossil of the Beast of Baluchistan, an ancient rhinoceros relative that stood fifteen feet tall. The Beast of Baluchistan served as the model for the AT-ATs in The Empire Strikes Back. Everything circles back to Roy Chapman Andrews, eventually.Meanwhile, in a corner of camp, Roy Chapman Andrews pulls his battered hat over his eyes and dozes. When you are digging for fossils, you must examine each fragment for meaning. What is this, where did it come from, what might it mean? You throw aside nothing until you know for sure that it is valueless. You learn to collect, then cull. Slowly, you build your museum. Roy Chapman Andrews writes in chapter one of his autobiography, Under a Lucky Star, “I don't think anyone but myself would give a tinker's damn about those boyhood years. As a rule, nothing of much interest happens to a young man until he is out of college.”As a child, he learned how to shoot a double-barreled shotgun. In his teens, he taught himself taxidermy from a text, became the best in Beloit, Wisconsin. His best friend drowned in a canoeing accident and Roy Chapman Andrews nearly did too. He clawed and crawled through the icy water and collapsed on a farmhouse porch. He lost nearly all his hair within a year. After graduation, he traveled to New York, where he talked his way into a job at the American Museum of Natural History. Years later, he would become the museum's director.Tinker's damn. Roy Chapman Andrews on the importance of self-discovery: Cocaine, morphia, heroin, hashish—I tried them all to satisfy my insatiable curiosity . . . [Cocaine] took effect within the hour. I got, I suppose, what alcohol gives to some men: a sense of the most wonderful well-being, a feeling of power unlimited, and the ability to do anything in the world. The ability to do anything in the world.Roy Chapman Andrews was the first to organize a desert expedition that used camels as well as motor cars, and he drove them deep into Mongolia. He spent nearly all of the 1920s planning, raising funds for, and executing his massive Central Asiatic Expeditions.Roy Chapman Andrews adopted baby antelopes and crows as pets, fended off bandits, and found a shitload of fossils. During their time back in Peking, he drank noon cocktails and played polo in an unsettled China. Outside the club walls, political prisoners were beheaded.I put the syllables of Roy Chapman Andrews into my mouth and I hold them there until they soften slightly. They roll around on my tongue: Roy Chapman Andrews. Roy Chapman Andrews Roy Chapman Andrews Roy Chapman Andrews Roy Chapman Andrews Roy Chapman Andrews. Roy Chapman Andrews!Roy Chapman Andrews: a mantra. In Dragon Hunter, the 2001 biography of Roy Chapman Andrews, author Charles Gallenkamp acknowledges Roy Chapman Andrews's propensity for exaggeration:The encounter with bandits, the foiled mutiny in the Korean wilderness, and the tiger hunt at Musan . . . all ended up in Andrews’ popular books and articles as partly romanticized, but to what extent it is difficult to determine . . . They are clear-cut examples of his liberal use of literary license as a means of appealing to general readers; moreover, such suspenseful stories greatly enhanced his adventurous image.Roy Chapman Andrews, despite his scientific training, constructed narrative. Would we say that the facts do not add up to his truth? Would we trot out our tired tropes about the tension inherent in the phrase creative nonfiction? Do we point out the techniques of the fictioneer, borrowed by the essayist?And what of the lawyer's question, that of intent? Does Roy Chapman Andrews, writing in 1940, draw more or fewer comparisons to James Frey? Are we still talking about goddamn James Frey? Did I really just bring up James Frey, and am I really going to leave him here, in the same paragraph with Roy Chapman Andrews?Without the narrative mode, I might not get out of bed. But even then, lying on my back, staring at the ceiling, I would build pattern from the popcorn. Roy Chapman Andrews: origin story. I do not think of Roy Chapman Andrews as father figure, nor do I want him as one. I have a father already. Once we were close, extremely close, and now he is remarried and we rarely speak.If you asked my father why we don't talk much anymore, he would have his account. If you were to ask me, I would have mine. Both accounts are true, though we fail to recognize each other's as true.Truths are not mutually exclusive.I have hurt my father, and he has hurt me. The details of these hurts may not be impressive, nor may they matter. What matters is that we have each turned our hearts into little pain museums, and every so often we visit the displays.At night, when everyone else is asleep, I like to dust my pains. I arrange them so that in the morning, they will catch the light.I align the pains into something resembling story. I visit them regularly, telling myself each time that it is not an obsession but a dissection. Not dwelling, but diagnosing.Surely I deserve some credit for this distinction, I lie to myself. In one of my favorite pictures of Roy Chapman Andrews, he is captured in profile, gazing at a vulture. He stares into the beady eyes of the bird, the nearest living relative of the dinosaurs. This is years before Ostrum, before Gauthier, before cladistics. Evolution, it turns out, is science plus narrative.Man and raptor's gaze is steely-eyed. It is confident. It is reflected in the bird's, reflected in Roy's, an endless bounceback. Behind them, the Gobi Desert stretches to the edge of the horizon. Still they hold each other's eyes. Roy Chapman Andrews: metaphor. What do we do with these rocks we gather, these fossils of our pains? We are traveling exhibitions. I take mine with me from town to town. For the price of admission, I will reveal each to you.Here is every comment my father ever made about my weight, its shape and its similarity to my mother's. Here is how I hear that, still, naked in the shower.Here is the time he, in the heat of an argument, called me by my mother's—his ex-wife's—name. Here is how he refused to acknowledge me as I lost my temper, taught me that I was not worthy of attention until I learned to chain my rage.How he did not understand me, and later, more painfully, refused to try.My exhibit lacks contextualization; I have not built you a diorama of my happy suburban childhood or the nights my father sat with me at the dining room table while I laboriously wrote out logic proofs. I have not built a display of the picnics we had on the shores of Lake Erie with pizza subs, our laughs steaming in the March wind.There is no accompanying plaque announcing that the exhibitor understands that on the spectrum of this planet's suffering, among the famines and floods and extinctions, her problems are tiny, little chips of bone. I thought that Roy Chapman Andrews was my father's childhood hero, but I was wrong. My father read the books, sure, and was captivated by the giant sloth. But it was my imagination alone that made Roy Chapman Andrews the reason that my father studied geology.My mind alone conflated the two men, created narrative. Or perhaps it gave me a reason to reach out to my father, some way of feeling close to him. To reach over the years, stretch way back to the good ones, when we were a team.Roy Chapman Andrews: stand-in. Roy Chapman Andrews was just a man. My father is just a man. title: Innovaciones tecnológicas para la elaboración de brotes de hortalizas foliáceas mínimamente procesadas en fresco
abstract:
Los alimentos vegetales minimamente procesados en fresco (MPF), tambien conocidos como productos de la ?Cuarta gama? de la alimentacion, cobran cada vez mayor importancia ante el progresivo interes de los consumidores por la alimentacion saludable y la practicidad de su facil preparacion. Cada dia son mas las personas preocupadas por incluir en su dieta alimentos ricos en compuestos bioactivos, los cuales se asocian a la prevencion de enfermedades cardiovasculares, cancer, artritis y mejora del sistema inmunologico, entre otras. Es sabido que una dieta equilibrada, abundante en frutas y hortalizas, favorece la salud y reduce el riesgo de enfermedades. Las hortalizas son alimentos baratos, pobres en grasas y ricos en vitaminas, minerales, antioxidantes y fibra. Entre los productos MPF (PMPF) estan de moda las mezclas de hortalizas foliaceas y hierbas cultivadas, que incluyen brotes de espinaca y lechuga o escarola, entre otros, procedentes de cultivo hidroponico.
El consumo en fresco de hortalizas foliaceas se ha incrementado en los ultimos anos y entre ellas se encuentran brotes de gran interes por sus propiedades saludables como la espinaca (Spinacia oleracea L.), la rucula (Eruca sativa) y la colleja (Silene vulgaris). A pesar de ello existe muy poca informacion acerca de su comportamiento postrecoleccion, especialmente como PMPF. Ademas, se dispone de escaso conocimiento sobre el efecto en la postcosecha de cultivar dichos productos en el sistema de bandejas flotantes y de utilizar distintas dosis de abonados nitrogenados. Por todo ello, los objetivos de investigacion en esta Tesis se enfocan a caracterizar diversas variedades de espinaca, rucola y colleja y determinar su vida util bajo diferentes factores y tecnicas pre y postcosecha. Para ello se estudian distintas condiciones de cultivo, determinando los principales atributos de calidad de los productos, ademas de alternativas tecnologicas eco-innovadoras para sustituir al hipoclorito sodico en la etapa de desinfeccion de su procesado minimo industrial.
En cuanto a los resultados obtenidos destaca que la espinaca ha mostrado una muy elevada intensidad metabolica y que la mayor tasa respiratoria (TR) inicial se determino en la variedad ?Eagle?, con 179 mg CO2 kg-1h-1. La produccion de etileno fue muy baja, inferior a 1 ?L kg-1h-1 en todas las variedades y en los diferentes brotes estudiados. Este comportamiento metabolico es el tipico de un organo vegetal no climaterico. Las variedades ?Koala? y ?Eagle? presentaron una apariencia visual y calidad global inferior a la observada en las demas variedades, por lo que se consideran menos recomendables comercialmente.
La TR de la rucula a 5 y 8oC no presento diferencias notables, salvo un ligero aumento inicial a 8oC. El incremento observado al final de su almacenamiento refrigerado se ha atribuido al desarrollo microbiano. Las atmosferas modificadas (AM) de equilibrio fueron 5-10 kPa O2 + 10-15 kPa CO2 a 5oC mientras que a 8oC fueron 1-5 kPa O2 + 15-20 kPa CO2. Respecto del color, la rucula lavada en una solucion de ClO2 u O3 durante la etapa de desinfeccion de su procesado minimo, preservo la luminosidad de las hojas durante 19 dias a 5oC, sin producirse diferencias en el Chroma y oHue.
El analisis sensorial reflejo como la rucula lavada con O3 y la testigo presentaron una peor calificacion global tras 19 dias a 8oC, aunque ambas permanecieron por encima del limite de comercializacion. Tras 19 dias, los brotes no presentaron diferencias entre los lavados, pero si con respecto a la temperatura de conservacion, ya que se calificaron como no comercializables los brotes almacenados a 8oC. El recuento de microorganismos mesofilos mostro que a 5oC los brotes de todos los tratamientos, excepto el testigo, permanecieron hasta el dia 19 por debajo de los niveles legales vigentes en su momento, mientras que a 8oC la vida comercial fue de solo 14 dias. Los brotes lavados con 4 ppm ClO2 y 100 ppm NaClO presentaron los menores recuentos microbianos a ambas temperaturas.
Los brotes tratados con 9,08 kJ UV-C m-2 previamente a su envasado en AM presentaron la mayor deshidratacion tras 9 dias a 5oC, situandose en el limite de comercializacion. El recuento de mesofilos para la variedad ?Coltivata? no presento diferencias entre tratamientos, manteniendose por debajo de los limites permitidos por la legislacion hasta el final de la conservacion. Para la ?Accesion local 02-248?, tras 11 dias de conservacion a 5oC, el testigo cultivado en bandejas flotantes bajo un abonado de 70/30 mmol / L (NO3 - / NH4 +), y la combinacion de un pre-tratamiento con 2,04 kJ UV-C m-2 en los abonados 30/70 y en el 50/50 mmol / L, superaban los limites legales microbiologicos entonces permitidos.
Las concentraciones en el interior de los envases de rucula ?Coltivata? y ?Accesion local 02-248? conservadas en alto O2 fueron 72-60 kPa O2 y 15-18 kPa CO2 respectivamente, por lo que su conservacion se ha realizado en una AM sobreoxigenada, moderadamente enriquecida en CO2. Las hojas de rucula de ambos cultivares presentaron una tendencia similar, en donde las conservadas en alto O2 fueron las que menor degradacion de clorofilas presentaron durante el tiempo de almacenamiento y, en consecuencia, las que tuvieron mayor aceptacion sensorial.
El comportamiento observado en los cuatro cultivares de colleja estudiados fueron los siguientes: la TR inicial fue mayor para las Accesiones 04-403 y 04-404 que en el resto, encontrandose en rangos de 85-87 mg CO2 kg-1h-1. Tras 13 dias a 5oC la respiracion se incremento, probablemente debido al desarrollo microbiano. La evolucion de la atmosfera para todas las Accesiones fue similar, sin presentar cambios importantes durante 22 dias a 5oC, registrandose niveles de 6-10 kPa O2 y 10-14 kPa CO2, que se consideran muy apropiados para su conservacion. Los brotes de la ?Accesion 01-309? presentaron una apariencia visual y una calidad global superior a las evaluadas en las demas Accesiones. La tendencia de la evolucion de la capacidad antioxidante total fue de disminuir ligeramente en todas las accesiones hasta el final de la conservacion. Por su parte, la evolucion de los polifenoles totales en la ?Accesion 04-403? aumento durante la vida comercial, a diferencia de la ?Accesion 01-309?, que presento una disminucion. La clorofila total se encontro entre 1y 1,3 g kg-1 pf, siendo el mayor contenido para la ?Accesion 02-255?, y sin existir diferencias importantes durante la conservacion.

abstract: ---New since 2026-07-03 VV3 Geometric Grammar of Wildfire Fields: Field-Theoretic Structure of Firefront Stability and Atmospheric Coupling "fire is the emergent validity condition of a constrained geometric language under incomplete observation." VV3__Geometric_Grammar_of_Wildfire__Fields-Theoretic-Structure_of_Firefront_Stability_and_Atmospheric_Coupling__Vening20260703.pdf "Collaboration " StatementThis work emerged from sustained human persistance in a non-linear development where LLM AI has been productive in the formatting and styling of the documents., the author notes that no single unique pattern emerged from collaboration, this is due to the nidek also the nature of this work, is also speculative, The collaboration should be understood as an expensive iterative research dialogue in which hypotheses, mathematical structures, notation, and scientific narratives were progressively refined through interactive exchange. De kwaliteit en de toon kan op sommige delen van deze documenten distinct anders zijn., of een verlaten undruk wekken. Q & A E.J..Vening : chargen@gmail.com ---New since 2026-07-03Lo-Fi Geometric Sensing Architecture for Wildfire Early Warning and Firefighter Tooling VV4__Ideas_for_networks_deployment_sensors_circuitry_notes.pdf Wildfire response is one of the few human professions where individuals routinely walk toward danger rather than away from it. This manuscript is dedicated to all mission specialists worldwide: firefighters, incident commanders, air‑operations crews, drone pilots, sensor engineers, meteorologists, ecologists, and volunteers who protect lives, land, and species. The author wishes to honor and pay respect to these individuals, acknowledging that every conceptual advance in sensing, modeling, or mitigation is ultimately meant to support their safety and effectiveness. These theories are offered in the hope that they may someday contribute to practical tools, improved situational awareness, and reduced risk. People, you are not alone; together we inform each other and share knowledge. Every insight, every sensor, every algorithm is part of a shared global effort. Especial thanks to the people in New Zealand and Australia who ran into a wildfire because a koala was burning alive and could not escape from its position in a eucalyptus tree. Their act reflects the deepest human instinct: to protect life, even at personal risk. This manuscript is written in the spirit of that courage. ---New since 2026-07-03 Lo-Fi Geometric Sensing Architecture for Wildfire Early Warning and Firefighter Tooling {Integrated Geometric Wildfire Mitigation System: Vening Field-Tuned Bio-Organic Ice Projectile Delivery with Lo-Fi CSOTA Telemetry Conceptual Synthesis and Engineering Specification shades_vii_lofi_drone_sentry.pdf This publication-ready specification details a closed-loop system combining Vening's Geometric Field Framework with lo-fi CSOTA sensing and bio-organic ice projectiles. Real-time telemetry from passive nodes feeds precise targeting of wildfire velocities, humidity collapse fields, and vortex points. Hollow-point munitions with aerogel-biodegradable shells deliver compressed payloads that expand into cold/moist/gas bubbles upon impact, disrupting key geometric fields for effective mitigation. chargen_iceviii_moisture_exp_delivery.pdfThis document details a closed-loop wildfire mitigation system integrating Vening's Geometric Field Framework with a bio-organic ice projectile delivery mechanism. The system combines lo-fi CSOTA sensing for real-time targeting with hollow-point NATO-style munitions containing cryoprotected bio-agents in high-density ice (Ice VII polymorphs). Upon impact, phase transitions and autocatalytic reactions produce targeted cold/moist/gas bubbles disrupting key fire geometry. Aerogel-biodegradable shells ensure flight stability and ecological compatibility. Rate-of-fire estimates and Vening equation tuning are provided. Integrated Geometric Wildfire Mitigation Architecture: Vening Field-Tuned Cryogenic Environmental Intervention System hippies_i_d_wei__Heijssens2026__prolif...pdf Wildfires are not merely combustion events; they are dynamic, evolving atmospheric systems shaped by geometry, energy transport, moisture gradients, and coupled environmental feedback loops. This document presents a conceptual closed-loop wildfire mitigation architecture combining geometric sensing, multi-scale environmental reconstruction, and precision delivery of localized cooling and moisture-restoring interventions. The proposed framework integrates Vening's Geometric Field perspective with advanced sensing networks, atmospheric state estimation, and phase-transition-based environmental response mechanisms. Rather than treating wildfire suppression as a purely reactive process, the system approaches fire behavior as a measurable evolving field: a structure of heat, airflow, humidity collapse, aerosol transport, and convective organization. Through distributed sensing, real-time field reconstruction, and targeted intervention, the architecture explores a future where wildfire management becomes increasingly predictive, adaptive, and environmentally intelligent. The objective is not simply to extinguish fire, but to restore stability within the physical conditions that allow ecosystems and communities to persist. This work represents a speculative synthesis of atmospheric physics, materials science, ecological engineering, and computational sensing. It explores how geometry itself may become a language for understanding, anticipating, and mitigating extreme environmental events. --- Wildfires002: A Geometric, Multi‑Scale, and Field‑Theoretic Framework for Adaptive Wildfire Mitigation please note: the default 'in focus' document has been set to wildfires002_en.pdf". title: The Seven Deadly Sins, Quintessence Theatre Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
abstract: For the past year restrictions on public gatherings necessitated by the Covid pandemic have precluded live performances, leaving most theaters dark. Yet, as most theater practitioners recognize, constraints—rather than depressing and inhibiting action—often conduce creativity and innovation. Philadelphia's Quintessence Theatre has risen to this challenge admirably in their digital presentation of Thornton Wilder's one-act play cycle The Seven Deadly Sins as radio plays, available for streaming in June 2021. Although audience members could listen to the seven recorded performances in any sequence, the company presented them in the order Wilder intended, made available on demand in two batches. The plays representing Gluttony, Pride, Sloth, and Envy played from 10 to 13 June; Wrath, Lust, and Avarice ran 17–20 June. With these expert performances, aided by excellent digital program notes, Quintessence has made a great contribution to Wilder's drama in presenting all seven plays in one production. When experienced as a unified whole the one-act plays reveal compelling thematic threads and connections.In the late 1950s and early 1960s, Wilder experimented with two seven-part play cycles—one based on the Christian sins and the other on Shakespeare's Ages of Man. Three of the cycle plays received their first productions in 1961 directed by José Quintero at New York's Circle in the Square: Infancy and Childhood from The Seven Ages of Man and Someone from Assisi (Lust) from The Seven Deadly Sins. In anticipation of this production Wilder gave an interview to Arthur Gelb of the New York Times, in which he expounded on his interest in the “sins” and “ages”: “I am interested in the drives that operate in society and in every man… . Pride, avarice and envy are in every home. I am not interested in the ephemeral—such subjects as the adulteries of dentists. I am interested in those things that repeat and repeat and repeat in the lives of the millions.” (Wilder's “dentist” remark may have been directed at Clifford Odets's Rocket to the Moon [produced in 1938; published in 1939].) Wilder praised Circle in the Square for its arena staging (“We have to kick the proscenium down”) and anticipated the current audio production: “The box set encourages the anecdote… . The unencumbered stage encourages the truth operative in everyone. The less seen, the more heard. The eye is the enemy of the ear in real drama” (74). In successfully recreating the intimacy of Golden Age radio drama, Quintessence's presentations allowed listeners to hear rather than see Wilder's drama.Each of the plays opened with a spoken welcome from “Thornton Wilder” (voiced with charming avuncularity by Michael Brusasco) with comments gleaned from Wilder's writing. This conceit worked splendidly in providing a brief background to each play and setting the appropriate mood—a wonderful benefit for audience members who fail to read program notes. Unfortunately, none of the productions used this conceit within the performances themselves in which a voiced narration would have been very helpful to describe stage actions and settings. Several times listeners without access to a script could have been confused, especially with Wilder's final tableaus.The first play, The Drunken Sisters, represents Gluttony and unlike other parts of the cycles, serves a previous purpose as the satyr play to Wilder's Greek tragedy The Alcestiad (1955; Collected Plays 370–430). This connection to ancient mythological drama (it features the god Apollo and the Three Fates) marks the playlet as an outlier in form among the other “sin” plays that are otherwise realistic. The Drunken Sisters is also the most farcical of the seven, and as “Wilder” declared in the spoken introduction to the Quintessence production, “it is best to begin with a comedy.” The actors portraying the Fates (Hanna Gaffney, Leigha Kato, and Marcia Saunders) enriched their portrayals with marvelous crone cackles and inebriated leerings—making the most out of their voices to evoke the play's farcical elements. But, as would occur in some of the other presentations, the actors' voices—while resonant and compelling—too often sounded too similar, confusing the listener as to which character was speaking. This production also failed to make the most of the differences among the fates (one “weaves” the thread of life, one “measures,” and one “cuts” [Collected Plays 435])—differences that Wilder emphasizes in his stage directions. Steven A. Wright as Apollo performed well in transforming from a disguised slave to a revealed god, but could have been broader and funnier in his comic song evoking the Nine Muses. The production ended with a non-textual addition. In the script Apollo speaks the final line of “Alcestis! Alcestis!” calling for the doomed queen as he “runs stumbling from the scene” (Collected Plays 443). Quintessence's production added a canny coda of the three sisters laughing and repeating the Oedipus riddle which had fascinated them. This mini-epilogue served as a nice reminder of the Fates' continuing role as deciders of destiny.The second play, Bernice, illustrates Pride and premiered in Berlin in 1957, with Ethel Waters as the title character (a housekeeper/cook) and the playwright himself as Mr. Walbeck (recently released from prison for his crime of embezzlement). “Thornton Wilder” informs the listener that the author based the play on the 1956 movie version of Ben Hecht's novella Miracle in the Rain. In the tradition of Hattie McDaniel, Zuhairah McGill performed expertly as the witty and wise black servant and also successfully brought out the character's darker aspects. But Kevin Bergen sounded too young to be the grave and stolid ex-convict. For the expository role of “Driver,” the production again failed to differentiate the characters' voices. Wilder's script describes the driver as “Irish, slightly drunk” (Collected Plays 497). If the actor had adopted a brogue—a choice clearly supported, even encouraged, by the script—the Irish accent would have not only helped differentiate the voices but added some needed levity to the otherwise somber scene. More than any of the other plays Bernice benefits from a joint production. On its own the brief play reads as thin and unsatisfying (Wilder himself withdrew it from performance). Yet when placed in context with its companion pieces, it emphasizes Wilder's recurring theme of regretful consequences, particularly among parents. In the Times interview Wilder claimed that “the reason why the world is in such a sloppy state … is that our parents were so stupid” (74).In the production of The Wreck on the Five-Twenty-Five (Sloth), the actors performed excellently in varying their voices, each one making strong tonal choices. The mother, Mrs. Hawkins (Sarah Gliko), and her daughter, Minnie (Leigha Kato), sounded completely believable as members of different generations. Kevin Bergen as the neighbor Mr. Forbes stood out as a comically superficial car salesman. The actor astutely exploited Wilder's ability to evoke a compelling character with only a few lines. The play's motif of voyeurism resonated particularly well in a “radio” presentation, as the audience overheard the characters as they watched the world pass by through windows. This production also employed many suitable sound effects, an element sometimes missing from the other presentations. Even mundane sounds of household bustling can greatly enrich the listening experience in terms of verisimilitude. The play is also the most modern of the cycle in its setting, making several references to the looming threat of atomic war.A Ringing of Doorbells, which concerns an elaborate scheme to defraud a rich woman, recalls Wilder's earlier one-act play Queens of France (1931; Collected Plays 80–92), which similarly illustrates how an imaginative scam can positively affect the “mark” or “pigeon.” The Quintessence production began well with Sabrina Profitt as Mrs. McCullum, the housekeeper, taking a cue from her character's name by speaking in a lilting Irish accent. A listening audience requires strong, even eccentric, character voices for clarity as well as variety. Charlotte Booker, as Mrs. Beattie, the wealthy widow, and Erika Rolfsrud (Mrs. Kinkaid) and Leigha Kato (Daphne), as the mother–daughter grifters, performed their parts very well, but the lack of narration greatly marred this production. The plot hinges on Mrs. Beattie's ultimate reaction to the exposed mother and daughter's attempt to swindle her. The aged widow—who has lost a daughter—envies the relationship of the two con women. Unfortunately, the author left the play unfinished. Wilder scholar and friend F. J. O'Neil provided an ending for the one-act, based on his discussions with the playwright, published in the first volume of The Collected Short Plays of Thornton Wilder. He revealed that Wilder wished to bring the play “to a logical, but unconventional conclusion” (Collected Plays 861). O'Neil ends the scene: [Mrs. Beattie and Daphne look at one another. Mrs. Kinkaid and Mrs. McCullum are frozen where they stand. Mrs. Beattie glances at Mrs. Kinkaid and then toward the antique cabinet on which stand the telephone and a writing kit with a pen holder and a checkbook. She moves carefully to the cabinet and pauses as if coming to an important decision.]MRS. BEATTIE:[Alive and together … that's the point.][Mrs. Beattie picks up the pen and checkbook, and turns back to face Daphne and Mrs. Kinkaid, as the lights fade.] (Collected Plays 532) As presented by Quintessence—without narrated stage directions—the spoken words alone of this ending left a listener confused, mystified, and unsatisfied.The first batch of four plays strongly emphasizes the “Deadly” in the cycle's title. All four feature death in some way, sometimes murder. The second group of three concerns the less dire consequences of sin in their focus on manners and reputation. Wilder ascribed the sin Wrath to In Shakespeare and the Bible. Although anger plays a major part in John Lubbock's past, it does not seem ultimately to have damaged the young attorney (voiced by Lee Cortopassi). His ambition, rather than his temper, causes the break with his fiancée Katy Buckingham (Leigha Kato). Zuhairah McGill excelled as Mrs. Mowbrey, Katy's estranged aunt and a retired madam. She captured all the nuances of charm and steely resolve in Wilder's character. As written and performed, Mrs. Mowbrey eclipses the supposed exemplum of Wrath, John Lubbock. Katy exhibits the true illustration of Wrath in her fascination with her namesake in The Taming of the Shrew. She claims not to have a temper, instead “turning all cold and stormy inside”—yet this coldness is the expression of her anger that ends the engagement (Collected Plays 543). As with his The Ringing of Doorbells, Wilder also left this play incomplete at his death. The published script, as edited by O'Neil, ends with Lubbock uncertain whether to pursue his recently exited fiancée or to stay with the retired madam who offers him social and political advancement. He finally “exits in the direction Mrs. Mowbrey has taken” (551). Sadly, listeners to the Quintessence production not privy to the stage directions are left with an uncertain, truncated ending.Along with The Drunken Sisters, Someone from Assisi (Lust) is the only other play without a modern or middle-class setting. The title refers to St. Francis (Stephen A. Wright) and his effect (both disastrous and revelatory) on women. In the introduction “Thornton Wilder” quotes from the author's journals: “The difficulty of ‘Someone from Assisi’ is to carry the burden of two tremendous elements as subordinate to elements that must overweight them … the idea of the Erotic as Destroyer and the Erotic as Creative” (Journals 272). Marcia Saunders perfectly embodied Wilder's erotic duality as the passion-plagued Mona Lucrezia. Hanna Gaffney also succeeded as the precocious child Pica, another example of this production allowing secondary characters to shine momentarily. This presentation used sounds to great effect, beginning with nuns chanting (non-scripted)—perfectly setting the scene through showing (broadcasting) rather than telling.The final play, Cement Hands, illustrates Avarice, “America's favorite sin” according to the spoken introduction. The title refers to a slang expression that describes the stingy unwillingness to extract money from one's pockets. This one-act with its sour ending could serve as a satyr play for Wilder's farce The Matchmaker (Collected Plays 285–367). Both dramas comically depict a miser, set the action in the private room of an expensive New York restaurant, and examine the relationship between money and marriage. The Quintessence production took proper advantage of the restaurant setting in its employment of suitable background sound effects. As with the previous two plays, Cement Hands dramatizes a sin that may be hurtful but not necessarily “deadly” in that it may be accommodated. At the end of Cement Hands, Diana (Leigha Kato) returns to the restaurant to leave a tip for Paul the waiter, an act that her fiancée (Lee Cortopassi), a chronic miser, cannot perform himself. Wilder's script reads: Paul, alone, picks up the tip. No expression on his face. Diana appears quickly.DIANA:I dropped a glove.(She drops a dollar bill on the table) Goodbye, Paul. (Collected Plays 583) Again, Quintessence's otherwise exceptional presentations (uniformly well-acted), by not supplying narration, leave the listener confused, diluting another Wilder ending.Although the Covid pandemic has temporarily robbed theatergoers of the thrill and immediacy inherent in live performances, recorded productions such as this one of The Seven Deadly Sins allows listeners, both present and future, nonetheless to experience Wilder's drama as it should be experienced, enlivened, and enacted by theater artists.

title: Barbara A. Hanawalt and Lisa J. Kiser, eds., Engaging with Nature: Essays on the Natural World in Medieval and Early Modern EuropeEngaging with Nature: Essays on the Natural World in Medieval and Early Modern Europe. Edited by Barbara A. Hanawalt and Lisa J. Kiser. Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press, 2008. Pp. vi+236.
abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeBook ReviewBarbara A. Hanawalt and Lisa J. Kiser, eds., Engaging with Nature: Essays on the Natural World in Medieval and Early Modern Europe Engaging with Nature: Essays on the Natural World in Medieval and Early Modern Europe. Edited by Barbara A. Hanawalt and Lisa J. Kiser. Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press, 2008. Pp. vi+236.Elizabeth OldmanElizabeth OldmanUniversity of Miami Search for more articles by this author PDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreIn medieval and early modern Europe, Barbara Hanawalt and Lisa Kiser indicate in the introduction to their collection of essays, the subject of the human engagement with nature for the first time becomes a primary object of inquiry rather than an ancillary consideration encountered on the road to some “more essential” matter. The seven essays included in their volume confirm a growing resistance to rigidly constructed categories and assumed outcomes in the study of and writing about science. How various writers, artists, philosophers, and others position themselves in relation to these imperatives serves as a common consideration in these analyses.Several of the essays, accordingly, are devoted to charting the recognition of potentialities, instances in investigations of the natural world in which incipient knowledge precedes language on the way to innovative insight. Whether in the realms of hunting, collecting, or animal inspection and analysis, the impulse to press nature to reveal its secrets—particularly efforts to master, rein in, or replicate in art—becomes paramount. Some of the most delightful outcomes emphasized by this volume are nature’s frequently unpredictable responses to, or downright rebellions against, human efforts to know completely.The opening essay, by Richard C. Hoffman, analyzes the shaping of the perception of the relationship between man and nature when natural scientists no longer assume that nature inexorably pushes toward some sort of balance. Hoffman investigates climate fluctuations and related atmospheric phenomena and concurrent cycles of drought, famine, and disease as a means of convincingly demonstrating that medieval Europeans were not merely passive victims of the vicissitudes of natural forces but rather partnered with nature in the evolution of history.In the particularly strong essay that follows, Jeffrey Jerome Cohen shows how medieval people created “thought experiments” in which animals served as opportunities to “try on” or sample identities that had the potential to exceed constricting limits of race, gender, and sexuality. Noteworthy is Cohen’s consideration of representations of the “promiscuous” and “hermaphroditic” hyena (yena) in the Physiologus and manuscript illustration in the Aberdeen Bestiary (manuscript illustration included) as allegory for stereotypical Jewish “duplicity” or “shiftiness” (46). Sinking its fangs and claws into a corpse in an act of savage desecration, this beast at once serves as paradigm for human limitation, bound by stereotype, and a means of seeing beyond the suffocation of being merely Christian or, more generally, merely human. No sooner does the “inherently unstabl(e)” (52) animal serve as a model for what humans think of each other and what they might develop into, then it departs on an unanticipated path to an undisclosed location. It goes, quite simply, “on its own way” (57).Susan Crane turns to an analysis of the hunt à force as occasion for the elite body of the aristocratic household to celebrate and perpetuate its privileged status via management and mastery over its natural surroundings. Crane emphasizes this ritual’s “staged” aspect, a woodland chase on horseback, led by tracking hounds, toward a hart or boar, depending on the season, by those in want for little. Certainly, Crane reminds us, trapping and snaring would be more effective methods, if this event were not more than a gestural confirmation of noble prerogative. This essay is most pioneering when it anatomizes the close human-animal interaction the hunting tradition perpetually requires in, for instance, the formulation of a verbal language that enables cross-species communication between hound and human or, more intimately, the parsing or examination of fumets (feces) as a means of securing comprehensive understanding, and thus more successfully dominating, the hunted.Before equilibrium became a formal subject of analysis, Joel Kaye persuasively argues, a speculative understanding of balance was combined with articulated concepts of equality and equalization through an intermediary “model of equilibrium” (87). Kaye focuses on natural philosopher Jean Buridan’s speculations in a domain of scientific inquiry that we would today term “geology,” speculations that audaciously seek to surpass foundational principles of Aristotelian physics long predicated upon, and circumscribed by, isolated events and rigid preconditions. “Abandon(ing) fixed natures, fixed meanings, fixed places, fixed times, fixed hierarchies, and mind-directed ‘purpose’ as he follows the logic of the moving system in equilibrium” (101), Buridan’s groundbreaking determinations proved essential to the history of a science more and more committed to overcoming timeworn paradigms.Pamela H. Smith contextualizes her investigation of man’s strivings to render natural processes humanly reproducible on a study of early modern collections of natural and fabricated objects. Identifying the dense holdings and subcategories of Samuel Quiccheberg’s (1529–67) plan for a Kunstkammer of curiosities and wonders (with particular attention to life-casts of animals, such as the lizard, photo included, which evidences its visual similitude to the real thing), and the ten-foot-high, five-feet-across, multitiered “chamber fountain” of Quiccheberg’s contemporary and fellow collector, Nuremberg goldsmith Wenzel Jamnitzer (1510–85), Smith reveals how these vast amassments affirmed princely authority and wealth and substantiated how collecting served as a key aspect of a new conception of philosophy that prioritized knowledge derived from direct engagement with nature.Marjorie Swann analyzes Thomas Browne’s preference for nonsexual modes of generation—his desire that mankind could in fact “procreate like trees” (137)—in his Religio Medici (1642). Vigorously striving to maintain the integrity of individual identity, the Norfolk physician and philosopher sought to resist forces that threaten to transform the self. Thus Browne lauded nonsexual production of plants by seeds and longed to follow along these lines in his own life, where, Swann reports, he venerated the exchange and comradeship of friendship over heterosexual marriage. In a volume that prioritizes active engagement as a path to innovation, this essay swims against the tide in its nostalgia for stasis.The collection concludes with Julie Berger Hochstrasser’s comprehensive elucidation of the methods by which Europeans perceived and generated images of the natural surroundings of the new Portuguese colony of Brazil. Her inclusion of a wide range of images (replications of pen and ink drawings, woodcuts, watercolors, and oil paintings, twenty-one plates in all) are essential to her account of the multifarious and often contradictory manner in which the sloth, in particular—an animal unknown in Europe and often reproduced by travelers to the New World—was represented. Who does the looking, Hochstrasser compellingly reminds us, determines how that which is perceived is received.
