title: Proverbs.
abstract: The Yorubas have an extraordinary number of proverbial sayings, and regard a knowledge of them as a proof of great wisdom, whence the saying, “A counsellor who understands proverbs soon sets matters right.” They are in constant use, and another saying runs, “A proverb is the horse of conversation. When the conversation droops a proverb revives it. Proverbs and conversation follow each other.” Several of the proverbs given in the volume on the Ewe-speaking peoples are known to and used by the Yoruba-speaking peoples; but they have hundreds of others which appear to be peculiar to themselves, and from these the following are taken as examples:— Secrets should never be told to a tattler. What is not wished to be known is done in secret. He who has done something in secret, and sees people talking together, thinks they are talking of his action. A whisperer looks suspiciously at the forest when he hears a noise, but the forest does not tell tales. Rags make up a pad. Continuai sweepings make a dust-heap. One here: two there: a great crowd. One here: two there: the market is filled up. (Nos. 5 to 8 are equivalent to our “Many a mickle makes a muckle.”) Boasting is not courage. He who boasts much cannot do much. Much gesticulation does not prove courage. It is easy to cut to pieces a dead elephant. (Nos. 9 to 12 resemble our “Deeds, not words.”) “I nearly killed the bird.” No one can eat nearly in a stew. (Answers to “Catch your hare before you cook him.”) A hog that has wallowed in the mud seeks a clean person to rub against. A man in a white cloth is never looked for in the palm-oil market. (Is something akin to “You cannot touch pitch without being defiled.”) The cross-roads do not fear sacrifices. The sieve never sifts meal by itself. Disobedience will drink water with his hands tied up. Disobedience is the father of insolence. Calamity has no voice; suffering cannot speak to tell who is really in distress. He who owns the inner square of the house is the master of the outer. Peace is the father of friendship. Strife never begets a gentle child. He who forgives ends the quarrel. A sharp word is as tough as a bow-string. A sharp word cannot be cured, but a wound may. A peacemaker often receives blows. There is no medicine against old age. The afomo (a parasitical plant) has no roots; it claims relationship with every tree. A man with a cough can never conceal himself. Full-belly child says to hungry-belly child, “Keep good heart.” A jealous woman has no flesh upon her breast, for however much she may feed upon jealousy, she will never be satisfied. Houses that are not adjacent do not readily catch fire. Do not attempt what you cannot bring to a good end. Each coloured cloth has its name. He who marries a beauty marries trouble. A man of the town knows nothing about farming, or the seasons for planting, yet the yam he buys must always be large. A witch kills but never inherits. Unless the tree falls you will never be able to reach the branches. Another’s eye is not like one’s own. The bite of the sand-fly is not so bad as poverty. Poverty destroys a man’s reputation. A poor man has no relations. Poverty never visits a poor man without visiting his children also. The white man is the father of merchants, and want of money is the father of disgrace. A man may be born to a fortune, but wisdom only comes with length of days. People think that the poor are not so wise as the rich, for if a man be wise, why is he poor? The appearance of the wise differs from that of the fool. The labourer is always in the sun, the plantation-owner always in the shade. (Answers to “One sows, another reaps.”) A lazy man looks for light employment. Laziness lends assistance to fatigue. The potsherd goes in front of the man who has taken embers on it from the fire. (Means that every enterprise requires a leader.) The partridge says: “What business has the farmer to bring his cloth here?” (fearing it may be a bird-trap). The farmer says: “How could I go to my farm without my cloth?” (This means that there are two sides to every question.) Ear, hear the other before you decide. He who annoys another only teaches him to strengthen himself. He who waits for a chance will have to wait for a year. When the jackal dies the fowls do not mourn, for the jackal never brings up a chicken. When fire burns in the bush, smuts fly into the town. (Answers to “Evil communication corrupts good manners.”) Tale-bearing is the elder brother, vexation the younger. He who knows a matter beforehand confuses the liar. Time may be very long, but a lie will not go to forgetfulness. A lie costs nothing to a liar. A man walks calmly in the presence of his defamer; a man walks proudly in the presence of his slanderer, when he knows that the slanderer has only twenty cowries in his house. To be trodden upon here, to be trodden upon there, is the fate of the palm-kernel lying in the road. The sole of the foot is exposed to all the dirt of the road. He who eats akashu does not know that a famine prevails. (Akashu is a large ball of agidi, and hence emblematic of plenty.) Consideration is the senior, calculation the junior, and wisdom the third-born. Want of consideration and forethought made six brothers pawn themselves for six dollars. (Instead of one brother pawning himself for the whole amount, in which case the others would be free to work and earn money with which to redeem him.) An obstinate man soon falls into disgrace. Inquiry saves a man from making mistakes. He who makes no inquiry gets himself into trouble. Though a man may miss other things, he never misses his mouth. Not to aid one in distress is to kill him in your heart. Charity is the father of sacrifice. Covetousness is the father of disease. Never did our fathers honour an orisha of this kind. (Is used to discountenance innovations.) A white cloth and a stain never agree. Thorns do not agree with the foot. The stream may dry up, but the watercourse still keeps its name. When water is poured on the head it finds its way down to the feet. A gift is a gift, and a purchase is a purchase; so no one will thank you for saying “I sold it you very cheap.” Hawks go away for the nesting-season, and fools think they have gone away for ever. Ashes fly back in the face of him who throws them. (Is equivalent to our “Curses come home to roost.”) It is the path of the needle that the thread is accustomed to follow. If a matter be dark, dive to the bottom. He who is pierced with a thorn must limp off to him who has a knife. Every man’s character is good in his own eyes. (This resembles “Self-praise is no recommendation.”) Wherever a man goes to dwell, his character goes with him. Frogs’ spawn does not attract the attention of the robber. (Frogs’ spawn is supposed to resemble a mass of beads.) The white ant may well admire the bird, for it loses its wings after flying for only one day. Gently! gently! still hurts the snail. A bribe blinds the judge’s eyes, for bribes never speak the truth. A witness speaks the truth; a witness is not a partisan. Iwo is the home of the grey parrot, Ibara the home of the hawk, but where is the home of the green parrot? (Is used to persons making false pretences.) Bank rises after bank, and ditch follows after ditch. When the rain falls into the ditch the banks are envious. (Is said of those who are dissatisfied with their station in life.) The strength of a mortar (made of wood) is not like the strength of a pot (made of clay). Place a mortar on the fire and it will burn; pound a yam in a pot and it will break. (Means that there is a proper use for everything.) When the monkey jumps from the tree he jumps into the house. (Inculcates the danger of leaving one’s proper station.) A tick having fixed itself on the mouth of a jackal, a fowl was asked to take it off; but the fowl knew that she was food for the jackal just as the tick was for her. Gossip is unbecoming in an elder. Three elders cannot all fail to pronounce the word ekulu; one may say elkúlu, another ekulú, but the third will say ekulu. (Ekulu is the name of an antelope. The saying means that there is safety in a number of counsellors.) The younger should not thrust himself into the seat of the elders. The young cannot teach the elders traditions. As a calabash receives the sediment of the water, so must an elder exercise forbearance. A man does not run among thorns for nothing. Either he is pursuing a snake or a snake is pursuing him. As no subject may keep a herald, so it is not every man who may own a palace. Everyone in the assembly has a name, but when you are summoned “in the name of the assembly” (instead of in the name of some individual in it) evil awaits you.. A near neighbour need not say good-bye till to-morrow. A thing thrown forward will surely be overtaken, and a thing put in the ground will be there to be dug up; but if nothing has been thrown forward, what shall be overtaken? and if nothing has been buried, what shall be dug up? (Is used to inculcate provident habits.) The name given to a child becomes natural to it. Gold should be sold to him who knows its value. Time is longer than a rope. The dawn does not come twice to wake a man. If clothes remain long in the bag they rot. The agbi (a bird with blue plumage) is the dyer in blue; the aluko (a bird with purple plumage) is the painter of purple; but the lekileki (the white crane) is the owner of the white cloth. (Means each to his own pursuits.) When the rain fell upon the parrot the aluko rejoiced, thinking that the red tail of the parrot would be spoiled, but the rain only increased its brilliancy. The akala (vulture) smells the carrion, no matter how high in the air he may be. The bat hangs with his head down, watching the actions of the birds. (Is used to inculcate silent observation.) He that has copper ornaments looks after the lime; he that has brass ornaments looks after the awedi. (The lime is used for cleaning copper an the awedi for cleaning brass.) Though the dengi is cold on the top, yet the inside is very hot. (Dengi is a kind of gruel made of pounded maize. The proverb means “Do not judge by appearances.”) A small bed will not hold two persons. The elephant makes a dust and the buffalo makes a dust, but the dust of the buffalo is lost in that of the elephant. Though you appear very sharp you cannot tell nine times nine. A large morsel chokes a child. He who cannot lift an ant, and yet tries to lift an elephant, will find out his folly. He who tries to shake the trunk of a tree only shakes himself. The world is the ocean and mankind is the lagoon. However well a man can swim he cannot cross the world. (Nos. 119 to 124 are used to check presumption and over-confidence.) When the eya (a wild cat) has reached to the ferocity of the leopard he will kill animals to feed on. Though the fire is burning the walls do not shrink from it, and yet the fire is trying to burn the water. (Is said of persons who aim at the greater when they cannot accomplish the less.) The cry of the bird kegio does not reach the sky. (Is used of one whose opinion or advice is not valued.) Cocoa-nut is not good for a bird to eat. (This is used in the same way as our “sour grapes.”) The bill-hook cuts the bush, but receives no profit from the bush. It clears the road, but receives no profit from the road. The bill-hook is badly bent, the bill-hook is badly bent. The billhook is bent; it pays five cowries to bind its neck (handle) with a ring. When the bill-hook reaches its owner’s farm with the ring on its neck, it is girded tightly for new works. (This saying refers to the labour of slaves, which brings them no remuneration. In the original it forms a kind of verse. Thus:— Ada shan igbo, Ko ri ere igbo. O ro ona, Ko ri ere ona. Ada da ida kuda, Ada da ida kuda. title: What a Difference a Couple Hundred Million Years Can Make
abstract: Cat Bohannon's book has a story arc. It's the arc of how we came to be what we are. It rises steadily through six chapters and then has an inflection point on page 332 of Chapter 7. After suggesting that Neanderthals possessed language, she asks whether it is language that makes us human. She answers her own question with a bold “I don't think so.” This is bold because there is wide agreement among scientists that language is what makes us special. Bohannon presses on. She wrote about the power of grammar earlier in Chapter 7, noting how it provides language with an infinitely flexible framework of cognition. “With human grammar,” she says, “we can make anything behave like an agent: a shoe can want, an eyelash can whisper.” But still no, she says, even that wouldn't have been enough. She continues, saying that there was still something, a dividing line such that “before it we were not human, and after it we were.” We became human “when a single human being told the very first story” (p. 332). I think she is on to something. More on that later.There is also a theme: “We have to put the female body in the picture. If we don't, it's not just feminism that's compromised. Modern medicine, neurobiology, paleoanthropology, even evolutionary biology all take a hit when we ignore the fact that half of us have breasts” (pp. 16–17). This theme spans the disciplines of history, anthropology, sociology, folklore, medicine, pop culture. And it is captured by a comment from Susan Sontag in her essay for Annie Leibovitz's book Women: “Any large-scale picturing of women belongs to the ongoing story of how women are presented, and how they are invited to think of themselves.” Thus, whether it is intentional or not, it raises a “question of women,” whereas “Men, unlike women, are not a work in progress” (Liebovitz & Sontag, 2000).And then there is the substance of the book, that is, the details of human female physiology. You might want to brace yourself for this one. I think I learned more new things per paragraph than I have from most other books I have ever read.I'm tempted to say that Eve is one of those “ahead of its time” books, rich with new understandings of female biology and accessible to both academicians and laypeople alike. But that would be less than accurate. Eve is something like 50 years too late! title: Why Arthur Miller Is Important
abstract: I have a Google alert for Arthur Miller and am thinking of canceling it. Every day my inbox fills up with news of productions around the world. It is especially bad this year. Theater directors and media alike have a fondness for anniversaries. They invite a backward look, a revisiting of works that at the time seemed to speak to the moment but which astonish by their continuing relevance. We have seen a world premiere of Miller's screenplay The Hook along with innovative stagings of his classic plays. British, French, and German television are making documentaries. BBC radio is preparing programs. Anyone vaguely knowledgeable about Miller has been writing program notes, delivering talks, advising companies. It is easy to forget the disregard and worse he suffered even for those early works as the American Legion picketed Salesman and it and All My Sons were banned from occupied Europe as anticapitalist. Easy to forget the contempt with which American critics received After the Fall and simply missed the boat with Incident at Vichy, The Price, The American Clock, The Archbishop's Ceiling.The ideological battles that once swirled around works of art now seem merely quaint but at the time could be poisonous. More remarkably, there were a number of American critics who never ceased dismissing him as a lightweight, a simple realist, resistant to experiment and an unrepentant critic of the American way. Even as his works were enthusiastically embraced abroad they were seen as irrelevant to those whose models were the new European theater or those groups rebelling against what they saw as the orthodoxies of drama with its stress on text and its fondness for the familiar architecture of presentation. But all the time Miller was finding his way to truths felt on the pulse by audiences who responded to the human situations he created as to the moral issues they engaged. He insisted that he never wrote political plays in the narrow sense except that all of his plays were political if we mean by that that they engaged with issues that linked the individual to society and society to the individual.His stress on the past may have been inspired originally by his admiration for ancient Greek theater and the work of Ibsen, but it was integral to his view of life. There is a reason that denial and betrayal were fundamental themes, and high on the list of those denials and betrayals was a refusal to grant the significance of the past. He could not abstract the individual from past actions or society from its culpabilities. title: Arthur Miller: American Witness
abstract: Sometimes in reading biographies we are looking for details about the author’s life and surrounding culture that can help us understand more clearly a particular event or work. Other times we are looking for broad perspectives, hoping to discover the lifelong desires, impulses, or needs that drive an entire oeuvre, hoping to understand not just an event or a work but a person. Although Arthur Miller: American Witness, at 202 pages of text, is only a third the length of his 2014 biography Tennessee Williams: Mad Pilgrimage of the Flesh, John Lahr handles both of these tasks admirably, despite essentially ending his discussion of Miller’s life in 1968 with comments on The Price. Someone once said of the trumpeter Miles Davis that he did not play many notes, but he played all the right ones. I have the same feeling about Lahr’s exploration of Miller.The book is part of the extensive Jewish Lives series from Yale University Press, which includes volumes on people as diverse as Sarah, Moses, Kafka, Einstein, Houdini, Bugsy Siegel, and Barbra Streisand. Certainly, Miller’s Jewish ethnicity was a significant part of his identity. Citing Harold Clurman, Lahr agrees that “Miller’s moral talent was rooted in the intellectual fervor and moral intensity of the Jewish community” (20), and Lahr explores this most directly in his discussion of Miller’s novel Focus. But ethnicity is not the key to Miller here. Lahr uses Miller’s correspondence with his parents, letters to his University of Michigan mentor Kenneth Rowe, Miller’s unpublished manuscript for a novel titled The Best Comedians about his marriage to Mary Slattery, and Lahr’s own email correspondence with Ross Miller, Miller’s brother Kermit’s son, to build a variegated portrait from sources that are not easily available. In addition, he makes good use of sources with which many of us are familiar: Miller’s autobiography Timebends, Christopher Bigsby’s magisterial two-volume biography of Miller, and Elia Kazan’s autobiography A Life. In this way, Lahr’s short book becomes a tour guide to these larger accounts.The place to start to understand Lahr’s Miller is with a quotation he cites three times (42, 61, 187) from Kazan’s A Life: “Art was not a writer who made up stories. His material had to be experienced; he reported on his inner condition. . . . He had to have that living connection with a subject before he could make drama of it” (Kazan 367–68). Regardless of their topic, Miller’s plays through the years depict the unfolding of his own life, which enables Lahr to give his biography the underlying structure of a drama. Robert M. Dowling subtitled his 2014 study of Eugene O’Neill “a life in four acts.” Lahr’s narrative is similar, although he gives us only the first scene of act 4.What we can call “act 1” is Miller’s youth, where the seeds of his sense of self are planted in a household that Lahr characterizes as crippled by “an undertow of contempt and humiliation” (23), especially after Miller’s father’s business failed and he no longer could provide the wealth that for his wife was the only reason she had been thrust into what had been essentially an arranged marriage. Miller recalls how his “heart went out [to his father] in his humiliation, however imperturbably he seemed to bear it; somehow it had become my job to distract them from their conflict” (Lahr 20; Timebends 18).Sensitivity to people’s humiliation and Miller’s desire to be a savior pervaded his entire life, but he also was angered and felt thwarted by his self-adopted role. Lahr cites the following speech from Biff to Willy that Miller wrote in his notebooks for Death of a Salesman; the line was cut from his final version of the play:That tension between our sense of obligation to others, even commitments based on love, and our rights to our own self-interest is a theme in many Miller plays.Miller’s struggle with his vision of himself as a moral man—what Clurman called his public image as an icon of “resistance to our soul’s sloth” (Lahr 193)—seems to have arisen from Miller’s relationship with his older brother Kermit, whom we see in Lahr’s book most pointedly through remarks from Kermit’s son Ross. According to Ross, Arthur and Kermit had an agreement when Kermit went to work with their father after the family business failed. Arthur was to go to Michigan, earn some credits, and then return to New York to take a role in the family business while Kermit returned to New York University to pursue his own degree and his dream of being a writer. Doing this, they both would finish college. But when Kermit drove to Michigan to visit at the end of Arthur’s first term, he found that Arthur had “‘fallen in love with the place’ and with the idea of himself as a playwright.” Arthur continued at Michigan and Kermit continued to work in the family business for five years (188). Arthur was rejected for military service in World War II because of a high school football injury. Kermit enlisted as a private and was discharged as a captain, having fought in the Battle of the Bulge toward the war’s end, where he was trapped in a snowstorm by German troops for a week and suffered extreme frostbite. He was awarded the Purple Heart and returned home a hero but suffered such depression that in 1946 he underwent electric shock treatments. Despite his youthful dreams of writing, he spent the rest of his working life as a carpet salesman. “My father’s nobility of character drove Arthur crazy,” says Ross. “Arthur craved fame and celebrity and got it. . . . But after the war my father could never take Arthur’s moralizing and pontificating seriously. The price Arthur paid was the loss of his brother’s respect” (70, 85, 192). Nearly all of Lahr’s citations to Ross Miller’s opinions of his uncle contain this bitterness. There must be a deeper story here, which future biographers will be eager to explore.Miller’s yearning for fame may have arisen from a second kind of contempt and humiliation he experienced in his youth: not his parents’ but his own. For whatever reasons, Miller never engaged well in school until he arrived at the University of Michigan (Lahr 25; Timebends 19). His older brother Kermit, on the other hand, was an excellent student, as their mother had been. Miller failed to be admitted to any college when he graduated from high school. Later, he applied twice to the University of Michigan and was rejected both times. Applying a third time, he wrote directly to the dean and was admitted on academic probation (Lahr 29, 34–36). His resilience is remarkable.Winning the Hopwood Award at Michigan for his first play, No Villain, was a turning point in Miller’s life, a moment not just for joy in accomplishment overcoming his sense of personal humiliation but for vengeance, for example, against his Aunt Betty, who had predicted the night he left for college that he would be an immediate and dismal failure. He called the Hopwood “an artillery shell fired through the ranks of my opposing army—down went all my old algebra teachers” (Lahr 44; Bigsby, Arthur Miller: 1915–1962 99; Timebends 224–26).These are the psychological seeds Lahr plants in what we might call act 1 of his narrative of Miller’s life, which takes us through Miller’s late twenties. We see Miller developing a sense of himself as a moral champion of the humiliated who struggles with his own feelings of inauthenticity and fragile personal pride while seeking resolution of these misgivings through recognition by other people of his merit and virtue. In the years immediately after graduating from Michigan, he is driven by ambition tainted by a hope for dominance or revenge. These are the elements of Miller’s past that will drive his future, the “birds that will come home to roost,” as Miller would have called them, as the rest of Lahr’s narrative unfolds (Lahr 83; Bigsby, Arthur Miller: 1915–1962 267).Act 2 shows us the next step. It is about success. Lahr takes us through Miller’s developing friendship with Elia Kazan, his triumph in 1947 with All My Sons and then, even more resoundingly, in 1949 with Death of a Salesman. Miller, still young at thirty-four, emerged as a major public intellectual, an “American Witness,” a voice of wise national conscience with a pulpit generally reserved for someone older and more experienced. He embraced the role and the attention.Comparing Miller to Tennessee Williams at this time, Lahr writes, “Williams’s work was an exploration of the imperialism of the self, Miller’s was about society’s effect on sharpening the self. . . . Miller had no interest in theater that wrapped itself exclusively in what he called ‘the shroud of introspection,’” a fault for which he had dismissed Eugene O’Neill. “[Miller] saw himself as working in the illumination business, throwing [now quoting Miller] ‘light on the condition of man as a social animal. That’s where our fate is, and that’s where the great plays are written.’” Emulating what he had learned about Ibsen from Kenneth Rowe in Michigan, Miller saw his dramas as tools for social enlightenment and change, a view of the writer that served his personal ideal of being a savior. Miller complained that the social role of Salesman was being undermined by the audience’s personal engagement with Willy: “There was too much crying going on in the audience for my comfort,” Miller wrote. “The stringent quality of the play was its social theme. It was being drowned in tears of pity for Willy. When you are crying, you can’t see straight” (Lahr 45–47, 100–101).Beneath this joy in public acclaim and social influence, Miller’s private life was crumbling. Riding home with his wife Mary Slattery after the opening of Salesman, Miller sensed a discomforting awkwardness being forced into their lives. He had a “persistent dread that we were being cut from our past and being thrust into darkness.” As Lahr says, “Miller had grasped the live wire of fame, and as painful as it would prove to be, he couldn’t let go . . . its centripetal force drew him into turbulent emotional waters” (Lahr 103, 105–6).Miller’s response was to attempt escape into work with Kazan. They headed to California, seeking funding for a screenplay, The Hook, about the Brooklyn waterfront. There Miller met the as-yet-unknown young actress Marilyn Monroe, whose “pain called out of Miller a protectiveness that kept his desire hidden from him,” as Lahr says, while fulfilling the role of savior he had sought since his youth (112, 143). Soon, however, the desire could not be denied. Miller, for whom moral rectitude was fundamental to his identity, “knew that I must flee or walk into a doom beyond all knowing.” Ultimately, he would feel “I was alternately soaring and anxious that I might be slipping into a life not my own. My will seemed to have evaporated.” He made “a retreat into morals, to be sure, but not necessarily to truthfulness” and headed home to his family in New York and an attempt to save his marriage (Lahr 113, 144, 164; Timebends 307; Bigsby, Arthur Miller: 1915–1962 509). The marriage, however, continued to be strained by Miller’s one real mistress, his obsessive commitment to his work. His friend Kazan was called before HUAC to testify. Miller wrote The Crucible as a response to that and, in a more private way, as an attempt to understand and redeem his marriage. Monroe reentered his life. He divorced and wrote A View From the Bridge, in part an exploration of sexual tension that cannot be acted on. Miller himself was called to testify before HUAC. On 29 June 1956, Miller and Monroe married—and that begins act 3, the climax of the tragedy that for Lahr has been unfolding from seeds planted in Miller by the “contempt and humiliation” he lived with in his youth.From Miller’s perspective, Monroe’s neediness overwhelmed his ability to work as he increasingly was called on to tend to her moods and career. From her perspective, Miller’s obsession with his own work made him distant and cold. As they drifted apart, Monroe had a brutally publicized affair with Yves Montand, her costar in Let’s Make Love in 1959. Miller, who had sought to triumph over humiliations since his youth, now found himself humiliated in the world press. Lahr cites Freud’s definition of trauma as “helplessness experienced” to describe Miller’s feelings (175). Aunt Betty had won once again. Kazan wrote, “I was sympathetic to Art . . . I knew how unprepared he was for that kind of tension. I also knew the degree of anger and vengeance she felt; it had been unremitting and without pity” (Lahr 167; Kazan 674).Miller had tried to rescue their marriage by writing a screenplay based on his short story The Misfits as a vehicle in which Monroe could display her dramatic talents beyond comedy. He intended it as a gift of love. But the role he created seemed to Monroe merely his own self-serving, maudlinly sentimentalized vision of who she was. She went forward with the filming but only in a way that those around her felt demeaned them and especially Miller (171). She was furious: “If that’s what he thinks of me, well, then, I’m not for him and he’s not for me.” Once more, she felt exploited: “They don’t need me at all. Not to act—just for the money. title: In Defense of Diasporic Judaism: Adolphe Danziger De Castro's “Muscular Jew”
abstract: Adolphe Danziger De Castro (1859–1959) is a remarkable figure in Jewish American literature. Nonetheless, in spite of his sixty-year incessant literary production, no literary study has been devoted to his oeuvre, which includes a collaboration on a short novel with Ambrose Bierce,1 short stories, five volumes of poetry, five novels, essays, a film script, a monograph on Talmudic history, and articles in American and Jewish American journals. Probably such a neglect is due to Danziger De Castro's controversial personality and the literary scandal concerning the authorship of the popular novel The Monk and Hangman's Daughter, which he co-authored with Bierce. Danziger De Castro may be also seen as a controversial figure because he added incredulous details to his early biography. Hence Danziger De Castro, who frequently claimed Sephardic heritage and significant academic achievements, was an enigmatic figure with many of his assertions unverified. William M. Kramer notes that Danziger De Castro spent much of the twentieth century wrestling with his own identity, only to ultimately question if he had been living a masquerade.2 Danziger De Castro's claims of Sephardic identity, however, may be seen as part of this broader trend among German Jews, who viewed Sephardic culture as a model for transforming Ashkenazic identity and achieving acceptance within German society.3 An additional reason for literary disregard may be due to the fact that now and then Danziger De Castro's novels feature a curious mix of literary genres—sentimental, sensational, first-person confessional letters or memoirs, historical fiction, a “ghetto-story,” and a Bildungsroman—which at times verge on the edge of soapy melodrama, especially when depicting farfetched coincidences. Analyzing Danziger De Castro's novel The Children of Fate: A Story of Passion (1905), his theological manuscript Jewish Forerunners of Christianity (1903), and his articles, this essay probes into the depictions of “resilient Jews” living in the last decades of the nineteenth century. It also demonstrates how Danziger De Castro's social and political agenda is aimed at defending the male Jew against centuries-old stereotypical delineations. It shows how by portraying a Jewish super-hero, a morally elevated and physically fit “New Jewish male,” Danziger De Castro attempts to defy common prejudices, which have mostly become prevalent following the massive influx of eastern European Jews to America. Moreover, it examines the rapports among Jewishness, virtue, and masculinity. Finally, it illustrates how his depiction of virtuous Jews in the Pale and America is juxtaposed with the representations of Jews and Jewish immigrants to America by his non-Jewish American contemporaries.4Born Abram Dancygier in Poland in 1859, Danziger De Castro was a rabbi, journalist, writer, lawyer, dentist, and American vice-consul to Madrid in 1903–04. He emigrated to the U.S. in 1883 and settled in San Francisco, where he worked as a dentist and freelance journalist. He claimed a rabbinical certification from Poland and a Ph.D. from the University of Bonn. He also adopted the name De Castro from an ancestor, Israel De Castro, a Sephardic Jew. This helped him become a prominent member of the Sephardic Community of Los Angeles, where he served as its first president. Though he moved frequently and changed professions, writing was his most stable career.Christopher A. Powell, who published a biographical sketch of Danziger De Castro, writes that his “superior intellect” allowed him “to successfully master half a dozen other occupations” but “failed him in his quest to be an important literary figure.” This claim is debatable, because it disregards Danziger De Castro's contribution to creating the American “New Jew”—a strong, capable, and moral Jewish hero. In numerous newspaper articles and in Children of Fate, he defied stereotypes of Jewish weakness, challenging anti-Semitic views. Moreover, Powell's comment overlooks the fact that Danziger De Castro's books were well received and popular.5The Jewish body, specifically the Jewish male body, has been scrutinized from various perspectives, including racial, political, religious, and ideological ones. The conceptualization of the figure of the “muscular Jew” was a decisive moment in the history of the formation of the “New Jew,” who leaves the Russian or Polish Shtetl to build a new life in the Promised Land. In a speech at the second Zionist Congress in Basel in August 1898, Max Nordau, a writer and a Zionist leader, proclaimed that there is a necessity to generate a “new Muscle [Muscular] Jew,” one who would not just symbolize a healthy and well-made body, but “rather [be] an acknowledgment of the older German tradition, which saw an inherent relationship between the healthy political mind and the healthy body.” Nordau connects physical fitness to Zionist ideals and to the prophetic vision of reestablishing the Jewish state in Palestine. He maintains that “Zionism breathes new life into Judaism. This much I am sure of. It does this morally by refreshing the ideals of the People, physically by physical education of our offspring, who shall reestablish a bygone Muscular Judaism.”6 Nordau addressed his plea particularly to Eastern European Jews who “must rise up and reform their individual bodies in order to reform their people as a whole; the ‘Luftvolk’ of the Diaspora must become grounded as a ‘Nationvolk.’”7 For him, a full-scale citizen must have a fit body.The idea of a “Muscular Jew” developed as a response to challenges faced by Jews historically, particularly in the context of anti-Semitism. Supporters of “Muscular Judaism” proposed social and political change through the body. A fit body would provide people with the might and moral character necessary for the attainment of centuries-old national dreams. Hence, the notion of enhancing physical strength became an important theme within the Zionist movement, as it aimed to counter stereotypes and promote a self-reliant Jewish identity. According to Stephen H. Norwood, “during the early-twentieth century, Jewish activists organizing against antisemitism recovered the submerged heritage of Jewish military prowess,” believing that “promoting physical fitness and fighting capability encouraged contemporary Jews to be more combative in protecting their communities against physical assault and defamation.”8 The “New Jew” concept was intertwined not just with discussions on physical strength, but also included an engagement in manual and agricultural labor as means of return to the Land of Israel. It emphasized the transformation of Jewish identity from one associated with urban intellectualism and religious traditions to one that embraced physicality, productivity, and a connection to the land. Anita Shapira's analysis highlights the emergence of an ideological shift aiming to redefine the Jewish identity, predating the advent of Zionism in the late-eighteenth century. This transformation was intertwined with the concept of the “New Jew,” a notion deeply rooted in the significance of the Land of Israel. Shapira argues that Zionism emphasized the link between the Jewish people and their ancestral homeland as fundamental for this profound metamorphosis to occur.9The notion of re-creating a “Muscle/Muscular Jew” associates the Jewish heroic past with the present by drawing from the valiant tradition represented by the Maccabees, which exemplifies the epitome of heroism. This vision challenges the conjectures of social Darwinism since “Jews, overcoming the extenuating circumstances that rendered them weak and adapting to the new challenges of nation building, could now become ‘true moderns’ in order to thrive.”10 In response to Nordau's entreaty, a series of sport clubs, so-called “Bar Kochba clubs,” were established in Europe that attracted young male Jews. The image of a “muscle Jew” became the symbol of Jewish regeneration both on individual and social levels.The image of a “Muscular Jew” appeared in British literature as early as the 1830s. Nadia Valdman discovered connections among masculinity, Jewishness, and English national identity and representations of “tough Jews” in Benjamin Disraeli's writings in the 1830s and ’40s. She maintains that the connection between moral, political, and physical toughness was underscored by the “Muscular Christianity” movement in the 1850s.11 Disraeli's uniqueness lies in his association of masculinity, chivalry, and physical and moral prowess with the idea of “race” and by linking the latter values with the exemplar of Jews, hence reinforcing both English and Jewish national identities.In American literature, probably the first iteration of the notion of a “Muscular Jew” appears in Helen Wise Molony's “True Love Falters Not” (1886). The story was written twelve years before Nordau coined the phrase the “Muscular Jew,” thus envisaging the growing popularity the Zionist leaders’ campaign aimed at propagating the idea of fitness. It is a story of an adept Jewish man, Robert Stern, whose physical prowess and muscularity are emphasized. As I have argued elsewhere, the novella's “originality stems not just from the introduction of the ideal of a ‘Muscular Jew,’ which was quite revolutionary” in Jewish American literature during “the last two decades of the nineteenth century, but also by conceiving an innovative genre—the Jewish survival narrative, written according to the literary tradition of the Bildungsroman.”12 As a typical Bildungsroman protagonist, Stern needs to realize that his fall was brought about by reckless actions, specifically his gambling. He needs to be reeducated, pay his literal and symbolic debts, and then realize redemption. During hard years of physical labor on a farm, he saves some of his fellow laborers by intervening in their fights.Another early depiction of a gentle, righteous and “Muscular Jew” is presented in Rosa Sonneschein's “Between Two Worlds” (1897), the story of an upright Jewish man named Bamberg who saves a rich young American widow from a shipwreck. Tragically, when trying to rescue her son, he drowns with her son. Ironically, before the collision she and her cousin express anti-Semitic opinions. According to the cousin, Jews are plotting to “Judaize the world.” This young widow, who prides on being open-minded, disdainfully proclaims that all Jewish husbands deal in diamonds with which their wives adorn themselves. This malicious observation echoes a deep-rooted stereotypical view of Jews, ominously voiced by apparently progressive Americans. Upon discovering that Bamberg is a Jew, both women are stunned, considering him an exception which only proves the rule regarding Jews’ greed and rudeness.13 The title of Sonneschein's novella is important in this context, as Bamberg, the manager of a profitable iron factory and a true gentleman, is caught between two worlds—he is a successful American businessman but, as a Jew, he is considered a member of a lowly sect.In “The Empire of the Ghetto,” Danziger De Castro protests Americans’ prejudices toward Jewish immigrants to New York. He addresses American readers and asserts that “your information [with regard to Jews], dear Gentiles, is sadly incomplete,” adding that Gentiles misinterpret Jewish practices and character when looking just at the “uncleanly aspect” of “the bewigged and bargaining women [. . .] pathetic in their poverty” and “bearded merchants with their odd speech.”14 In another article he criticizes George C. Lorimer, a prominent American pastor, for defending Jews, stating that “it never strikes these gentlemen [priests and leaders] that vindication is next door neighbor to insult.”15 In Danziger De Castro's experience, philosemitic pronouncements are usually followed by offensive comments.He believes that Jewish newcomers want to become Americans and they learn eagerly to integrate themselves within American culture. title: Response
abstract: First I want to thank warmly the five participants in this Forum on my book with Ranjan Ghosh. They have all been generous but learned and penetrating in their comments. I am extremely grateful to them for writing their essays.Though all five are specialists in literary theory and literary studies, and though all teach at distinguished universities, four in the United States and one in England, they are in their training and scholarly orientations strikingly different from one another.Laurent Dubreuil was trained in philosophy at the prestigious École normale supérieure in Paris and at the Université Paris-VIII, where Hélène Cixous directed his thesis. Dubreuil teaches now in the Romance Languages and Comparative Literature Departments at Cornell University. Most of his published books are in one way or another about literature.Andrew Way Leong has a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. He teaches in the English Department at Northwestern University. Leong is a comparatist who works primarily in Japanese and American literature, as well as in Asian American literature.Nicholas Royle is a graduate of Oxford University. He teaches now at Sussex University in the United Kingdom. Royle is a specialist on recent literary theory, particularly on the uncanny, but he is also himself a distinguished novelist and literary critic.Marshall Brown (PhD Yale University) is the gifted editor of Modern Language Quarterly. He teaches Comparative Literature at the University of Washington in Seattle. Brown is a specialist in British and European Romanticism.R. Radhakrishnan and Ragini Tharoor Srinivasan are both originally from South India. Radhakrishnan's PhD is from the Binghamton University. He teaches now at the University of California at Irvine. He is a leading postcolonial critic. Srinivasan holds a PhD from the Department of Rhetoric at Berkeley. She is a brilliant interdisciplinary theorist and a specialist, among other things, in Postcolonial South Asian literature. She teaches at the University of Arizona.What an impressive diversity of scholars! Commenting in detail on their challenging essays might take a book in itself. I will say a few words about specific points in each and then conclude by specifying ways in which my own thinking has markedly evolved just since I wrote my parts of Thinking Literature across Continents a few years ago.First, though, a general comment about all these essays. All five of them write brilliantly about literary theory and about what literature is, but none of them applies his or her theoretical formulations to a single actual literary work. My contributions to our book, on the other hand, “read” in detail several literary works. I consider these readings the most important parts of my contributions to Thinking Literature across Continents. None of my readings is even mentioned, much less evaluated, in the Forum essays. In my strongly held view, literary theory is a handmaiden to literary works, an aid to reading them. It is of little use otherwise. What these authors do is present literary theory in a vacuum. It is analogous to doing astrophysics without any basis in actual data from the stars. You can say anything you like, since it has no explicit basis in anything real. You can say the moon is made of green cheese and the stars of a luminescent form of such cheese. You can develop any literary theory you like if you feel no need for empirical evidence drawn from actual literary works. I find this procedure truly amazing. I kept thinking to myself, “Example, please!” after some eloquent abstract formulation.Dubreuil's essay opens, as might be expected from a graduate of the École Normale, with a substantial and impressively accurate history of the origins and historical development down to the present of Western literary theory. He then astutely places my book with Ghosh in the present globalizing state of this context.One specific comment: Dubreuil takes issue with my categorizing of “what we Westerners have meant by literature for the last couple of centuries.”1 This, says Dubreuil, “is something I do not know much about, as I do not believe that ‘we Westerners’ exist and am rather convinced that, if ‘we’ ever were a group endowed with some consistence or content, we would yet be unable to determine consensually what ‘literature’ means. As for its date of birth (‘three centuries old,’ says Hillis Miller), we have so many different options on the table (from late Antiquity to the end of the 18th C.) that I doubt even more seriously of any valuable chronological response.” I would have much to say about these remarks. Dubreuil is kind enough to add: “This is to say that I share Hillis Miller's scruples.” The reference in “we Westerners” is obliquely to Jacques Derrida's remarks in his interview with Derek Attridge about literature in the sense of print literature (novels, poems, and plays) in Western languages. Literature in that sense, says Derrida, appeared with the change from a manuscript culture to a primarily print culture in Europe in the late seventeenth century and with the rise to dominance of a literate middle class. Print literature was published for, and read primarily from the eighteenth century on, by literate middle-class citizens of European and American countries. The ways literature is written, “published,” and read these days is changing rapidly again as digital media are swiftly replacing print media. My “we Westerners” was a slightly ironic reference to that restricted group defined above. I have noticed frequently that my irony is often not recognized as such. I am as aware as Dubreuil is that Sophocles's plays, Homer's epics, Chinese lyric poetry, and Sanskrit poetry, and so on, are generally called “literature,” but I believe that no single definition of so-called “literature” would fit so many kinds of literature at all easily. That is one reason I am dubious about the new discipline called “global literature,” good as it is to study works of imaginative writing from all over the world and from all times. I am greatly impressed that Dubreuil, as he says in his last paragraph, invented the term “more than global.” It was a formulation whose time had come, as Ghosh's crucial use of it attests.Leong's goal, like that of the other essays in this Forum, mutatis mutandis, is as much to understand the form of interchange our book represents as it is to understand the ideas about literature that each of us expresses in what might have been published as separate stand-alone essays. As is appropriate both for our book and for Leong's training in not only Japanese but in other Far Eastern languages and cultures, he uses an important form of logic from India, “Tetralemma” (Catuskoti in Sanskrit). He uses this logic to analyze the relationships among Ghosh's parts of our book and my parts. “Tetralemma” also exists, it happens, as a relatively minor form of ancient Greek logic associated with Democritus and with Pyrrhonism, Leong uses, however, the Indian form. “Tetra” means “four” in Greek. A “lemma” “is a subsidiary or intermediate theorem in an argument or proof.” “Tetralemma,” as its name suggests, is a form of logic stating that “with reference to any a logical proposition X, there are four possibilities: affirmation, negation, both, neither.” As Leong shows, when you apply Tetralemma to Thinking Literature across Continents, you get a Ghosh–Miller tetralemma: both (in)- fusion and induction; neither (in)fusion nor induction. Both Ghosh and Miller; neither Ghosh nor Miller. As Leong puts this: “Ghosh writes that Thinking Literature across Continents leaves ‘readers in the midst of three books, one by Ghosh, another by Miller, and the third by Ghosh-Miller.’2 My response must address the fourth book in which a reader might find herself: the book by neither-Ghosh-nor-Miller.” I leave it to the reader to follow through the brilliant way Leong uses Tetralemma to specify the articulations and disarticulations of the various sections of our book.I end my response to Leong by saying that I find fascinating what he writes about choosing between “profane” and “secular” as tetralemmic negations of “sacred.” “Profane” comes from Latin profanus, meaning “outside of the temple,” therefore nonsacred. As Leong recognizes, however, in today's idiomatic English, which I was trying to use, “profane” means “given to profanity,” in the sense of cursing and swearing, whereas I used “secular” to refer to literature that makes no pretense to being “sacred.” The Bible is a sacred text. Anthony Trollope's Framley Parsonage does not claim to be a sacred text in the sense the Bible is. Leong, like the other authors in this Forum, does not mention a single actual work of secular literature, much less the specific ones I comment on in detail in our book. Leong's discourse is almost exclusively at the level of abstract concepts about philosophy and literary theory.Royle is the only one of the contributors to this Forum who is personally known to me. I have met him a good many times and consider him a friend. I therefore, of course, agree with everything he says. My response to his essay is primarily to say, “Yea, Verily!” or “Yowza!” Royle is luminously intelligent, learned, witty, and original. He has written brilliantly over the years about the whole field of contemporary theory, especially authoritatively about Derrida. He has published admirable works of literary criticism. He has written with characteristic originality and distinction about the specific category of the uncanny in literature and in other forms of expression and experience. I have learned much from him that has been immensely useful in my own work. I have learned from Royle especially about the uncanny and about the way “telepathic narrator” is a better term than “omniscient narrator” for the characteristic storyteller of European novels. Royle has also published several wonderfully innovative novels, the latest of which, An Englishman's Guide to Birdwatching, contains, more or less in passing, what, if you are not reading attentively, at first appears to be a splendidly spoofing and ironically negative comprehensive review of Royle's own work by the novel's protagonist, Osmer.
